docs.title: PAROL6 Robot Manual
docs.text:
Document number: SR-1002

PAROL6 release: 1

Python API (parol6): v0.9.1

PAROL6 commander software: main

Revision: 2026.A

Published: 2026-11-03

Applies to: PAROL6 with the PAROL6 control board v2.0, PAROL6 release 1, Python API (parol6) v0.9.1, PAROL6 commander software main

Original instructions

Quick start About this manual

Source Robotics d.o.o. publishes this document as part of the open-source PAROL6 project. It is revised as the product changes; the document number, release, revision and date above identify the version you are reading, and the document history on the About page says what changed. Take care that the release named under Applies to matches the robot in front of you, and that the Python API version matches what pip installed: the version selector in the header switches between releases. The text and the images are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, the code examples MIT.

Gripper Printed parts Reset

Drag to turn the robot, scroll to zoom, move each joint with its slider, choose the gripper on the flange, try a colour for the printed parts (the motors stay black). The model is the robot's URDF; the sliders run over its joint limits.

  • Quick start

    One page from an assembled robot to a homed one that moves: power, the commander software, the first jog, homing, with a link into the manual at every step.

  • The robot manual

    Safety, Technical data, Installation, Operation, Peripherals, Maintenance, Troubleshooting.

  • Build guide

    From the BOM to the first run: what to print and how, the parts to buy, the assembly manual and videos, the wiring, the firmware upload, the first power-on.

  • Control board

    The board that drives the robot: specifications, connectors and pinout, the stepper drivers, the I/O and E-stop wiring, CAN, firmware upload, the test firmware, the serial protocol.

  • End effectors

    What goes on the flange: the pneumatic and vacuum grippers, the SSG-48 and MSG electric grippers, your own tool; mounting, connections, the homing offset, driving them.

  • GUI interfaces

    The graphical programs: the commander software, Waldo Commander in the browser, Motor GUI for the grippers.

  • Programming

    The programming guide: the interfaces, the concepts behind them, the Python API, RBTscript, ROS 2; and the reference, read from the API's source.

docs.title: Moving the robot
docs.text:
1. Home it, then bring it to the parked pose: joints 2 and 3 toward their limit switches so the arm folds over the base. The commander's Park button writes a program that moves there (Switching off). Or move it by hand once it is switched off (Moving the robot by hand).
  2. Switch off with the forearm held; unplug the supply, the USB and the E-stop.
  3. Carry it by the base, not by the arm.
Figure 9.1: The parked pose: the arm folded in over the base.

docs.title: Packing
docs.text: Fold the arm as above, put foam under the joint 3 limit switch so that the forearm rests on it and not on the switch, and tape the forearm to the upper arm so that the joints cannot swing. Pack the robot upright in a box with foam around the base; the gripper and the E-stop separately.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Dry, at room temperature, folded. The stepper motors and the drivers have no shelf-life issues; the PETG parts should not be stored where it gets hot, in a car or near a radiator. Before the first use after storage, run the Inspection.

docs.title: Scope and audience
docs.text:
The PAROL6 Robot Manual covers the PAROL6 desktop robotic arm from the box, or the printer, to a robot that runs programs: what the robot is, how to install it safely, how it is switched on, homed, jogged and run, which tools and grippers it takes, its inputs, outputs and pneumatics, how it is maintained and what to do when something fails. The Build guide, part of the same document, covers building one from the published files. Four more documents live on this site: the Control Board Manual, for the electronics inside the base; the End Effectors Guide, for the grippers and tools on the flange; the GUI Guide, for the graphical programs; and the Programming Guide with its API reference, for everyone who writes programs for the robot. The list under Related documents gives their numbers.

The manual is written for someone who has a PAROL6 or is building one: a maker, a student, a teacher or an engineer who can run a Python script and tighten a belt. It does not assume robotics training; the concepts the robot's software uses are explained in the Theory corner, which anyone can read first. Read the Safety chapter before you power anything. The Quick start is the first day on one page; the chapters are in the order you need them and go deeper.

docs.title: Finding your way
docs.text:
The header has seven tabs. PAROL6 Robot Manual is the document you read from the start: the quick start, then safety, technical data, installation, operation, peripherals, maintenance and troubleshooting, in numbered chapters, followed by the build guide. Control Board is the manual of the electronics inside the base: the connectors, the stepper drivers, the I/O wiring, the firmware, the serial protocol. End effectors is what goes on the flange: the pneumatic and vacuum grippers, the SSG-48 and MSG electric grippers, a tool of your own, and how each is mounted, connected and driven. GUI interfaces covers the graphical programs: the commander software, Waldo Commander, Motor GUI. Programming is for everyone who writes programs for the robot: the interfaces, the concepts, the Python API, RBTscript, ROS 2, and the reference where you look things up: every method of the Python API, read from its source, the RBTscript commands, the serial protocol byte by byte, the firmware parameters. Theory corner explains the robotics behind the software, from joint numbering and units to kinematics, singularities and motion profiles, for anyone who wants to read first. Support says where to get help and how to report a problem.

The whole site describes one PAROL6 release. The dropdown next to the site name switches between releases, and a page from an older release says so in a bar at the top. The repository card on the right of the header opens the repository the page belongs to; every page ends with a link to edit it and one to report a problem with it.

docs.title: Warnings and notes
docs.text:
Three kinds of warnings and notes appear in this documentation. Read every Danger and Notice before you act on the step it belongs to. A green Check box after a setup step says what you should see when the step worked, and where to go when it did not.

Note

Points out something that is easy to miss or that changes what follows: a default, a limit, a side effect.

Notice

The robot, the tool, or data on the control board or the PC can be damaged or lost if this is ignored. Nobody is at risk.

Danger

Someone can be injured if this is ignored. Stop and read the whole box before acting on the step it belongs to.

docs.title: Document history
docs.text:
The documents on this site describe one PAROL6 release; one revision is kept per release, and the version selector in the header switches between them. The Programming Guide and the API reference also name the Python API version they describe, because the API is released more often than the robot.

The text and the images of this documentation are licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0, the code examples under the MIT licence. The robot's mechanical files, firmware and software are published under GPLv3 in their repositories. The Source Robotics name, the product names and the logos are not covered by any of these.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
From the PAROL6 you have just built to one that is homed and moves on command, on one page. It assumes the robot is assembled and wired as in the Build guide (Mechanical assembly, Electronics and wiring), and nothing more: no firmware uploaded yet, no software on your PC, and no experience with Python or a terminal. Every step ends with a link to the page that explains it; follow it when a step is not clear or something fails.

Read first

PAROL6 has no brakes: when the power goes, the arm falls. It has pinch points, it moves fast, and it moves by itself while homing. Anchor it to the table, keep the E-stop within reach, keep hands out of the arm's path, and read the Safety chapter: it is five minutes long.

docs.title: 1. What you need
docs.text:
Where to get it Your PAROL6, assembled and wired, with the control board inside the base the Build guide; the parts in the BOM, or as kits from the shop A 24 V power supply, 5 A the BOM names one; any 24 V 5 A supply works A mains switch within reach, on the supply's mains side: a switched socket strip will do it is the stop that still works when the PC software has frozen (Emergency stop) An E-stop, a normally closed button on the base the BOM names one; any NC switch works A USB cable, type B, to the PC An ST-Link programmer and the programming adapter, to upload the firmware once the programming adapter in the shop A PC with Windows, Linux or macOS see the minimum PC

Read in more detail: What you need.

docs.title: 2. Anchor the robot
docs.text:
Bolt the base to the table through its six holes, or clamp it to the edge. A free-standing PAROL6 tips over when it extends.

Check

Push the top of the base sideways, firmly: it must not lift or slide.

Read in more detail: Mounting the robot.

docs.title: 3. Install Python and Git, and open a terminal
docs.text:
The PC software is written in Python, and Git downloads it. A terminal is the window where you type commands: type one line, press Enter, wait until it finishes.

WindowsLinuxmacOS
  1. Download Python 3.11.9 from python.org: the "Windows installer (64-bit)". 3.11.9 is the last 3.11 release with an installer.
  2. Run it. On its first screen tick Add python.exe to PATH, then press Install Now.
  3. Download Git from git-scm.com and install it with the settings it proposes.
  4. Open a terminal: press the Windows key, type cmd and press Enter. A black window opens.
  5. Type python --version and press Enter, then git --version.

The commands on this page start with cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents, which takes the terminal to your Documents folder. If Windows answers that it cannot find the path, your Documents folder is kept in OneDrive: type cd %USERPROFILE%\OneDrive\Documents instead. To open a terminal in any folder, open the folder in File Explorer, click the address bar, type cmd and press Enter.

  1. Open a terminal: Ctrl+Alt+T on Ubuntu, or Terminal in the applications menu.
  2. Install Git: sudo apt install git (it asks for your password).
  3. The software needs Python 3.11: the commander runs on 3.10 or 3.11 only, the Python API on 3.11 or newer. Ubuntu's own Python is 3.10 on Ubuntu 22.04 and 3.12 on Ubuntu 24.04, so install 3.11 next to it, with its virtual environments and its window toolkit: 
    sudo add-apt-repository ppa:deadsnakes/ppa
sudo apt install python3.11 python3.11-venv python3.11-tk
  4. Type python3.11 --version and press Enter, then git --version. Each program below gets its own virtual environment made with Python 3.11; inside it, python is that Python 3.11.
  1. Download Python 3.11.9 from python.org: the "macOS 64-bit universal2 installer". Run it.
  2. Open a terminal: press Cmd+Space, type Terminal and press Enter.
  3. Install Git with the Xcode command line tools: type xcode-select --install, press Enter and confirm the window that opens.
  4. Type python3.11 --version and press Enter, then git --version. Each program below gets its own virtual environment made with Python 3.11; inside it, python is that Python 3.11.

Check

The terminal answers Python 3.11 and a number, and git version and a number. If it says a command is not found, install that program again (on Windows, tick Add python.exe to PATH), then open a new terminal.

docs.title: 4. Upload the main firmware
docs.text:
A control board from the shop comes with the test firmware, which turns all six motors as soon as the board starts. Put the main firmware on it before you switch on the assembled robot. You do this once.

  1. Download the robot repository into your Documents folder: 
    cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents
git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm.git
    On Linux and macOS, the first line is cd ~/Documents.
  2. Install VS Code. Open it, click the Extensions icon on the left, search for PlatformIO IDE and install it. Restart VS Code when it asks.
  3. On Windows, install the ST-Link driver: in File Explorer, open PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm in your Documents folder, right-click en.stsw-link009.zip, choose Extract All, and run dpinst_amd64.exe from the extracted folder.
  4. Unplug the 24 V supply from the robot. Plug the programming adapter onto the 2×5 header next to the USB port, and the ST-Link into the PC. The adapter powers the board's microcontroller, not the motors.
  5. In VS Code: File, Open Folder, and choose PAROL6 control board main software inside PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm. The first time, PlatformIO downloads its tools for a few minutes: wait until the bar at the bottom is quiet.
  6. Click the → arrow (Upload) in the bar at the bottom of VS Code.
  7. When it has finished, unplug the programming adapter.

Check

The terminal at the bottom of VS Code ends with SUCCESS. If not, see the Firmware page and Control board troubleshooting.

Read in more detail: Firmware · Firmware and first run.

docs.title: 5. Install the robot software
docs.text:
Choose one, or install both: the commander software is a window with buttons, a program editor and a 3D simulator; the Python API drives the robot from Python programs you write. Each one goes into its own folder with its own virtual environment (.venv), a private copy of Python for that program: the two need different versions of the same packages, so they cannot share one.

Commander softwarePython API

In the terminal, download the commander software, make its virtual environment and install what it needs (a few minutes):

cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents
git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-commander-software.git
cd PAROL-commander-software
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

On Linux and macOS:

cd ~/Documents
git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-commander-software.git
cd PAROL-commander-software
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

After the activate line the prompt starts with (.venv).

In the terminal, download the Python API, switch to version 0.9.1, make its virtual environment and install it (a few minutes):

cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents
git clone https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API.git
cd PAROL6-python-API
git checkout v0.9.1
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install .

On Linux and macOS:

cd ~/Documents
git clone https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API.git
cd PAROL6-python-API
git checkout v0.9.1
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install .

After the activate line the prompt starts with (.venv). Git reports a "detached HEAD" after the checkout: that is expected.

Check

The install ends without an ERROR line. If one appears, see Commander installation or Python API installation.

docs.title: 6. Connect
docs.text:
1. The E-stop to the two E-stop terminals on the base. Without it the robot will not run.
  2. The USB cable to the PC.
  3. The 24 V supply to the power connector, and the supply's mains plug into the switched socket strip, or behind the mains switch, within your reach. Nothing happens yet: the board is off until the button is pressed.

Read in more detail: Connecting.

docs.title: 7. Switch on
docs.text:
Hold the arm by the forearm and press the power button on the base. The motors energise, you hear six clicks, and the arm holds its position. Let go.

Check

Six drivers initialise and the arm supports itself before you let go. If it does not, use First power-on: if nothing happens.

Read in more detail: First power-on · Switching on and off.

docs.title: 8. Start the software
docs.text:
First find the robot's serial port, the name the PC gives the USB connection:

  • Windows: open Device Manager (right-click the Start button), then Ports (COM & LPT): the robot is a "USB Serial Device" with a number, for example COM5.
  • Linux: ls /dev/ttyACM* in the terminal, usually /dev/ttyACM0. If the software later reports "permission denied", run sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER, then log out and in again.
  • macOS: ls /dev/cu.usbmodem* in the terminal.
Commander softwarePython API

For the first run, write the port into the program. Open PAROL-commander-software/GUI/files/Serial_sender_good_latest.py in a text editor (VS Code: File, Open File) and find these lines near the top: 

if my_os == "Windows": 
    STARTING_PORT = 8 # COM3
else:   
    STARTING_PORT = 0
On Windows, replace 8 with the number of your port, 5 for COM5. On Linux, 0 is /dev/ttyACM0; change it if yours has another number. Save the file. Then start the program in the terminal: 
cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents\PAROL-commander-software
.venv\Scripts\activate
cd GUI\files
python Serial_sender_good_latest.py
On Linux and macOS: 
cd ~/Documents/PAROL-commander-software
source .venv/bin/activate
cd GUI/files
python Serial_sender_good_latest.py
Two windows open: the commander and the simulator. At the bottom of the commander, type the serial port in the port field (COM5 on Windows, ttyACM0 on Linux) and press Connect, more than once if the first try fails.

  1. Start the controller, the program that talks to the robot, with your port, and leave its terminal open: 
    cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents\PAROL6-python-API
.venv\Scripts\activate
parol6-server --serial COM5
    On Linux and macOS: cd ~/Documents/PAROL6-python-API, then source .venv/bin/activate, then parol6-server --serial /dev/ttyACM0 (macOS: the /dev/cu.usbmodem… name).
  2. Open a second terminal and activate the same virtual environment in it: 
    cd %USERPROFILE%\Documents\PAROL6-python-API
.venv\Scripts\activate
python
    (Linux and macOS: cd ~/Documents/PAROL6-python-API, source .venv/bin/activate, python.) The prompt changes to >>>: Python now runs each line you type. Type these three lines: 
    from parol6 import RobotClient
rbt = RobotClient()
rbt.ping()
    Keep this second terminal open: the next steps type into it.

Read in more detail: The commander software · The Python API.

Check

The commander's response log shows the robot's data, or ping() answers with hardware_connected=True. If it does not, use Communication troubleshooting.

docs.title: 9. Jog each joint
docs.text:
Before homing, check that every joint turns the way the software thinks it does: each one briefly, a few degrees. The figure shows each joint's positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey.

Figure 1: Each joint turned 30 degrees in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey.

Before homing, both programs check each jog against the joint limits with a position count that starts at 0 when the board is switched on. That count puts joint 2 past its positive limit and joints 3 and 6 at or below their negative limits. So, until the robot is homed:

  • Joint 2 jogs only in its negative direction. Check that it turns opposite to the figure.
  • Joints 3 and 6 jog only in their positive direction, which is the one to check.
  • Joints 1, 4 and 5 jog both ways.

A refused jog does not move: the commander logs Error: Robot jog -> Position out of range, the Python API stops the joint before it starts.

Commander softwarePython API

In the Joint jog menu, press the left arrow (positive) of joints 1 and 3 to 6 briefly, and the right arrow (negative) of joint 2.

rbt.jog_j(0, speed=0.2, duration=0.5)     # joint 1, positive, half a second
rbt.jog_j(1, speed=-0.2, duration=0.5)    # joint 2, negative
The first number is the joint: 0 is joint 1, 5 is joint 6. A negative speed jogs the negative way.

A joint that turns the wrong way is fixed in the firmware, not by trial: Firmware and first run.

Read in more detail: Jogging · Joint limits and directions.

Check

Joints 1 and 3 to 6 turned the way the figure shows, and joint 2 turned the opposite way on its negative jog. If one did not, fix it before you home: A joint turns the wrong way.

docs.title: 10. Home
docs.text:
Homing finds each joint's reference at its limit switch or sensor. Joints 1, 2 and 3 move to their switches together, then 4, then 6, then 5, and the arm ends in the after-homing pose: the standby pose turned 90° about joint 1. Stay at the E-stop: a joint that grinds at its end stop has a switch that does not trigger.

Before you press Home:

  • Joint 6 stands so that it finds its sensor within one turn in the negative direction, with the tool's cables and tubes not wound up. The figure shows the pose: the gripper as drawn, the sensor (blue) and the homing pin (red); joint 6 turns along the green arrow.
  • The tool is mounted, and the firmware's joint 5 homing offset matches it. Joint 5 homes against a feature of the tool holder; j5_homing_offset in main.cpp is 8900 for the pneumatic gripper holder (as shipped) and 8035 for the SSG-48. If you change it, upload the firmware again as in step 4 (Joint 5 and the tool).
Figure 2: Joint 6 before homing: the sensor, the homing pin and the direction of rotation. Commander softwarePython API

Press Home.

rbt.home(wait=True)

Read in more detail: Homing · Homing failures.

Check

Homing finishes, the physical arm matches the simulator, and the pin passes through the witness marks of each joint, which line up in the after-homing pose (Witness marks). If a joint keeps travelling or the pose is wrong, stop and use Homing failures.

docs.title: 11. Move it
docs.text:
The robot now knows where it is. Three simple moves: bend the arm a little, turn the base, and come back. The Python API adds a short straight line down and up from the bent pose.

Commander softwarePython API

Paste this program into the program window and press Start; Stop halts it. 

Begin()
MoveJoint(90,-70,160,0,30,180,t=3)
Delay(1)
MoveJoint(60,-70,160,0,30,180,t=3)
Delay(1)
MoveJoint(90,-90,180,0,0,180,t=3)
End()
MoveJoint takes the six joint angles in degrees; t=3 makes the move take three seconds. Jogging in the Cartesian jog menu moves the tool in straight lines instead.

Type these lines at the >>> prompt, one at a time; each waits until its move is done: 

rbt.move_j([90, -70, 160, 0, 30, 180], speed=0.3)       # bend the arm: six joint angles in degrees
rbt.move_l([0, 0, -30, 0, 0, 0], rel=True, speed=0.3)   # a straight line 30 mm down
rbt.move_l([0, 0, 30, 0, 0, 0], rel=True, speed=0.3)    # and 30 mm back up
rbt.move_j([60, -70, 160, 0, 30, 180], speed=0.3)       # turn the base
rbt.move_j([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180], speed=0.3)        # back to the after-homing pose
speed is a fraction of the maximum: 0.3 is gentle. With rel=True, move_l takes a change from where the tool is: x, y and z in mm in the world frame, then three rotations in degrees.

Read in more detail: RBTscript · The Python API.

docs.title: 12. Switch off
docs.text:
Bring the arm to the parked pose first, folded in over the base, so that it has the least distance to fall:

Commander softwarePython API

Press Park: it writes a three-line program into the program window. Press Start to run it.

rbt.move_j([90, -144.683, 108.171, 2.222, 25.003, 180], speed=0.3)   # the commander's park pose
Type exit() to leave Python.

Then hold the forearm and press the power button. The arm goes limp the moment the motors lose power.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: After-homing pose Where homing leaves the robot: the standby pose turned 90° about joint 1, joints at 90°, −90°, 180°, 0°, 0°, 180°. The firmware (standby_position) and the Python API (STANDBY_ANGLES_DEG) call this pose standby. The witness marks line up in it. Blending (blend radius) Passing through a waypoint without stopping: the path cuts the corner within the given radius. The Python API's r parameter. Commander software Source Robotics' desktop program for PAROL6: a GUI with jogging, a simulator, a program editor for RBTscript, I/O and gripper control, talking to the control board over USB. Control board The electronics inside the base: an STM32 microcontroller, six TMC5160 stepper drivers, the inputs, outputs, E-stop input, CAN and USB. It runs the low-level firmware; the PC runs the high-level software. Controller (Python API) The parol6-server process: it talks to the control board over serial at 100 Hz, plans the motion and accepts commands over UDP from any number of clients. Direction, positive The direction in which a joint's angle increases, shown in the figure on Joint limits and directions. The commander's left arrows jog positive. E-stop The normally closed button on the base. Pressing it, unplugging it or cutting its wire opens the circuit, and the robot stops. It must be connected for the robot to run. Firmware The program on the control board. The main firmware runs the robot with the PC software; the test firmware checks the board and the wiring from a serial terminal. Flange The mounting face at the end of joint 6, where the tool is screwed on. With nothing on it, the TCP is the flange face. Forearm (lower arm) The link from the elbow (joint 3) to the wrist. It carries joint 4. Forearm and lower arm mean the same link. Homing (referencing) Finding each joint's position after power-up by driving it to its limit switch or sensor, then moving a known number of steps to the after-homing pose. Needed after every power-up; the robot does not know where it is before. Jogging Moving a joint, or the tool along an axis, at a chosen speed for as long as a button is held or a command repeats. Joint names Joints 1 to 6 by number, from the base up. Other names for the same joints: base, shoulder and elbow for 1 to 3, and wrist 1, wrist 2 and wrist 3 for 4 to 6, as in the robot model and ROS. Limit switch, inductive sensor The references for homing: mechanical switches on joints 2, 3 and 5, inductive sensors on joints 1, 4 and 6. Mastering Fine-tuning the number of steps from a joint's limit switch to its witness mark, so that a homed robot stands exactly in the after-homing pose. Motion profile The shape of the speed curve of a move: trapezoidal, polynomial, time-optimal, and so on. The Python API offers several; the commander uses trapezoidal and quintic polynomial. Parked pose The arm folded in over the base, joints 2 and 3 toward their limit switches: how the robot rests when it is off, and the pose to switch off in, since the arm has the least distance to fall from it. The commander's Park button writes a program that moves there (90°, −144.683°, 108.171°, 2.222°, 25.003°, 180°). Pose The position and the orientation of the tool together: six numbers, x, y, z in millimetres and three angles in degrees. The standby, after-homing and parked poses are poses of the whole arm, given as six joint angles. RBTscript The commander software's program language: one command per line, MoveJoint, MoveCart, Delay, Gripper and so on. Standby pose The pose of the Denavit-Hartenberg table and the reference of the joint angles: joints at 0°, −90°, 180°, 0°, 0°, 180°, the upper arm vertical, the forearm horizontal, the arm pointing away from the electronics case at the back of the base. After homing the robot stands in it turned 90° about joint 1 (joint 1 at 90°): the after-homing pose, which the Python API calls its standby. Stepper motor The motors of PAROL6: open-loop motors that move in steps, 200 full steps per turn, 6400 with the 32 microsteps the control board uses. The position is counted, not measured. Test firmware The firmware every control board from the shop carries when it ships. It reports each driver at power-on and answers a few text commands (#LIMIT, #IO) from a serial terminal, and it turns all six motors slowly from the moment it starts until the power is switched off. Replace it with the main firmware before the robot is used (The test firmware). TCP (tool center point) The point on the tool the robot positions and the origin of the tool frame. Selecting a tool in the software sets it; an offset moves it. TRF, WRF The tool reference frame, fixed to the tool, and the world reference frame, fixed to the base. Cartesian jogs and relative moves can be made in either. Upper arm The link from the shoulder (joint 2) to the elbow (joint 3). Witness marks Holes in the printed parts of neighbouring links that line up, so that a pin passes through, when the joint stands exactly in the after-homing pose. Wrist 1, wrist 2, wrist 3 Other names for joints 4, 5 and 6. See Joint names.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text: PAROL6 is a 3D-printed six-axis desktop robotic arm with a 408 mm reach and a 1 kg payload, built to work like an industrial arm in its mechanics, its control software and the way you use it. Everything about it is open source: the printable parts, the bill of materials, the control board's firmware, the commander software and the Python API. You can buy it assembled, as the full kit or as the partial kit of the hard-to-find parts, or print and build one from the published files: the Build guide compares them.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• The robot system: the arm, the control board, the PC software, and how they divide the work
  • What you get: what is in the box of an assembled robot or a kit
  • What you need: the power supply, the PC, the tools and the knowledge the robot asks of you

docs.title: The robot system
docs.text:
A working PAROL6 is three things: the arm, the control board inside its base, and a PC running the high-level software. Each does a part of the job.

Figure 1.1: PAROL6 with the connections on its base.

docs.title: The arm
docs.text:
Six revolute joints, driven by NEMA 17 stepper motors through planetary gearboxes and belts, in PETG printed links. Joints 1, 2 and 3 position the wrist; joints 4, 5 and 6 form a spherical wrist that orients the tool. Joint 6 ends in the flange the tool mounts on. The tool connections are on the forearm: an M8 connector for an electric gripper and two push-in fittings for pneumatic lines. Each joint has a limit switch or an inductive sensor that gives it a reference when the robot homes.

Figure 1.2: PAROL6 with the pneumatic gripper, its parts numbered.
  1. Base, with the control board inside
  2. Joint 1 motor
  3. Shoulder, turned by joint 1
  4. Joint 2 motor
  5. Upper arm
  6. Joint 3 motor
  7. Elbow
  8. Forearm, also called the lower arm, turned by joint 4
  9. Wrist, turned by joint 5
  10. Flange, turned by joint 6
  11. Air fittings for a pneumatic tool
  12. Gripper, here the standard pneumatic gripper

The arm has no brakes and no joint encoders. The motors hold the arm while they are powered; the position is counted in steps from the homing reference. Both facts shape how the robot is used, and the Safety chapter returns to them.

docs.title: The control board
docs.text: The PAROL6 control board sits in the base: an STM32F446 microcontroller, six TMC5160 stepper drivers, two isolated inputs and two isolated outputs, the E-stop input, a CAN bus for electric grippers, and USB to the PC. Its firmware generates the step pulses, runs the homing sequence, reads the switches and the inputs, drives the outputs and the gripper, and exchanges a packet with the PC at 100 Hz. It does not plan motion: it executes the joint speeds and positions the PC sends it, 100 times a second.

docs.title: The PC software
docs.text:
The PC does the thinking: kinematics, trajectory planning, the simulator, the program interpreter, the interface. There are two first-party programs, and others:

What it is For Commander software A desktop GUI with jogging, a 3D simulator, a program editor for RBTscript, I/O and gripper tabs Using the robot by hand, teaching points, simple programs Python API A controller process that talks to the board, and a Python client library with blocking and asynchronous calls, planned and streamed motion, tools, collision checking Programs, integrations, research, teleoperation, AI agents ROS 2 and MoveIt A MoveIt configuration and a ros2_control hardware interface that drive the Python API's controller ROS users Community interfaces Web GUIs, alternative firmware, vision demos

All of them speak the same serial protocol to the control board, so a board with the main firmware works with any of them.

docs.title: How a move happens
docs.text:
1. You press a jog button, run a program line or call move_j.
  2. The PC software computes the trajectory: the joint angles over time, with the speed profile you chose, within the joint limits.
  3. One hundred times a second it sends the control board a packet with the target position and speed of each joint, the output states and the gripper command.
  4. The board sets the stepper speeds and runs the steps; the drivers turn the motors.
  5. The board answers with the actual position and speed of each joint, the switch and input states, the errors and the gripper's status, which the PC software shows and uses for the next cycle.
sequenceDiagram
    participant PC as PC software
    participant B as Control board
    participant M as Motors
    Note over PC: a jog button, a program line, move_j: the trajectory is planned
    loop every 10 ms
        PC->>B: targets: joint positions and speeds, outputs, gripper
        B->>M: step pulses at the commanded speeds
        B-->>PC: actual positions and speeds, switches, inputs, errors
    end

docs.title: Where everything is published
docs.text:
Mechanical files, BOM, building instructions, control board firmware, URDF PAROL6-Desktop-robot-arm Commander software PAROL-commander-software Python API PAROL6-python-API ROS 2 MoveIt configuration PAROL6-ROS2-MOVEIT This documentation PAROL-docs Shop, videos, community source-robotics.com, YouTube, Discord

The full list is on Downloads and files.

docs.title: An assembled robot
docs.text: A PAROL6 from the shop comes assembled, wired and tested, with the control board in the base running the main firmware, the E-stop button, the pneumatic gripper holder, and the robot homed once on the bench. Check the contents against the order; the power supply, grippers and the programming adapter are separate items unless the order includes them.

docs.title: A kit
docs.text: The full kit contains every part of the BOM except the printed parts and the power supply. The partial kit contains the hard-to-find parts: the board, the drivers, the bearings, belts, pulleys, connectors, sensors, switches and the pneumatics; you add the gearboxes, the motors, the power supply and the printed parts. The Build guide lists every kit. You assemble a kit with the Build guide and the assembly manual. The control board in a kit carries the test firmware, as every control board from the shop does: it turns all six motors as soon as it starts. Upload the main firmware before you switch on the assembled robot (Firmware and first run).

docs.title: A control board on its own
docs.text: Every control board is tested end to end before it ships and comes with the test firmware, which exercises the drivers, the switches and the I/O from a serial terminal. Upload the main firmware before you use it with the commander software or the Python API: Firmware.

docs.title: The files
docs.text: Everything else you get is on GitHub: the STL and STEP files, the BOM with purchase links, the building instructions PDF and the video playlist, the firmware sources, the software. Downloads and files lists them.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
A 24 V DC supply of at least 5 A. The BOM names a Mean Well 120 W DIN-rail unit; any regulated 24 V 5 A supply with the robot's GX16 power connector wired to it does. The control board accepts 18 to 24 V; below 24 V the motors lose torque and speed. The robot draws about 40 W in typical use and more when all six motors accelerate at once.

Plug the supply in through a mains switch within reach, a switched socket strip for example. It is the stop that still works when the PC software has frozen (Emergency stop), and the switch you reach for when the E-stop has no effect.

docs.title: The E-stop
docs.text: A normally closed emergency stop button, wired to the two E-stop terminals of the control board. The robot does not run without it. The kit's button mounts on the base in the printed holder; any NC switch works for a bench setup (Emergency stop).

docs.title: The PC
docs.text:
The PC runs the kinematics and the planner and must send a packet to the robot every 10 ms without hiccups. A machine that falls behind makes the robot stutter. Tested systems and the minimum are in the commander repository's confirmed working systems: at least an Intel i5 six-core processor of 2017 or newer, or an AMD equivalent. The tested systems include two Windows 10 PCs with six-core AMD Ryzen processors, a Radxa ROCK 5B on Linux and a six-core MacBook Pro.

Commander software Python API Operating system Windows, Linux, macOS Windows, Linux (x86-64 and ARM64), macOS (ARM64) Python 3.10 or 3.11 3.11 or newer Connection USB (a serial port, 3 Mbaud) USB on the PC that runs the controller; clients anywhere on the network

A USB type B cable connects the robot to the PC. USB does not power the board.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: For an assembled robot: hex keys (2, 2.5, 3 mm) for the mounting screws and the gripper, a small screwdriver for the terminal blocks. For a build, the Build guide lists the rest, down to the blue threadlocker and the thermal cement.

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text: You should be able to use a hex key. Python and the terminal you can learn on the way: the Quick start gives every command to type, for someone who has never used either. The Theory corner explains the robotics vocabulary the software uses, from joint numbering to singularities, in the order you meet it.

docs.title: 2. Safety
docs.text:
PAROL6 is a desktop robot, light enough to lift with one hand, and it can still hurt you: it pinches, it moves fast, it moves by itself when it homes, and it falls when it loses power. This chapter is short. Read all of it before the first power-on, and have everyone who works at the robot read it.

Danger

The project's Safety Warning and Disclaimer applies to everything on this site: the hardware, the firmware, the software and this documentation are under development, and you build, modify and operate the robot at your own risk.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Intended use: what the robot is for, and what it is not
  • Hazards: pinch points, the fall on power loss, induced voltage, hot motors, the tool
  • Emergency stop: what the E-stop does, and what it does not
  • Moving the robot by hand: when it is allowed and the two things never to do
  • What the robot protects against, and what not
  • Planning the cell: the person, the guarding, the program

docs.title: Emergency stop
docs.text:
The E-stop is the red button on the base, a normally closed contact wired to the control board's E-stop input. It must be connected for the robot to run.

Figure 2.2: E-stop wiring to the control board.

docs.title: What pressing it does
docs.text:
The control board reads the E-stop input in every command cycle and reports it to the PC in every packet. The PC software acts on it:

  • the commander software disables the robot: it sends the disable command, the firmware stops accepting motion commands, and the log shows Robot disable; button or estop. A running program is stopped. The motors stay energised and hold the arm. Release the button and press Enable to continue; Start runs a program again from its first line.
  • the Python API's controller cancels the move in progress and the queue, sends the disable command to the firmware, and refuses every motion command with SYS_ESTOP_ACTIVE while the button is pressed. When the button is released, the controller clears that error by itself and accepts commands again, but the firmware stays disabled and the arm does not move until reset() sends the enable command. Call reset() after every E-stop, before the next move.

The E-stop is a software stop

The control board's firmware (release 1) reports the E-stop and does not itself cut the motor power or the step pulses: the PC software stops the motion. A PC that has crashed, a program that has frozen, or a USB cable that has fallen out leaves the E-stop without effect, and the firmware keeps executing the last packet it received: a joint that was jogging in the commander keeps turning until it reaches its blocker. For those cases the hard stop is the power supply: a switch on the supply's mains side within reach, and the knowledge that the arm will fall when you use it.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It does not cut power to the motors, so the arm does not fall when it is pressed.
  • It does not stop the gripper: an electric gripper keeps its grip, a pneumatic one stays where the valve left it.
  • It does not stop a Python script of your own: the script keeps running. Its commands are refused while the button is pressed and accepted again after the release, before the arm can move. Stop the script before you release the button, then call reset().

docs.title: If someone is caught by the arm
docs.text:
The E-stop does not free anyone

Pressed, the E-stop leaves the motors holding the arm where it is, and a joint cannot be pushed back by hand against a holding motor. To free a trapped hand or finger, either release the E-stop, enable the robot and jog that joint away slowly, the smallest step at a time; or support the arm with one hand and switch off the power supply with the other, knowing that the arm goes limp and falls. Decide which before you need it, and keep the supply's switch within reach (Planning the cell).

docs.title: The contact
docs.text: Normally closed, so that a cut wire, a loose terminal or an unplugged button is read as a stop. A normally open button does not work. The control board has two E-stop connectors on the same input: a second button can be wired in series, or a safety relay's contact. Inputs, outputs and E-stop has the wiring.

docs.title: Pinch and crush points
docs.text:
Every joint is a pinch point, and the elbow and wrist fold against the upper arm and forearm. The motors are geared: a finger between two links when a joint closes is crushed, not pushed away. Keep hands, cables and tubes out of the arm's path while it is enabled, and never reach into the workspace of a running program. Under the elbow, the belt that drives joint 3 runs onto its pulley: a finger or a loose cable there is drawn in.

Figure 2.1: The pinch points of PAROL6, after homing: the wrist, the elbow, the belt and pulley under the elbow, the shoulder and the base.

docs.title: Clothing, hair and eyes
docs.text: A joint that closes catches more than fingers: its belts and pulleys pull in hair, loose sleeves, scarves, lanyards and jewellery. Tie back long hair and take those off before you work at a powered robot, and keep them out of the arm's reach while it moves. Wear safety glasses with a pneumatic gripper, with a sharp or pointed tool, and whenever the robot can drop or throw a part.

docs.title: The arm falls when the power goes
docs.text:
PAROL6 has no brakes. The moment the motors lose power, from the button, the supply, a blown fuse or a pulled cable, the arm goes limp and falls under its own weight, with whatever it carries. The gearing slows the fall of joints 2 and 3 a little; it does not stop it.

  • Never switch the robot off while it is extended or carrying something: bring it to the parked pose first, folded in over the base, where it has the least distance to fall (Switching on and off).
  • Hold the forearm when you press the power button.
  • Keep hands out from under the arm.
  • Expect the fall during any power failure, and place nothing fragile under the arm.

docs.title: Motion you did not command
docs.text:
• Homing moves every joint, at speed, toward its limit switch, as soon as Home is pressed. The arm must be free to move and the switches must work (Homing).
  • A program restarts where you told it to, and Loop() restarts it forever.
  • A lost step makes the arm move to a different place than the one on the screen. After a collision or a stall, stop and home again.
  • A wrong joint direction on a new build sends a joint the wrong way on the first jog, into its stop. Jog slowly and briefly the first time (Firmware and first run).

docs.title: Stepper-induced voltage
docs.text: A stepper motor turned by hand is a generator. Moving the arm quickly while the supply is connected and the board off can power the board on and energise the motors, with the arm wherever you left it. Move an unpowered robot slowly, and only toward the parked pose or into its box.

docs.title: Hot motors
docs.text: After hours of motion the wrist motors reach 70 °C (Currents and temperatures). That is hot to the touch and close to the limit of the plastic around them.

docs.title: Electricity
docs.text: The robot runs on 24 V, which is safe to touch. The power supply you plug it into is connected to the mains: use a closed, approved supply, never an open-frame one on the desk. The control board has no reverse-polarity protection on its power input.

docs.title: The tool
docs.text: A pneumatic gripper closes with the force of the compressed air behind it, whatever is between its fingers; the electric grippers close with up to 80 N. A vacuum gripper drops its load the moment the air stops. Treat the tool as part of the robot in every rule above.

docs.title: Intended use
docs.text:
PAROL6 is made for education, research, hobby robotics and light automation on a bench: pick-and-place of light objects, camera and sensor experiments, teaching robot programming, prototyping a task before buying an industrial arm. It is an open-source, 3D-printed machine assembled by its owner or by a small workshop, and it is not a certified industrial robot.

Use it

  • on a bench or frame it is bolted to, in a dry room
  • with a payload within its rating: 1 kg near the base, 0.5 kg at full reach, tool included
  • with the E-stop connected and within reach
  • with the person who runs it able to see the whole arm

Do not use it

  • around people who do not know it is a robot: children, visitors, a crowded desk
  • for anything that must not fail: it has no brakes and no joint position feedback, and a lost step is silent
  • with tools that cut, heat or spray without your own guarding and risk assessment
  • in wet, dusty or hot places, or outdoors

A self-built robot is the builder's responsibility from the first screw: the currents, the wiring, the limit switches and the mechanical stops are all yours to get right, and the Build guide says where the mistakes are made.

docs.title: Moving the robot by hand
docs.text:
An unpowered PAROL6 can be moved by hand: the joints turn against the friction of their gearboxes and belts, and the arm has no brakes to release. This is how you pose it for packing and how you lift it. Two rules:

Never more than one turn, except joint 6

No joint may ever be turned more than one full turn, by hand or by software. Cables and pneumatic tubes run through the joints, and a second turn wraps and tears them. The one exception is joint 6: with the bare flange it can turn without limit; with a gripper or a tool, the tool's cables and tubes wrap as it turns, and they set how far it may go. Joints 1 to 5 have printed blockers that stop them; on a build without them, the rule is yours to keep.

Figure 2.3: Joint 5 at its lower and upper limit, -120 and +120 degrees, over the standby pose in grey. A gripper can reach the forearm before that: check the clearance with a slow jog.

Not while the supply is connected

A stepper turned by hand generates voltage, and a quick move can switch the board on with the arm in your hands. Unplug the power supply, or move slowly, and only toward the parked pose.

docs.title: When the robot is powered
docs.text: Do not force a powered joint. The motor holds it with its full holding current; what gives is a belt, a set screw or a printed part, and afterwards the position the software reports is wrong. To move a powered robot, jog it.

docs.title: After moving by hand
docs.text: The robot does not know it was moved: the firmware counts steps and sees none. Home again before any program or Cartesian move. The commander's position display and the simulator are wrong until you do.

docs.title: Lifting
docs.text: Bring the arm to the parked pose, joints 2 and 3 toward their limit switches so that the arm folds over the base, then lift by the base, not by the arm. Transport and storage has the packing.

docs.title: Planning the cell
docs.text: A robot cell is the robot, what it works on, and the people around it. For a PAROL6 on a bench the plan fits on a page, and it is worth writing.

docs.title: The person
docs.text: One person runs the robot and sees all of it. Nobody else reaches into the workspace while it is enabled. The E-stop is within that person's reach, and so is the power supply's switch.

docs.title: The space
docs.text:
• The arm's reach, 408 mm from the axis of joint 1 to the flange, plus the tool, and a margin for the elbow, which swings behind the base when the arm folds: a sphere of about half a metre.
  • Nothing fragile inside it, and nothing that the arm could knock onto the floor.
  • The cables and tubes outside the sweep, or fixed so the arm cannot catch them.
  • For a robot that runs unattended or near others, an enclosure: acrylic panels on the profile frame are enough to keep hands out; the robot cannot break them.

docs.title: The program
docs.text:
• Run every new program in the simulator first, at full speed, and watch for the arm folding into the base or the table.
  • Start on the real robot at low speed: in the commander, low v= or long t= in the moves (the speed slider only scales jogging); in the Python API, the speed fraction of each move.
  • Make the first move of a program go from the after-homing pose to a known pose, so that a program started right after homing always begins safely.
  • Use Delay() and the inputs to wait for the world, rather than assuming it.

docs.title: The tool and the parts
docs.text:
• The payload includes the tool. A gripper and a camera together can be most of the 0.5 kg the arm carries at full reach.
  • A pneumatic gripper needs 5 to 7 bar (check your gripper's rating) and a valve wired to an output; the valve's two tubes decide whether it is normally open or closed (Pneumatics).
  • Know what the gripper does at an E-stop and at a power loss. The E-stop leaves the gripper as it is: an electric gripper keeps its grip, and a pneumatic or vacuum gripper stays where the valve left it. When the power or the air goes, the vacuum gripper drops its part.

docs.title: When something changes
docs.text: Changing the tool, the base, the table height or the fixture changes the kinematics and the clearances. Update the tool in the software, check the limits with a slow jog, and run the programs in the simulator again.

docs.title: What the robot protects against, and what not
docs.text: Know what the hardware and the software catch, and what they do not, before you decide how the robot is guarded.

docs.title: What is protected
docs.text: Against How Where A target outside the joint limits The planner refuses it; a jog stops at the limit. Firmware 1, the commander and the Python API check the earlier, partly wider limits (Joint limits) Commander, Python API A speed or acceleration above the limits Clamped to the robot model's limits Commander, Python API A move through a singularity (Cartesian) The commander stops the move; the API's IK fails and refuses the command Commander, Python API A pose the arm cannot reach The IK fails and the command is refused Commander, Python API Self-collision and collision with declared obstacles Collision checking of planned moves and jogs against the robot's meshes and your keep-out shapes Python API (set_shapes) The E-stop pressed Reported by the board, acted on by the PC software (Emergency stop) Commander, Python API A driver overheating The TMC5160 shuts its outputs down when it gets too hot; the fan keeps it far below that. The joint then goes limp, and firmware 1 does not tell the PC Control board A short on a motor output The TMC5160 switches the output off. Firmware 1 reads the driver's short and open-load flags once at start-up and does not report them Control board

docs.title: What is not protected
docs.text:
Not against Why What you do instead A collision with something the software does not know There are no joint encoders and no force sensing: the stepper pushes until it stalls, then loses steps silently Keep the workspace clear; check programs in the simulator first; declare obstacles to the Python API's collision checker Lost steps Open-loop motors; the position is counted, not measured After a stall or a collision, home again; keep speeds and payloads within the limits A fall on power loss No brakes Switch off only in the parked pose; keep hands and objects out from under the arm A frozen PC The E-stop acts through the PC software; the firmware does not stop on its own A mains switch on the power supply within reach Lost communication with the PC The firmware has no timeout: it keeps executing the last packet until the next one arrives. After a move to a position (programs, the Python API) the joint stops near that target. After a jog in the commander the joint keeps turning at the jog speed until it reaches its blocker Keep the mains switch within reach; a short, direct USB cable Motor temperature Only the drivers are measured, not the motors Reduce the current for long runs (Currents and temperatures) The tool The robot does not know what the tool does Guard the tool as you would the robot A wrong joint direction on a new build The firmware trusts its configuration Jog each joint briefly before homing

The commander's safety functions are described in Errors and recovery; the Python API's in Errors.

docs.title: 3. Technical data
docs.text: The numbers of PAROL6 V1: the specifications, the joint limits and their directions, the dimensions and the kinematic model, the drives with their ratios and resolutions, and the motor currents with the temperatures they lead to.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Specifications
  • Joint limits and directions
  • Dimensions and kinematics
  • Drives, ratios and resolution
  • Currents and temperatures

The control board's own specifications are in the Control Board Manual.

docs.title: Motors and gearing
docs.text:
Joint Motor Gearing Ratio Joint 1 NEMA 17, 65 N·cm (60 mm) HTD3 belt, 15-tooth pulley to a 96-tooth printed pulley 6.4 : 1 Joint 2 NEMA 17, 65 N·cm (60 mm) EG planetary gearbox 20 : 1 Joint 3 NEMA 17, 45 N·cm (40 mm) EG planetary gearbox 20 : 1, then a belt 38 : 42 18.095 : 1 Joint 4 NEMA 17, 45 N·cm (40 mm) HTD3 belt, 12-tooth pulley to 48 teeth 4 : 1 Joint 5 NEMA 17, 45 N·cm (40 mm) HTD3 belt, 12-tooth pulley to 48 teeth 4 : 1 Joint 6 NEMA 17, 16 N·cm (20 mm) EG planetary gearbox 10 : 1

The planetary gearboxes are the precision EG series with 15 to 20 arc-minutes of backlash; the cheaper MG series fits and works, with more backlash. The belts are 6 mm wide HTD3, tensioned by small bearings; their lengths are in the BOM.

docs.title: Steps and microsteps
docs.text:
The stepper motors have 200 full steps per turn. The control board runs the TMC5160 drivers at 32 microsteps, so one motor turn is 6400 microsteps, and every position and speed the firmware and the PC exchange is in these steps. Through the gearing, one step at the joint is:

Joint Steps per joint turn Step size Joint 1 40 960 0.00879° (0.000153 rad) Joint 2 128 000 0.00281° (0.000049 rad) Joint 3 115 810 0.00311° (0.000054 rad) Joint 4 25 600 0.01406° (0.000245 rad) Joint 5 25 600 0.01406° (0.000245 rad) Joint 6 64 000 0.00563° (0.000098 rad)

Conversions: degrees per step = 360 / (200 × 32) / ratio; the software's DEG2STEPS and STEPS2DEG do exactly this. A microstep is not a guaranteed position: the motor's holding torque at a fraction of a full step is small, so the real resolution under load is coarser than the table, which is why the repeatability is specified at 0.1 mm rather than at the step size.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Joint Joint 1, ratio 6.4 Joint 2, ratio 20 Joint 3, ratio 18.095 Joint 4, ratio 4 Joint 5, ratio 4 Joint 6, ratio 10 Joint angle, degrees Joint speed, degrees per second

16 000 steps from the standby pose · one step is 0.00281° at the joint

10 667 steps per second · the motor turns at 100 rpm

The conversions of this page, with your numbers: 6400 microsteps per motor turn, through the joint's ratio.

docs.title: Why open loop works here
docs.text: The motors are not fitted with encoders: the position is the count of steps commanded since homing. This works because the planner never asks a motor for more than its torque at the commanded speed and acceleration, with margin; a stepper that is not overloaded does not lose steps. If one is overloaded (a collision, a payload over the limit, too high a speed with a reduced current) it loses steps silently, the arm is then not where the software thinks it is, and the only cure is to home again. Steppers, open loop and backlash goes deeper.

docs.title: Joint numbering and positive directions
docs.text:
Joints are numbered from the base up. Joints 1, 2 and 3 are also called the base, shoulder and elbow joints, and joints 4, 5 and 6 wrist 1, wrist 2 and wrist 3, the names the robot model and ROS use. Each picture shows one joint turned 30° in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey. The arrow at the joint points the same way, and the commander software's left arrows jog in that direction.

Figure 3.1: Each joint turned 30 degrees in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey. Joint Also called Positive direction J1 base counter-clockwise, seen from above J2 shoulder leans the upper arm forward, the way the forearm points in the standby pose J3 elbow raises the forearm J4 wrist 1 clockwise, seen from the tool J5 wrist 2 tips the tool up, in the standby pose J6 wrist 3 clockwise, seen from the tool

docs.title: Standby and after homing
docs.text:
The standby pose is the pose of the Denavit-Hartenberg table and the kinematics sheets, and the reference for the limits below: the upper arm vertical, the forearm horizontal, the arm pointing away from the electronics case at the back of the base. After homing the robot stands in the same pose turned 90° about joint 1, counter-clockwise seen from above: the firmware sets joint 1 to +90° when it finishes homing.

Pose Joint 1 Joint 2 Joint 3 Joint 4 Joint 5 Joint 6 Standby 0° −90° 180° 0° 0° 180° After homing 90° −90° 180° 0° 0° 180°

The Python API calls the after-homing pose its standby (STANDBY_ANGLES_DEG), and a later home() moves there; the commander software's standby is the standby pose above.

Figure 3.2: The standby pose, from the front and from the side, with the joints marked.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
The joint limits of PAROL6's model in robot_descriptions (version 2.15.1), in degrees, in the angles the software shows (the standby pose above).

Joint Negative limit Standby Positive limit Range J1 −97.40° 0° +97.40° 194.8° J2 −146.15° −90° −32.70° 113.4° J3 105.52° 180° 294.59° 189.1° J4 −114.59° 0° +114.59° 229.2° J5 −120.32° 0° +120.32° 240.6° J6 none 180° none no limit with the bare flange; with a tool, its cables and tubes set it Figure 3.3: Each joint at both its limits, in its colour, over the standby pose in grey; the arc spans the range, in the angles the software shows. Joint 1 is seen from above, with the after-homing position marked; joint 4 is seen from the tool, with joint 5 at 90 degrees so that the tool's swing shows; joint 6 has no limit.

The firmware and the software still use the earlier limits

Firmware 1, the commander software and the Python API (0.9.1) enforce the limits of the earlier model until they are updated: J1 ±123.05°, J2 −145.01° to −3.38°, J3 107.87° to 287.87°, J4 ±105.47°, J5 ±90°, J6 0° to 360°. A target between the two is accepted by them; keep to the table above. Before homing they apply these limits to a position count that starts at 0 at power-up, so joint 2 cannot be jogged in its positive direction, nor joints 3 and 6 in their negative one, until the robot is homed (Jogging).

Joints 1 to 5 are stopped at both ends by printed blocker parts, the mechanical stops a little past the limits above. The limit switch or sensor that homes a joint sits near its blocker, so that it triggers just before the joint reaches it. Joint 6 has no blocker: with the bare flange nothing stops it, and with a tool only the tool's cables and tubes do.

Grippers and bases change the limits

A gripper changes where joint 5 can go without colliding with the forearm, and a riser under the base changes what joint 2 can reach. The software limits do not know about either: check the real clearances with a slow jog before you run a program near a limit.

The limits are not a safety function

The limits only stop the software from commanding a joint further. Inside them the arm can still hit a person, the table or itself, no safety-rated part checks them, and a wrong homing shifts them with it. They protect the robot's cables and parts, not the people near it (Safety).

Never more than one turn, except joint 6

No joint may ever be turned more than one full turn, by hand or by software: the cables and pneumatic tubes that pass through the joints wrap and tear. The one exception is joint 6: with the bare flange it can turn without limit; with a gripper or a tool, the tool's cables and tubes wrap as it turns, and they set how far it may go (Moving the robot by hand).

docs.text:
Gripper Printed parts Reset

Drag to turn the robot, scroll to zoom, move each joint with its slider, choose the gripper on the flange, try a colour for the printed parts (the motors stay black). The model is the robot's URDF; the sliders run over its joint limits.

The sheets below come from PAROL6's models in robot_descriptions (version 2.15.1). Each shows the robot's own meshes in the standby pose (every joint of the model at 0), in one orthographic side view at one scale, with the dimensions taken from the URDF, not measured from the picture, and the standard DH table to the tool centre point (TCP) of that configuration. Click a sheet to enlarge it.

Flange onlyPneumatic gripperSSG-48SSG-48 fin-rayMSGMSG soft jaws

Figure 3.4: PAROL6 with nothing on the flange: dimensions and the DH table to the TCP.

Figure 3.5: PAROL6 with the standard pneumatic gripper: dimensions and the DH table to the TCP.

Figure 3.6: PAROL6 with the SSG-48 gripper, solid jaws: dimensions and the DH table to the TCP.

Figure 3.7: PAROL6 with the SSG-48 gripper, fin-ray jaws: dimensions and the DH table to the TCP.
