Figure 3.9: PAROL6 with the MSG gripper, soft TPU jaws: dimensions and the DH table to the TCP.

Dimension What it is Value a1 Base height: the floor to the joint 2 axis 110.5 mm a2 Shoulder offset: the joint 1 axis to the joint 2 axis 23.42 mm a3 Upper arm: joint 2 to joint 3 180 mm a4 Elbow offset 43.5 mm a5 Forearm: the joint 3 axis to the wrist centre 177 mm a6 The joint 6 centre to the TCP, along the tool axis depends on the tool, below a7 Sideways offset of the TCP depends on the tool, below Tool a6 a7 Flange only (the TCP is the flange face) 50.5 mm 0 Pneumatic gripper 62.3 mm 45.25 mm SSG-48, solid or fin-ray jaws 134.3 mm 0 MSG, solid or soft jaws 134.3 mm 28.35 mm

A riser under the base changes a1, and a tool of your own changes a6 and a7: tell the software about the tool (Tools and the TCP), or the poses it reports will be wrong.

The software still computes with the earlier model

These pages give the model's dimensions. Until the software is updated, the Python API (its built-in URDF) and the commander software compute with a5 = 176.35 mm, and the commander with a6 = 62.8 mm for the pneumatic gripper, so a pose they report can differ from these sheets by up to about 0.65 mm.

docs.title: Kinematic structure
docs.text: The first three joints place the wrist centre; the axes of joints 4, 5 and 6 intersect in one point, a spherical wrist, which is what makes the inverse kinematics tractable. The Theory corner explains forward and inverse kinematics, and Configurations and singularities the eight ways the arm can reach one pose.

docs.title: Denavit-Hartenberg parameters
docs.text:
Standard DH, each joint's transform being A_i = Rz(theta_i) Tz(d_i) Tx(a_i) Rx(alpha_i), from the base to the TCP. q1 to q6 are the model's joint angles (the URDF's), all 0 in the standby pose; the theta column already contains the joint offsets, so do not add them twice. Theta is the angle the software shows: joint 2's software angle is q2 − 90°, joint 3's is q3 + 180° and joint 6's is q6 + 180°, the others are equal. The sheets above give the same table for each tool.

Joint Link theta alpha a d 1 Base q1 -90° a2 = 23.42 mm a1 = 110.5 mm 2 Shoulder q2 - 90° 180° a3 = 180 mm 0 3 Elbow q3 + 180° 90° -a4 = -43.5 mm 0 4 Wrist 1 q4 -90° 0 -a5 = -177 mm 5 Wrist 2 q5 90° 0 0 6 Wrist 3, to the TCP q6 + 180° 180° -a7 -a6

The models were checked at 128 poses including the joint limits: the DH table, the URDF and the MuJoCo model agree to within 0.006 mm and 0.002°. The Python API does not use the table directly: it loads its URDF and computes the kinematics numerically. The commander software uses a Robotics Toolbox DH model.

docs.title: Mounting holes
docs.text: Six holes in the base, on a pattern made for 30×30 mm aluminium profiles. The mounting plates folder of the repository has STEP drawings of a small and a big base plate: Mounting the robot.

docs.title: Motor currents
docs.text:
The control board sets each motor's running current in the firmware. The values are chosen for the motors of the BOM and for the printed parts around them; joints 4 and 5 run below their motors' rating because their motors are enclosed in the forearm.

Joint Maximum current (constants.h) Current while moving Holding current Joint 1 2000 mA 85 % of the maximum: 1700 mA 70 % of that: 1190 mA Joint 2 2000 mA 1700 mA 80 %: 1360 mA Joint 3 1900 mA 1615 mA 80 %: 1292 mA Joint 4 1700 mA 1445 mA 80 %: 1156 mA Joint 5 1700 mA 1445 mA 80 %: 1156 mA Joint 6 965 mA 820 mA 88 %: 722 mA

The firmware calls rms_current(MOTORx_MAX_CURRENT * 0.85, hold_multiplier); the hold multiplier is 0.7 for joint 1, 0.8 for joints 2 to 5 and 0.88 for joint 6 (motor_init.cpp; Firmware parameters). Lower currents give less torque, which means lower reachable speeds and accelerations and a higher chance of lost steps; higher currents heat the motors and the plastic around them.

docs.title: Temperatures
docs.text:
Stepper motors are rated for 100 °C and more, but PAROL6 is plastic, and PETG softens around 80 °C. These are the motor case temperatures measured on a robot at the default currents, at room temperature:

Joint Holding position for 5 h Moving for 2 h Joint 1 51 °C 64 °C Joint 2 54 °C 64 °C Joint 3 48 °C 52 °C Joint 4 60 °C 73 °C Joint 5 60 °C 72 °C Joint 6 61 °C 65 °C

Through a thermal camera, a powered PAROL6 shows where the heat is: the motors of joints 2 and 3 beside the shoulder, the elbow (the hottest point in this picture, 50 °C) and the wrist motors in the forearm, and the control board at the back of the base. The scale runs from 29.6 to 50.0 °C.

Figure 3.10: A powered PAROL6 through a thermal camera: warm motors at the shoulder, the elbow and in the forearm, and the control board in the base.

Long runs

Joints 4 and 5 come within 10 °C of the plastic's limit after two hours of continuous motion. For a robot that runs for hours, reduce the currents in the firmware (MOTORx_MAX_CURRENT in constants.h, or the hold_multiplier in motor_init.cpp), lower the duty cycle, or let it rest in a pose that does not load the motors. A deformed forearm cannot be straightened: it has to be printed again.

The stepper drivers protect themselves: a TMC5160 that gets too hot shuts its outputs down, and its joint goes limp. The fan in the base keeps them well below that (Control board technical data). Firmware 1 does not tell the PC when a driver is hot: the joints' temperature error bits in its packet are always 0. The driver temperature is not the motor temperature.

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Value Degrees of freedom 6 revolute joints Reach 408 mm to the flange, 434 mm to the standard pneumatic gripper's TCP, from the axis of joint 1 Payload 1 kg near the base, 0.5 kg across the full workspace Repeatability 0.1 mm Weight 5.5 kg Material 3D-printed PETG, steel shafts and bearings Motors NEMA 17 stepper motors, one per joint Gearing Planetary gearboxes (joints 2, 3, 6) and HTD3 belts (joints 1, 3, 4, 5) Position reference Limit switches (joints 2, 3, 5) and inductive sensors (joints 1, 4, 6); no joint encoders Brakes None: the arm falls when the motors lose power Power supply 24 V DC, 5 A, recommended for optimal robot performance (18 V minimum) Power consumption About 40 W typical Control PAROL6 control board (STM32F446, six TMC5160 drivers) in the base PC connection USB, serial at 3 Mbaud, 100 Hz command cycle Inputs and outputs 2 isolated inputs, 2 isolated outputs, E-stop input Buses 1 CAN bus for electric grippers (a second is on the board, not populated) Tool connections M8 4-pin gripper connector (24 V, CAN) at the forearm; 2 pneumatic lines, 4 mm tube, base to forearm Mounting 6 holes in the base, spaced for 30×30 mm aluminium profiles; clamps Operating temperature Room temperature; the printed parts limit the motor temperatures (Currents and temperatures)

docs.title: Joint ranges
docs.text:
Joint Range Joint 1 194.8° (±97.4°) Joint 2 113.4° Joint 3 189.1° Joint 4 229.2° (±114.6°) Joint 5 240.6° (±120.3°) Joint 6 360° in software; mechanically unlimited, but see Moving the robot by hand

The ranges are those of the robot's model (robot_descriptions 2.15.1); the exact limits are on Joint limits and directions.

docs.title: Speeds
docs.text:
The speed limits are set in the PC software, not in the firmware, and the two programs differ: the commander allows less on joints 1, 2, 3 and 6 and on the tool, and more on joints 4 and 5.

Joint Python API: maximum speed Python API: acceleration Commander: maximum speed Joint 1 132 °/s (15000 steps/s) 395 °/s² 57 °/s (6500 steps/s) Joint 2 70 °/s (25000 steps/s) 211 °/s² 51 °/s (18000 steps/s) Joint 3 99 °/s (32000 steps/s) 298 °/s² 62 °/s (20000 steps/s) Joint 4 141 °/s (10000 steps/s) 422 °/s² 309 °/s (22000 steps/s) Joint 5 141 °/s (10000 steps/s) 422 °/s² 309 °/s (22000 steps/s) Joint 6 152 °/s (27000 steps/s) 456 °/s² 124 °/s (22000 steps/s) Tool, linear 200 mm/s 550 mm/s² 60 mm/s Tool, angular 100 °/s 275 °/s² 25 °/s

The steps per second are converted with the ratios of Drives, ratios and resolution. In the Python API a joint's acceleration is three times its speed, so a joint reaches full speed in a third of a second, and jogging is limited to 80 % of the maxima. The commander jogs within lower limits of its own, which its speed slider scales: 13 °/s on joint 1, 8 °/s on joint 2, 11 °/s on joint 3, 98 °/s on joints 4 and 5 and 101 °/s on joint 6 at 100 % (1500, 3000, 3600, 7000, 7000 and 18000 steps/s), and 60 mm/s for the tool. A joint driven at its maximum with a reduced motor current or a heavy payload loses steps: lower the speed before you lower the current.

docs.title: 4. Installation
docs.text: Where to put the robot, how to fix it, what to connect, and the first power-on.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Installation site
  • Mounting the robot
  • Connecting
  • First power-on

Building the robot is the Build guide; wiring the control board inside the base is in the Control Board Manual.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
The robot needs three connections to run. They are on the back of the base.

Figure 4.3: The power (green), USB (blue) and E-stop (yellow and pink) connections, and the power button (red). Connection Connector Notes 24 V power GX16 2-pin From the 24 V 5 A supply. Mind the polarity when you wire your own cable: the board has no reverse-polarity protection USB USB type B To the PC. USB does not power the board E-stop Two screw terminals A normally closed contact between them. Open means stop

Plug the power supply into the mains through a switch within your reach, a switched socket strip for example: it is the stop that still works when the PC software has frozen (Emergency stop).

docs.title: The E-stop
docs.text:
The E-stop must be a normally closed contact: pressing it, unplugging it or cutting its wire opens the circuit, and all of these stop the robot, which is what you want. A normally open button does not work. The control board has two E-stop connectors on the same input, so a second button can be wired in series.

The kit's button comes with a printed housing and a PG7 cable gland. Emergency stop says what happens when it is pressed, and the Control Board Manual has the wiring diagram.

docs.title: The gripper
docs.text: An electric gripper (SSG-48, MSG) plugs into the M8 connector at the forearm, which carries 24 V and CAN: Electric grippers. Pneumatic tubes from the valve go to the two push-in fittings at the base: Pneumatics.

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text:
The two inputs, two outputs and their supply terminals are on the side of the control board, reachable through the base: Inputs and outputs.

Nothing else on the programming port

The 2×5-pin programming header next to the USB port is for the ST-Link programming adapter only. An ST-Link connected with plain jumper wires without the adapter has destroyed boards. See Firmware.

docs.title: First power-on
docs.text:
The first time, and every time after that:

  1. Check the E-stop is connected and released.
  2. Hold the arm by the forearm. The motors energise with a jolt, and until they do the arm is limp.
  3. Press the power button on the base. The 24 V stage switches on, each driver initialises with a click, six clicks, and the arm holds its position.
  4. Let go. The robot is now enabled, not homed, and waiting for the PC.

Check

Six clicks, the fan runs, and the arm holds when you let go. If not: If nothing happens.

Nothing moves until the PC software commands it. Start the commander software or the Python API's controller, connect, check the jog directions and home: the Quick start walks through it.

docs.title: What the button does
docs.text: The button is not a switch in the power line: it tells the firmware to turn the 24 V stage on, and the firmware keeps it on. A short press while the robot is on turns it off. The board stays powered, and turns itself on, as long as 3.3 V is present on the programming header, which is why a connected ST-Link keeps the robot on and the button useless: Switching on and off.

docs.title: If nothing happens
docs.text:
• No clicks, no fan: no 24 V. Check the supply, the GX16 cable and its polarity.
  • Clicks, but the PC software does not connect: the serial port name, or the board runs the test firmware. See Communication.
  • The board turned on by itself when the supply was plugged in: something supplies 3.3 V to the programming header, or the arm was moved while unpowered (Hazards).

docs.title: Installation site
docs.text:
• A rigid table or frame. The arm accelerates its 5.5 kg quickly; a wobbly table shakes and spoils the repeatability. An aluminium profile frame or a solid bench is right.
  • Clearance. The arm reaches 408 mm from the axis of joint 1 in every direction, plus the tool, and its elbow swings further back than the tool when it folds. Keep a free sphere of about 500 mm around the base, and nothing fragile in it. The simulator shows the sweep of a program before the robot runs it.
  • Room temperature, dry, dust-free. The base draws air through its fan over the stepper drivers.
  • The E-stop within reach of the person at the PC, and reachable from where someone would stand to load the robot.
  • Cables. The power, USB and E-stop cables leave the base at the back; route them so that nothing pulls on them and so that the arm cannot sweep over them.
  • Pneumatics. If you use the pneumatic gripper, a valve and an air supply at 5 to 7 bar near the base; check your gripper's rating (Pneumatics).
  • A mains switch within reach on the power supply's mains side, a switched socket strip for example: the stop for when the PC software has frozen (Emergency stop).

The Planning the cell page covers the safety side: who can reach the robot, guarding, and what the software can and cannot stop.

docs.title: Mounting the robot
docs.text:
An unanchored robot falls over

When the arm extends, the centre of gravity leaves the base. Never run PAROL6 free-standing, not even for a test.

docs.title: The base holes
docs.text:
Six holes in the base, spaced for 30×30 mm aluminium profiles. Bolt the base to a plate or a profile frame with M5 screws and T-nuts.

Figure 4.1: The six holes in the base.

docs.title: Clamps
docs.text: For a desk, clamp the base to the edge with two screw clamps over the base's rim. Check that the clamps do not interfere with the fan intake and the connectors at the back.

docs.title: A profile frame
docs.text:
The repository's STL/UTILITY folder has connectors_4_alu_profiles.STL, which prints a set of corner connectors for a frame of 30×30 profiles, as in the figure. You need M5 T-nuts, M5 × 12 mm screws for the connectors and M5 × 18 to 20 mm screws for the base.

Figure 4.2: PAROL6 on a 30×30 aluminium profile frame.

docs.title: Mounting plates
docs.text: The mounting plates folder of the repository has STEP files of a small and a big base plate, with the hole pattern, for a plate you have machined or cut.

docs.title: Orientation
docs.text: PAROL6 is designed to stand upright on its base. Wall and ceiling mounting are not supported: the payload, the motor currents and the speed limits are set for an upright arm, and with no brakes the arm would fall into the mount when powered off.

docs.title: 5. Operation
docs.text: How the robot is switched on and off, homed, jogged and run, what happens when something goes wrong, and how it is mastered.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Switching on and off
  • Homing
  • Jogging
  • Running programs
  • Errors and recovery
  • Mastering

Each page says what to do in the commander software and in the Python API; the details of either are in the Programming Guide.

docs.title: What the robot reports
docs.text: Every 10 ms the control board sends the PC the joints' positions and speeds, which joints are homed, the state of the inputs, outputs and E-stop, the gripper's status, and two error bytes reserved for the drivers' temperature and position flags. The PC software adds its own: inverse kinematics failures, limit violations, timing problems.

docs.title: The commander software
docs.text:
The response log shows what the robot and the program are doing and why a command was refused. The common entries:

Log Meaning What to do Robot disable; button or estop The E-stop is open, or Disable was pressed Release the E-stop; press Enable An inverse kinematics error The target pose has no solution, or lies past a singularity Change the pose or the approach; move in joint space to get near it A joint limit error The move would leave a joint's range Choose a reachable target Jogging stops in Cartesian mode A singularity Jog a joint away from it The time between commands rises above 10 ms The PC cannot keep the 100 Hz loop Close other programs; a faster PC (Communication)

Enable clears the errors and enables the robot; Clear error resets the homing state but does not re-enable a disabled robot; Disable stops the firmware from accepting motion commands while the motors keep holding.

docs.title: The Python API
docs.text: A refused command raises MotionError with a code, a cause and a remedy, from the controller's error catalog: IK_TARGET_UNREACHABLE, MOTN_NOT_HOMED, SYS_ESTOP_ACTIVE, SYS_SELF_COLLISION, MOTN_CANCELLED and the others on Errors. error() returns the current error, activity() what the robot is doing. After an E-stop is released, call reset(): it enables the firmware again, and until then the arm does not move. After stop() nothing needs clearing.

docs.title: After a collision or a stall
docs.text: The motors have lost steps and the arm is not where the software says. Stop the program, move the arm clear if it is trapped (disable it, or switch off with the forearm held), check the belts and the printed parts, and home again before anything else.

docs.title: After the arm fell
docs.text: Power was lost with the arm extended. Check every joint by hand for free movement, look at the belts and the couplers, switch on with the forearm held, and home.

docs.title: A joint moves the wrong way
docs.text: On a new build or after work on the wiring: stop at once. The direction is set per joint in the firmware (Firmware and first run); do not try to home until every joint jogs in the right direction.

docs.title: The gripper reports an error
docs.text: The electric grippers report their own errors through the robot: not calibrated, E-stop, timeout. The commander's Gripper tab has Clear gripper error and Calibrate gripper: clear the error first, then calibrate, and wait until the calibration has finished before the first move. The Python API's tool.calibrate() calibrates but has no clear (SSG-48, MSG). The gripper manuals explain each error.

docs.title: Homing
docs.text: After power-up the robot does not know where its joints are: the motors count steps, and the count starts at zero wherever the arm happens to stand. Homing gives each joint a reference by driving it to its limit switch or sensor, then moving a known number of steps to the after-homing pose. It must be done after every power-up, and again after a collision, a stall or any move by hand.

docs.title: Before you press Home
docs.text:
• The arm can move freely to every limit: nothing on the table in the way, no cable caught.
  • The tool is mounted: joint 5 homes against the tool's feature on the SSG-48 and the pneumatic gripper, and the homing offset in the firmware matches the tool (Joint 5 and the tool, SSG-48).
  • Joint 6 stands so that it finds its sensor within one turn in the negative direction, with the cables and tubes not already wound up. The figure shows the pose: the gripper as drawn, the sensor (blue) and the homing pin (red); joint 6 turns along the green arrow.
  • You are at the E-stop.
Figure 5.1: Joint 6 before homing: the sensor, the homing pin and the direction of rotation.

docs.title: The sequence
docs.text:
The firmware runs the sequence; the PC only starts it and watches.

flowchart TD
    S([Home]) --> A[Joints 1, 2 and 3 drive together to their sensor and switches]
    A --> B[Each backs off about a thousand steps and approaches again slowly:<br>the second trigger is the reference]
    B --> C[Joints 1, 2 and 3 move to their after-homing positions]
    C --> D[Joint 4: the same against its inductive sensor, then its after-homing position]
    D --> E[Joint 6 turns in the negative direction until its sensor sees the pin,<br>backs off, re-approaches, moves on so that joint 5 can home]
    E --> F[Joint 5 homes against its switch]
    F --> G[Joints 5 and 6 move to their after-homing positions together]
    G --> H([Every counter set to its after-homing value: six joints homed])
  1. Joints 1, 2 and 3 move together toward their switches: joint 1 to its inductive sensor, joints 2 and 3 to their limit switches. Each stops when it triggers.
  2. Each backs off, 850 steps on joint 1 and 1050 on joints 2 and 3, and approaches again slowly, and the position where it triggers the second time is the reference: the first hit may have pressed the switch too far.
  3. Joints 1, 2 and 3 move from the reference to their after-homing positions (13500, 19588 and 23020 steps away).
  4. Joint 4 does the same against its inductive sensor (backing off 1550 steps) and moves to its after-homing position.
  5. Joint 6 turns in the negative direction until its sensor sees the homing pin, backs off, re-approaches, and moves on to the position from which joint 5 can home.
  6. Joint 5 homes against its switch, and joints 5 and 6 move to their after-homing positions together: joint 5 by j5_homing_offset, joint 6 back to the point where its sensor triggered.
  7. The firmware sets every joint's counter to its after-homing value (standby_position in the firmware), and reports all six joints as homed.

A video of a correct homing: Homing reference. It takes about half a minute. The result is the after-homing pose: the standby pose turned 90° about joint 1, with joint 1 at +90° (Joint limits and directions).

Commander softwarePython API

Press Home. The response log reports the joints as they home; the position display and the simulator are right once all six are homed.

rbt.home(wait=True)
The first home() after power-up runs the referencing sequence. A later home() on a referenced robot is a planned, collision-checked joint move back to the after-homing pose; home(calibrate=True) runs the sequence again. Planned motion is refused with MOTN_NOT_HOMED until the robot is referenced.

docs.title: If it goes wrong
docs.text: Press the E-stop when a joint grinds at its end without stopping: its switch does not trigger. Joints 1, 4 and 6 use inductive sensors whose LED lights when they see metal; a sensor that does not light needs its trigger screw adjusted. If joint 6 keeps turning, its homing pin is not where the sensor looks. Homing failures has the cases.

docs.title: Mastering
docs.text: A homed robot stands within a few steps of the after-homing pose. The exact number of steps from each switch to the witness marks differs between builds; Mastering says how to measure and set it.

docs.title: Jogging
docs.text: Jogging moves one joint, or the tool along one axis, for as long as you hold a button or repeat a command. It is how you check a new robot, teach a pose and get out of trouble.

docs.title: Joint jog
docs.text:
Each joint has a pair of arrows in the commander's Joint jog menu: the left arrow is the positive direction, the right arrow negative, as in Joint limits and directions. The speed slider sets the speed as a percentage of the commander's jog maximum, which is lower than the speed a program may use (Speeds). A jog stops at the joint limit.

Python API 

rbt.jog_j(0, speed=0.3, duration=0.5)               # joint index 0 = J1, 30 % speed, 0.5 s
rbt.jog_j(joints=[1, 2], speeds=[0.2, -0.2], duration=1.0)
A jog command runs for duration and the arm brakes to rest when no newer jog arrives; a GUI repeats it while the button is held. Joints are indexed from 0 in the API.

docs.title: Cartesian jog
docs.text:
The tool moves along X, Y or Z, or rotates about them, in the world frame (WRF, fixed to the base) or the tool frame (TRF, fixed to the tool). The commander's Cartesian jog menu has the six pairs of arrows and the WRF/TRF switch; a jog in the tool frame moves the tool along its own axes, which is the natural way to approach a part.

Python API 
rbt.jog_l("WRF", "X", speed=0.2, duration=0.5)
rbt.jog_l("TRF", axes=["Z", "RZ"], speeds_list=[0.2, 0.1], duration=0.5)

A Cartesian jog needs a homed robot, and it can run into a singularity, where the planner cannot find joint speeds for the tool's motion: the commander stops the jog, and the Python API refuses it. Jog a joint away from the singular pose and continue (Configurations and singularities).

docs.title: Jogging a robot that is not homed
docs.text:
Joint jog works before homing: it is how you check the directions on a new build. The positions shown are meaningless until the robot is homed, and a Cartesian jog is refused.

Both programs still check each jog against the joint limits, with a position count that starts at 0 when the board is switched on. That count puts joint 2 past its positive limit and joints 3 and 6 at or below their negative limits, so until the robot is homed:

  • joint 2 jogs only in its negative direction (the right arrow);
  • joints 3 and 6 jog only in their positive direction (the left arrow);
  • joints 1, 4 and 5 jog both ways.

A refused jog does not move: the commander logs Error: Robot jog -> Position out of range, the Python API stops the joint before it starts.

Warning

Before homing, the limits are checked against a count that does not match the arm, so they do not protect the joint: nothing stops it at its real limit except the printed blocker. Jog briefly and slowly.

docs.title: Mastering
docs.text: Homing brings each joint to its switch and then a fixed number of steps to the after-homing pose. That number is in the firmware, measured on the reference robot. Printers and parts differ, so on your robot the homed pose may be off by a fraction of a degree per joint. Mastering measures the difference and corrects the number, so that a homed robot stands exactly at its witness marks.

docs.title: Witness marks
docs.text:
Holes in neighbouring links that line up when the joint stands where homing should leave it, in the after-homing pose (90°, −90°, 180°, 0°, 0°, 180°): a pin pushed through them proves the pose. PAROL6 has them on every joint.

Figure 5.2: Witness marks of PAROL6.

docs.title: The procedure
docs.text:
1. Home the robot.
  2. For each joint, jog it in small steps until the pin fits through its witness marks. Jog at the lowest speed and read the joint's position from the commander's position display or rbt.angles().
  3. Convert the angle you jogged by to motor steps with the joint's ratio (Drives, ratios and resolution), or read the step count from the firmware's telemetry.
  4. For joints 1 to 4: in motor_init.cpp, add that number of steps to the joint's homed_position (subtract if you jogged in the negative direction), upload the firmware, and home again. The pin should now fit without jogging. Joints 5 and 6 work differently, below.
/// @brief Number of steps from when the limit switch is hit to the standby position
Joint__->homed_position = 13500;   // joint 1: raise or lower by the steps you measured

The values of the reference robot are on Firmware parameters.

docs.title: Joint 5 and the tool
docs.text: Joint 5 homes against a feature of the tool, so its number depends on the tool: 8900 steps with the pneumatic gripper holder and 8035 with the SSG-48, set as j5_homing_offset in main.cpp. Master joint 5 by changing that value, not its homed_position. A custom tool needs its own value, found the same way.

docs.title: Joint 6
docs.text: Joint 6 has no offset to master in firmware 1. Its homed_position (15900) is only the position from which joint 5 homes: when joint 5 is done, joint 6 turns back to the point where its sensor saw the homing pin, and that point is its after-homing position. If joint 6 does not line up with its witness marks after homing, move its sensor or its homing pin.

docs.title: When to master again
docs.text: After replacing a belt, a switch, a sensor or a printed part of a joint, or when the robot's absolute accuracy matters more than its repeatability. The repeatability does not depend on mastering: a homed robot returns to the same place every time, whether or not that place is exactly the witness mark.

docs.title: Running programs
docs.text: A program is a list of moves, delays, I/O and gripper commands. PAROL6 runs programs in two ways.

docs.title: RBTscript in the commander software
docs.text:
The commander's Program window takes an RBTscript program: one command per line, MoveJoint, MoveCart, MoveCartRelTRF, Delay, Output, Gripper, with Begin() and End() or Loop() around it. The command list next to the window inserts a command with the robot's current pose as its arguments, which is how you teach points: jog to the pose, click the command. Start runs the program, Stop halts it.

Begin()
MoveJoint(90,-90,180,0,0,180,t=3)
MoveCart(0,263,242,90,0,90,t=2)
Output(1,HIGH)
Delay(1)
Output(1,LOW)
End()

RBTscript has the language and Examples has programs to start from. Programs are plain text files you can keep and share.

docs.title: Python with the Python API
docs.text:
A Python script that calls the client is a program: every motion call queues a move on the controller, and the script waits for it or not, as you choose.

from parol6 import RobotClient

with RobotClient() as rbt:
    rbt.home(wait=True)
    rbt.select_tool("SSG-48")
    rbt.tool.calibrate()
    rbt.delay(2)                  # the SSG-48 needs about 3 s; calibrate() waits only 2 s
    rbt.move_j([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180], speed=0.5)
    rbt.move_l([0, 263, 200, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.3)
    rbt.tool.close(speed=0.5, current=0.4)
    rbt.move_l([0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.3)
    rbt.tool.open()

The Python API also runs programs written for other tools, and from other machines: the controller accepts commands over the network from any client, so a program can run on a laptop while the controller runs on the PC at the robot. The Python API is the guide.

docs.title: Simulate first
docs.text: Both programs have a simulator. The commander opens its 3D window with the GUI and mirrors the robot; the Python API's controller runs with simulator(True) or the DryRunRobotClient without hardware, through the same kinematics and collision checks. Run a new program in the simulator at full speed, then on the robot at low speed.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: The commander's speed slider scales jogging only; a program's speed is in its moves, v= and a= or t=. The Python API takes a speed fraction per move and set_execution_speed() scales the queue while it runs; pause() and resume() hold and continue it.

docs.title: Stopping a program
docs.text:
• Stop in the commander, or stop() in the API: the current move is cancelled, the queue cleared, the robot stays enabled and holding.
  • The E-stop: the robot is disabled and the program or the queue is stopped; in the Python API, call reset() after releasing it (Emergency stop).
  • Closing the software: stop the program first. The firmware has no timeout: it keeps executing the last packet it received until the next one arrives. After a move to a position the joints stop near that target and hold.

When the PC stops sending during a jog

If the commander closes, crashes or loses the USB connection while a joint jogs (in joint or Cartesian jog), the firmware keeps that joint turning at its jog speed until it reaches its blocker. Programs that use speed tracking (speed as the last argument of a move) behave the same way. Use the mains switch of the power supply (Emergency stop).

docs.title: Switching on
docs.text:
1. E-stop connected and released; power supply on; USB to the PC.
  2. Hold the arm by the forearm.
  3. Press the power button on the base. The fan starts, the six drivers initialise with a click each, and the motors hold the arm.
  4. Start the PC software and connect. The robot is enabled and not homed; nothing moves until you command it.

The firmware energises the motors at the moment the 24 V stage comes up, whether or not a PC is connected, and holds them with the holding current from then on.

docs.title: Switching off
docs.text:
Not while it moves

Never switch the robot off while it is running a program or carrying something. If it behaves unexpectedly, press the E-stop; if the E-stop has no effect, switch off the power supply. The power button is the last resort, and only with the arm held.

  1. Stop the program and bring the arm to the parked pose, folded in over the base, where it has the least distance to fall. In the commander, Park writes a three-line program into the program window that moves there; press Start to run it. In the Python API, rbt.move_j([90, -144.683, 108.171, 2.222, 25.003, 180], speed=0.3) moves to the same pose.
  2. Disconnect in the software, or stop the controller.
  3. Hold the forearm.
  4. Press the power button. The motors release at once and the arm goes limp in your hand.

docs.title: The button and the programming adapter
docs.text: The button does not switch the power line: it tells the firmware to turn the 24 V stage on and off. The microcontroller itself runs from 3.3 V derived from that stage, or from the programming header. While an ST-Link or the programming adapter is connected, the board has 3.3 V, turns on by itself when the supply is plugged in, and cannot be switched off with the button. Upload firmware with the 24 V supply disconnected, then unplug the adapter, then plug the supply in and press the button (Firmware).

docs.title: After a power failure
docs.text: The arm has fallen. Check that nothing is damaged and nothing is trapped under it, switch on as above, and home before anything else: the position is lost.

docs.title: 6. Peripherals
docs.text:
Everything the robot talks to besides the PC and the tool: switches and sensors on its inputs, valves and lamps on its outputs, the air for the pneumatic gripper, and the CAN bus for the electric grippers.

Figure 6.1: The control board's connections to the outside world.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Inputs and outputs
  • Pneumatics
  • CAN bus

The electrical details of the connectors are in the Control Board Manual.

docs.title: CAN bus
docs.text:
The control board has a CAN bus for the electric grippers, wired to the M8 connector at the forearm. The board is the master: it sends the gripper the command from the PC's packet every cycle (a move, a calibrate, a clear error, or an empty status poll when nothing changed) and relays the gripper's answer back to the PC.

  • Bit rate: 1 Mbit/s, the grippers' rate.
  • Node ID: the gripper's CAN ID, 0 as shipped; the PC packet carries the ID the board addresses, so a gripper with another ID works if the software is told.
  • Termination: 120 Ω at each end of the bus. At the board end, the CAN1 JUMPER connects the board's 120 Ω resistor when it is on; at the other end, the gripper has its own termination switch, on as shipped (CAN bus).

A second CAN controller is on the board, but its transceiver is not populated: CAN 2 is for your own experiments. More axes on the bus, a seventh axis or a second gripper, are not supported by the firmware or the software yet; the protocol the grippers speak is documented in the STEPFOC and Spectral Micro references for anyone who wants to extend it.

The electrical side is in CAN bus of the Control Board Manual.

docs.title: Inputs and outputs
docs.text: The control board has two isolated inputs and two isolated outputs on screw terminals at the side of the board, reachable through the base. They are isolated from the robot's electronics through optocouplers, and they share a supply that you choose.

docs.title: The supply
docs.text:
• Isolated: connect an external supply's negative to GND_SEL and positive to HV_SEL. The inputs and outputs then work at that voltage, 12 or 24 V (the inputs need at least 12 V), and a fault on them cannot reach the robot.
  • Not isolated: link the robot's own 24 V and GND to HV_SEL and GND_SEL. Simpler, and the valve of the pneumatic gripper is usually wired this way. A 2 A fuse protects the outputs in this mode.
Figure 6.2: Isolated supply wiring. Figure 6.3: Non-isolated wiring from the robot's 24 V.

The E-stop is not part of this: it is wired to the robot's own supply whichever option you choose.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Switches, push buttons, light barriers and sensors. A switch goes between HV_SEL and IN1 or IN2; a three-wire sensor takes HV_SEL and GND_SEL for its supply and gives its signal to the input. Input voltage 12 to 50 V, 24 V nominal.

The robot reports the inputs in every packet: the commander's IO tab shows them, and the Python API's io() returns [in1, in2, out1, out2, estop]. RBTscript's Input() has no action yet: a program stops on it (Known issues).

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Relays, valves, lamps, small actuators, up to 0.5 A each (1 A peak), 48 V maximum. A load goes between GND_SEL and OUT1 or OUT2; the output switches it to the supply. An inductive load, a valve or a relay coil, gets a flyback diode across it.

RBTscriptPython API 
Output(1,HIGH)
Output(1,LOW)

Only output 1: in the current commander version Output(2,...) is refused by a bug in its check and stops the program (RBTscript).

rbt.write_io(0, 1)       # output 1 high (logical index 0)
rbt.write_io(1, 0)

The commander's IO tab switches the outputs by hand.

Figure 6.4: The IO tab of the commander software.

docs.title: Pneumatics
docs.text: Two 4 mm tubes run inside the arm from the push-in fittings at the base to the forearm, where the pneumatic or vacuum gripper connects. A 5/2 solenoid valve at the base, driven by an output, switches the air.

docs.title: Pressure
docs.text: 5 to 7 bar; check your gripper's rating, and stay below the lowest rating of the gripper, the valve and the fittings. The tubes and fittings are standard 4 mm pneumatic parts.

docs.title: The valve
docs.text: A 5/2 valve, 24 V coil, 4 mm ports: one port from the compressor, two to the base fittings, the exhausts open. The coil goes between GND_SEL and OUTPUT1 (Inputs and outputs). Which of the two outputs is pressurised when the coil is off decides whether the gripper is normally open or normally closed: swap the two tubes to change it.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text: The arm's tubes run inside it from the base to the push-in fittings on the forearm; they are one reason for the one-turn rule of the joints. From the forearm fittings, the gripper's own tubes cross joints 5 and 6 outside the arm, like an electric gripper's cable: give them enough slack for the range you use, since they, not the flange, limit joint 6. Outside the base, give the tubes a loop so the arm cannot pull them.

docs.title: A vacuum gripper
docs.text:
Needs one line only: block the valve's second port (Vacuum gripper).

In the Python API, a pneumatic or vacuum tool's open() switches output 1 high and close() switches it low, whatever the tubing does: lay the tubes so the two match (Pneumatic gripper).

docs.title: 7. Maintenance
docs.text:
PAROL6 needs little: belts that stay tight, set screws that stay put, switches that trigger. Check them at the intervals below and after any collision.

Interval What Before each session The E-stop works (press it with the robot enabled); nothing in the workspace; the cables and tubes free Monthly, or every 50 hours Inspection: belts, couplers, switches, fan, printed parts After a collision, a fall or a lost step Inspection, then Checking the homing When a belt slips or a joint is loose Belts, Couplers and threadlocker

Before any work inside the base, unplug the supply and touch earthed metal: static electricity damages the control board and its drivers.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Inspection
  • Belts
  • Couplers and threadlocker
  • Checking the homing

docs.title: Belts
docs.text: Belts drive joints 1, 3, 4 and 5. Over time they stretch a little and the joint loses stiffness; a belt that slips a tooth loses the robot's position.

docs.title: Tension
docs.text: The reference is the belt tension video: in it, maximum hand force is applied to the belt, and that is the tension to aim for on joints 3 and 5. Joints 1 and 4 take slightly less. A belt is tensioned by adding or moving the small tension bearings (3 × 8 × 4 mm and 3 × 10 × 4 mm) that press on its back; if a belt is not tight enough, add another bearing as in the photos. You may or may not need a tensioner on a given joint: it depends on your belts and printed parts, so fit one only where the belt is not tight enough without it.

docs.title: Joint 5 belt
docs.text: Figure 7.1: Joint 5 belt and tensioner.

docs.title: Joint 4 belt
docs.text: Figure 7.2: Joint 4 belt and tensioner.

docs.title: Joint 3 belt
docs.text: Figure 7.3: Joint 3 belt and tensioner.

docs.title: Joint 1 belt
docs.text: Figure 7.4: Joint 1 belt and tensioner.

docs.title: Grease
docs.text: A thin film of grease on the belts' teeth reduces noise and wear. Reapply when it dries out.

docs.title: Replacement
docs.text:
Joint Belt Joint 1 HTD3 396 mm, 6 mm wide Joint 3 HTD3 342 mm Joint 4 HTD3 201 mm Joint 5 HTD3 246 mm

Replacing a belt means opening the joint as in the assembly manual; afterwards home the robot and check the witness marks, and master if they do not line up.

docs.title: Couplers and threadlocker
docs.text:
The motor shafts, the gearbox outputs and the joint 6 shaft are joined by couplers and pulleys with set screws on flats or keys. Vibration loosens set screws; a loose one lets the motor turn without the joint, and the robot loses its position without noticing.

  • If a joint starts to slip, or its position drifts between homings, find the set screw, tighten it, and apply blue (medium) threadlocker. Do not move the robot for 24 hours while it cures.
  • Put a screw on the key as well as on the flat where the part has both.
  • Apply threadlocker to every metal-to-metal screw joint on the robot: the motor mounts, the gearbox flanges, the bearing clamps. Printed parts and brass inserts do not need it, and the solvent in some threadlockers attacks plastic: keep it on the metal.
  • Never use red (permanent) threadlocker; the parts cannot be taken apart again without heat.

After tightening a coupler, home the robot and check the witness marks.

docs.title: Checking the homing
docs.text:
Homing is the robot's only position reference, so check it after any mechanical work, after a collision, and whenever the robot's accuracy seems off.

  1. Home the robot and watch each joint: it must reach its switch, back off, re-approach slowly, and move on. A joint that grinds at a stop, or re-approaches at full speed, has a switch problem (Homing failures).
  2. At the end, try the pin at the witness marks of each joint (Mastering). It should slide in, or nearly. A joint that is off by more than a degree was knocked, slipped, or its switch moved.
  3. Home three times in a row and compare the witness marks each time. The pose should repeat exactly: if it does not, the switch or the sensor triggers inconsistently, or something in the joint moves.
  4. Jog to a taught pose from a program and check that the tool is where it was taught.

A joint that homes repeatably but to the wrong place is mastered; a joint that does not repeat is repaired.

docs.title: Inspection
docs.text:
With the robot switched off and the supply unplugged:

  • Belts (joints 1, 3, 4, 5): press each with a finger through its cover opening; it should give a little and spring back. A belt that sags or that you can push against the pulley needs tensioning (Belts). Look for frayed edges and missing teeth.
  • Couplers and set screws: hold the output of each joint and try to turn the motor side; any play that is not the gearbox's backlash is a loose set screw (Couplers and threadlocker).
  • Limit switches and sensors: press each switch lever; it should click. The inductive sensors' LEDs light when a screw head comes near.
  • Printed parts: cracks at screw bosses and bearing seats, especially on the elbow and the upper arm, and any warping of the forearm from heat.
  • Cables and tubes: chafing where the arm's cables pass through the joints, and where the gripper's cable and tubes cross joints 5 and 6 from the forearm; the gripper cable's connector tight.
  • The fan: turning when the robot is on, and the intake free of dust. A stopped fan overheats the drivers.
  • The base: the mounting bolts tight, the E-stop button firm in its housing.

Then switch on, home, and watch the homing: each joint should back off and re-approach its switch cleanly, and the pose at the end should match the witness marks (Checking the homing).

docs.title: Cleaning
docs.text: Clean the robot switched off and unplugged. Wipe the printed parts with a dry or slightly damp cloth; use no solvents on them, and never spray anything into the base, where the control board and the fan are open to it. Clear dust from the fan intake with a soft brush or a vacuum cleaner, not with compressed air, which drives the dust into the board.

docs.title: 8. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• By symptom: the robot does not turn on, does not connect, moves wrong, stops, makes noise
  • Homing failures
  • Communication: serial ports, the 100 Hz loop, slow PCs
  • Known issues: the faults in the firmware and software that are known and not yet fixed, and what to do until they are

For the control board itself, see the Control Board Manual's troubleshooting; for the software, Programming troubleshooting. When you ask for help, Report a problem says what to include.

docs.title: By symptom
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause What to do Nothing happens at the power button No 24 V; polarity; the button cable Check the supply's LED, the GX16 cable, the JST button cable on the board The board turns on by itself when the supply is plugged in 3.3 V on the programming header (an ST-Link or the adapter is connected); the arm was moved while unpowered Unplug the adapter; move an unpowered robot slowly The robot cannot be switched off with the button The same 3.3 V Unplug the programming adapter Clicks on power-up, but the PC does not connect Wrong serial port; the test firmware is on the board; Linux permissions Communication A joint jogs the wrong way Direction not set for that joint in the firmware; a motor's wires swapped A joint turns the wrong way A joint does not move at all Driver not seated or faulty; motor connector; the joint is at its blocker The test firmware: its driver report at power-on, and whether the motor turns with the others (The test firmware) A joint grinds at its end during homing Its switch or sensor does not trigger E-stop; Homing failures Joint 6 keeps spinning during homing The homing pin is not where the sensor looks E-stop; set the joint 6 pose as in Homing The pose after homing is off by a few degrees on one joint A loose coupler, a slipped belt, a moved switch Couplers, Belts, then Mastering The robot's position drifts during a program Lost steps: too fast, too heavy, a collision, a reduced current Lower the speed; check the payload; home again A joint hums or squeals and does not hold A driver in error, a lost phase The test firmware's driver report at power-on (its fault flags); check the motor cable Cartesian jogging stops by itself A singularity Jog a joint away (Configurations and singularities) A pose from the GUI cannot be reached by MoveCart The inverse kinematics finds no solution along the straight line Move in joint space; choose another orientation The robot stutters while moving The PC misses the 10 ms cycle Communication The forearm is hot Hours of motion at the default currents Currents and temperatures The gripper does nothing Not calibrated; an error latched; the cable Calibrate, clear the error; the gripper's manual The E-stop has no effect The PC software is frozen Switch off the power supply; see Emergency stop

docs.title: The serial port
docs.text:
The control board appears on the PC as a serial port over USB: COMx on Windows, /dev/ttyACMx on Linux and /dev/cu.usbmodem… on macOS. The commander takes COM5 or ttyACM0 in its connection field; the Python API's controller takes --serial COM5 or --serial /dev/ttyACM0, or finds the port from PAROL6_COM_PORT.

  • Windows: Device Manager, Ports, shows the number. If the board is missing, try another cable or port; the board enumerates only when it has power.
  • Linux: ls /dev/ttyACM*. Permission denied: sudo chmod 666 /dev/ttyACM0, or add yourself to the dialout group and log in again.
  • Connect fails the first time in the commander: press Connect again; two or three tries are normal.
  • The port is busy: another program has it, often a previous instance of the controller.

docs.title: The test firmware answers, the main firmware does not
docs.text: A board from the shop carries the test firmware, which talks in text. Upload the main firmware (Firmware).

docs.title: The 100 Hz loop
docs.text:
The PC must send a packet every 10 ms. The commander prints Time between 2 commands in ms in its terminal output; it should sit near 0.010. The number is in seconds, despite the label: 0.010 is 10 ms. If it is often higher, the robot stutters and the position tracking suffers.

  • Close browsers and other heavy programs; disable power saving on the USB port and the CPU.
  • A faster PC: six cores from 2017 or newer (What you need).
  • The Python API's controller logs loop overbudget by +N% when its loop runs late, and shows the figures in loop_stats(); it also accepts a lower PAROL6_CONTROL_RATE_HZ, at the cost of smoothness, and runs worse with TRACE or DEBUG logging on.

docs.title: The connection drops
docs.text: A USB cable without ferrite near the motors, a hub, or a long cable: use a short, shielded cable straight into the PC. When packets stop, the firmware keeps executing the last one: after a move to a position the joints stop near that target and hold, but a joint that was jogging in the commander keeps turning until it reaches its blocker. Keep the mains switch of the power supply within reach (Emergency stop).

docs.title: Homing failures
docs.text: Stop with the E-stop first; a joint driven against its stop strips a belt or cracks a part.

docs.title: A joint does not stop at its switch
docs.text:
• Joints 2, 3, 5 use mechanical limit switches. Check that the lever is pressed by the moving part, that the switch clicks, and that it is wired to 24 V and its signal terminal (polarity does not matter). The test firmware's #LIMIT shows the state live.
  • Joints 1, 4, 6 use inductive sensors that detect a screw head. The sensor's LED lights when it sees metal. If it does not light as the joint passes, adjust the trigger screw closer; the 4 mm sensors see about 1 to 2 mm. Wiring: brown 24 V, blue GND, black signal.
  • A switch on the wrong joint's terminal: wire each switch and sensor to the terminal the wiring diagram shows for its joint; the test firmware's #LIMIT shows which input changes when you press a switch.

docs.title: A joint stops too early
docs.text: The switch triggers before the joint reaches it: a wire shorted, a sensor too close to a screw it should not see, or a switch lever caught. Also the reason a homed pose is far off on one joint.

docs.title: Joint 6 turns more than a turn
docs.text: Its sensor never sees the homing pin. Before homing, turn joint 6 by hand so that the pin is just before the sensor in the direction of rotation (Homing), and check the sensor's gap.

docs.title: Joint 5 does not reach its switch
docs.text: The tool's homing feature is missing or in the wrong place, or the firmware's j5_homing_offset is for another tool (Your own tool).

docs.title: The homed pose does not match the witness marks
docs.text: By a fraction of a degree: master the joint. By more: the joint slipped, a belt or coupler, or the switch moved. Inspect, then master.

docs.title: Homing never finishes in the software
docs.text: The PC lost the packet stream, or the firmware is waiting for a joint that does not report. Check the log, press Clear error or reset(), and home again.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text: The faults in PAROL6's firmware and software that are known and not yet fixed, and what to do until they are. The pages that describe each part say the same where it matters; this page collects them in one place. Which versions work together is in Versions and compatibility.

docs.title: Control board firmware
docs.text:
Seen in: release 1.

What happens What to do More KI-1 Enforces the joint limits of the earlier robot model, which differ from those in these pages; a target between the two is accepted. Keep to the limits in the Joint limits table. Joint limits

docs.title: Control board test firmware
docs.text:
Seen in: release 1.

What happens What to do More KI-8 Enables all six drivers when it boots and turns every motor slowly, without a command, with no limits and no homing, until the power is switched off; no command stops them. Run it with the arm free to move or the motors unmounted, never on a robot folded against its stops. The test firmware KI-9 Most command names the parser knows (#STATUS, #STEP1 to #STEP6, #FLASH, #CAN) are answered with Unknown command: only #IO, #LIMIT, #STOP and #start do something. Use the four commands that work; CAN has its own test program. Test firmware commands

docs.title: Commander software
docs.text:
Seen in: main branch, 2025-09-23.

What happens What to do More KI-2 Enforces the joint limits of the earlier robot model, and computes with its dimensions (a5 = 176.35 mm, the pneumatic gripper's a6 = 62.8 mm), so its Cartesian positions are off by up to about 0.65 mm. Keep to the limits in the Joint limits table; teach the poses that need accuracy on the robot. Kinematics KI-3 Output(2,HIGH) and Output(2,LOW) are refused by a bug in the program check (Invalid Output() command), and the program stops. Use output 1 in commander programs, or switch output 2 from the Python API. RBTscript, I/O KI-4 SpeedJoint(), Input() and Home() pass the program check but have no action: the program stops on that line until you press Stop. Leave them out of programs; home with the Home button before you start a program. RBTscript, SpeedJoint and SpeedCart KI-5 SpeedCart(), Get_data and Timeouts are in the command menu but fail the program check: a program that contains one is refused. Leave them out of programs. RBTscript, SpeedJoint and SpeedCart KI-6 A move's profile written in quotes ("trap") or as func=trap is ignored without a message, and the move gets the default profile. Write the bare word, trap or poly, as the last argument. RBTscript KI-7 The Cartesian rotation jog buttons do nothing in the world frame (WRF). Rotate in the tool frame (TRF), the default. The GUI

docs.title: v0.8.1 — 2026-09-20
docs.text: A patch on v0.8.0: PR #51, the Cartesian streaming executor. No API changes.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• MOVECART and SERVOL hold their straight line. Ruckig's synchronization was never set, so it defaulted to Time — the six tangent components only finish together, each taking its own time-optimal route there, and the tangent bows. The executor now runs under Phase, one shared profile for all six.
  • A repeated target no longer costs that synchronization. A servo stream sets the same target every tick, and each re-plan drops to time synchronization unless the current velocity and acceleration line up exactly with the fresh profile; once out of phase the state drifts further out and the next tick fails too. Setting a target Ruckig is already tracking is now a no-op. On a 160 mm diagonal: 4.7 mm off the line before, 0.000 mm after.
  • The speed ceilings are TCP speeds again. Ruckig bounds each component on its own, so an isotropic envelope let a diagonal run the resultant up to sqrt(3) times the configured limit — 1.35x as measured. The per-component ceilings are now scaled by the motion direction's largest component over its norm, and the same move peaks at exactly the 0.160 m/s jog ceiling.

docs.title: v0.8.0 — 2026-09-19
docs.text: Everything since v0.7.0: PRs #41–#48, the PAROL6 side of waldoctl v0.14.0's skill runtime, full TCP calibration, bounded I/O, execution speed, demonstration metadata, held-object geometry and supervised restart. Pre-1.0, so breaking changes bump the minor.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
• The waldoctl pin moves v0.12.0 → v0.14.0. set_tcp_transform/tcp_transform and set_execution_speed/pause/resume are required of every client there and implemented here.
  • Completion waits query the exact command result (#47, #48), and client and controller must both speak the new query. A controller session change during a wait raises ConnectionError; unknown, cancelled and expired results stay unconfirmed instead of passing for success, and replies to timed-out queries are filtered by response type.
  • TCP queries fail explicitly when the controller does not answer (#43) rather than returning a stale value.
  • Unconfirmed blocking motion completion raises TimeoutError (#45); the queued motion stays until it completes or is stopped.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
• Python skills run on the connected client (#41). Decorated skills go through the existing synchronous connection and event loop, can use the typed PAROL6 async client internally, compose nested calls, and run unchanged under Commander's stepping wrapper. Live and dry-run clients advertise their skill capabilities. Stopping a planned trajectory now clears the segment player's activity, so status no longer sits at EXECUTING after a cancel.
  • Gripper skills discover PAROL6 gripper support on the live client and native preview (#42); the preview tool exposes its key and type as metadata, so a requirement check cannot dispatch a command. Streaming updates preserve unread configuration, query and stop packets across a polling batch boundary.

docs.title: Setup and calibration
docs.text:
• Full TCP transforms through planning and readback (#43). Translation and intrinsic XYZ orientation are queued, applied and confirmed before use; earlier queued motion keeps its frame, cancelled corrections do not leak into planning, and a tool/variant change clears the correction. The XYZ API stays and clears user rotation. Tool status reports its applied variant, so a calibration cannot silently bind to different jaws.
  • Bounded digital I/O (#44). Reads and writes take a per-call deadline covering endpoint setup and retries; a missing read returns None, an unconfirmed write raises TimeoutError, and neither is mistaken for cancellation. Both facades advertise io.digital; dry-run output writes use logical indices and report dispatch errors.

docs.title: Motion
docs.text:
• Queued execution speed and explicit pause/resume (#45). set_execution_speed(0.1..1.0) retimes the planned joint path; pause() decelerates to a hold with the queue retained and resume() continues at the selected speed, and changing speed while paused keeps the hold. Rate changes are checked against acceleration derived from the emitted positions, with preallocated buffers in the control loop; queued dwell pauses, while jog and servo-stream timing stay separate. Preview retimes durations and reports paused operations as unresolved. Physical transition tuning is unverified.
  • Held-object geometry under the flange (#47). Only declared contact pairs are exempt; attach/detach requires confirmed whole-world application and invalid contact names keep the previous geometry. Reference or controller-context changes invalidate declarations and gate arm motion until explicit reconciliation or removal. The controller retains 1024 successful indices, including every command consumed by a blend.

docs.title: Status surface
docs.text:
• Session and timing metadata on every status frame (#46): a nonzero session id, publication sequence and monotonic snapshot timestamp, so a client can record observation cadence and detect a controller restart. Missing metadata is explicitly unavailable. The offline client's no-tool identity matches the native controller.
  • Queue readback includes accepted commands still waiting for planning or paused (#48), and clears completed or cancelled indices, so a supervised restart can tell whether the controller still has pending work. Restart detection also watches status broadcasts when the command socket goes quiet after a peer reset.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: • interpolatepy is gone. Both profiles it supplied were only ever asked for rest-to-rest motion, so the trapezoidal and quintic curves are now evaluated here in closed form, across a numpy array rather than one Python call per sample. Positions match the previous output to within a thousandth of a motor step. This also removes a compiled dependency that, as of its 3.3.0, ships no Windows or Python 3.14 wheels.

docs.title: v0.7.0 — 2026-09-04
docs.text: Everything since 0.3.2, the last release. Four tags landed in between without notes, so this collects them. Pre-1.0, so breaking changes bump the minor.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
• RobotError comes from waldoctl rather than being defined here. A frontend represents a refusal the same way whichever backend raised it. It is an exception now, not a frozen dataclass, so a client can raise it as-is; anything that built one positionally or called dataclasses.replace on it needs updating. Tool-error attribution rebuilds the error from its wire form for exactly that reason.
  • stop, estop and reset replace halt and resume, and a stop cancels the whole motion pipeline rather than just the active command.
  • home(calibrate=) replaces the separate CALIBRATE command. Unhomed, or with calibrate=True, the arm runs the full end-stop referencing sequence; already homed, it takes a planned collision-checked move back to standby.
  • Planned motion is refused while unhomed. Jogging stays available.
  • The waldoctl pin moves v0.7.0 → v0.12.0, which removes the Plane keep-out shape. Persisted worlds containing a plane now raise on load.

docs.title: Status surface
docs.text:
• The control loop broadcasts its own health. The p99 period and the deadline-miss count ride every STATUS frame in a loop_health mapping, so a display no longer polls the loop-statistics query for them. drive_health sits beside it and stays empty on this backend: the drives report per-joint error flags, not analog registers, and empty distinguishes "no such sensor" from "all zero".
  • StatusBuffer, homing progress and loop statistics conform to waldoctl, and homing progress now survives a cancel.
  • A hardware e-stop disables the controller, rather than only halting motion.

docs.title: Motion
docs.text:
• Trajectory settling is gated on progress, not elapsed ticks.
  • Fast-path home: an already-referenced arm takes a planned return move instead of re-running the firmware seek.
  • Command indices stay monotonic across a reset.
  • The dry-run snapshot carries the pending blend chain, so a preview mid-blend matches what the runtime will execute.

docs.title: Fixes and hygiene
docs.text:
• A system command's Command_out was clobbered in the same tick by the executor fallback.
  • The MSG gripper is seated on the flange rather than inside the wrist, and its built-in camera mount is declared.
  • Test fixes surfaced by loaded runners: the unreachable-client test takes a free port instead of adding to the live one, which overflowed past 65535; the loop-health comparison waits for a frame that has caught up instead of demanding two samples of a climbing counter be equal.
  • Typing: scipy stubs pinned per Python version, stale suppressions dropped, sync tool wrappers typed as SyncTool.
