docs.title: PAROL6 Control Board Manual
docs.text:
Document number: SR-2002

PAROL6 release: 1

Revision: 2026.A

Published: 2026-11-03

Applies to: PAROL6 control board v2.0 and v1.2, PAROL6 release 1

Original instructions

The PAROL6 control board is the controller of the PAROL6 arm: a 32-bit microcontroller, six stepper drivers, the inputs and outputs, the E-stop input, CAN and USB on a board the size of a pack of playing cards, which is what lets PAROL6 run without a control cabinet. This manual covers the board itself: its specifications, connectors and pinout, the stepper drivers and their installation, the I/O and E-stop wiring, the CAN bus, uploading the firmware, the test firmware, and the serial protocol the PC software uses. How the robot is used is in the Robot Manual; how it is programmed in the Programming Guide.

  • The board

    Overview, Safety, Technical data, Connectors and pinout, Stepper drivers.

  • Wiring

    Inputs, outputs and E-stop, CAN bus.

  • Firmware

    Uploading the firmware, the test firmware, the serial protocol, troubleshooting.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
The control board sits in the base of PAROL6 and does the low-level work: it generates the step pulses for six stepper motors, runs the homing sequence, reads the limit switches, the inputs and the E-stop, switches the outputs, drives an electric gripper over CAN, and exchanges a data packet with the PC over USB 100 times a second. It plans nothing: the PC computes every trajectory and sends the board the joint speeds and positions to execute, cycle by cycle.

Figure 1.1: Features of the control board.

It works out of the box with PAROL6 and the commander software or the Python API, and it drives any six-axis stepper arm that is wired like PAROL6.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Version Status Difference v2.0 Current, in the shop Pluggable terminal block connectors v1.2 Discontinued Spring-loaded Phoenix contacts

The two are functionally identical and run the same firmware.

Figure 1.2: Control board v2.0. Figure 1.3: Control board v1.2 (discontinued).

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Every board is tested end to end before it ships, and comes with the test firmware preloaded, so that you can check the wiring of your robot before the main firmware goes on (The test firmware).

docs.title: Where it is published
docs.text:
The firmware, main and test, is in the robot repository: PAROL6 control board main software and PAROL6 control board test code. The board is sold in the shop.

The board schematics and PCB design are not available as open source materials due to licensing agreements and confidentiality terms established with our development partners. These proprietary design elements are subject to contractual obligations that restrict their public distribution.

docs.title: 2. Safety
docs.text:
Figure 2.1: Four ways to destroy the control board.

Four ways to destroy the board

  1. A stepper driver module inserted the wrong way round. Check the orientation against the DIAG pins before the first power-on (Stepper drivers).
  2. A driver without its heatsink cemented on. The TMC5160 modules need the heatsink and the fan.
  3. An ST-Link connected with jumper wires without the programming adapter. Use the adapter, or only the four pins named on Firmware.
  4. Reversed supply polarity. The XT30 power input has no reverse-polarity protection.
  • The board runs on 24 V, which is safe to touch; the power supply you connect it to is the mains device.
  • The outputs switch up to 1 A at up to 48 V; the inputs take up to 50 V. The isolation between them and the robot holds only if you power them from an isolated supply (Inputs, outputs and E-stop).
  • The E-stop input is read by the firmware and acted on by the PC software; it does not cut the motor power (Emergency stop in the Robot Manual).
  • With 3.3 V on the programming header the board turns on when the supply is connected and cannot be switched off with the button. Disconnect the 24 V supply before you connect the programmer.
  • The drivers are hot after use; the fan must run whenever the motors are energised.
  • Static electricity damages the microcontroller and the drivers. Unplug the supply and touch earthed metal before you handle the board or a driver module, and hold them by the edges.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Microcontroller STM32F446RE: Arm Cortex-M4 with DSP and FPU, 180 MHz, 512 KB flash Stepper drivers 6 × TMC5160 modules, SPI configured, 10 to 35 V, with stall, short and temperature protection; currents below Microstepping 32 (set by the firmware) Inputs 2, isolated, 12 to 50 V, 24 V nominal Outputs 2, isolated, 48 V maximum, 0.5 A continuous, 1 A peak; 2 A fuse for the non-isolated mode E-stop One input on a dedicated pin, two connectors in parallel, normally closed contact CAN 2 controllers; CAN 1 with its transceiver, CAN 2 transceiver not populated USB USB 2.0 full speed, a virtual serial port; the PC software opens it at 3 000 000 baud, a setting USB ignores Additional memory W25Q64FV SPI flash, 64 Mbit Programming SWD through the 2×5-pin header (ST-Link with the programming adapter) Fan 5 V, 3-pin header, 0.3 A maximum, not PWM Power button Soft switch: the button tells the firmware to switch the 24 V stage on and off Supply voltage 18 V minimum, 24 V maximum; 24 V is recommended for optimal robot performance Supply voltage sense The firmware reads the supply voltage (VBUS) Size Three M3 mounting holes; dimensions in the drawing below

docs.title: Operating limits
docs.text:
Stepper driver rated current 2.5 A per motor Stepper driver maximum current 3.6 A, short bursts or with extreme cooling only Driver overtemperature The driver shuts its outputs down and its joint goes limp; firmware 1 does not tell the PC Isolated input voltage 12 V minimum, 24 V nominal, 50 V maximum Isolated output voltage 48 V maximum Isolated output current 1 A maximum Fan current 0.3 A maximum; around 0.1 A recommended

The PAROL6 firmware runs the motors well below the drivers' ratings: 0.8 to 1.7 A (Currents and temperatures).

docs.title: Dimensions
docs.text: Figure 3.1: PCB dimensions in millimetres.

docs.title: Mounting and cooling
docs.text: Three M3 holes. The drivers need active cooling: a 40 × 40 × 20 mm 5 V fan, a Noctua NF-A4x20 or any 5 V fan of that size that is not PWM controlled, blowing over the heatsinks. In PAROL6 the fan sits in the base's fan cover.

docs.title: 4. Connectors and pinout
docs.text: Figure 4.1: The connections of the control board.

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text: Connection Connector 24 V power XT30 male Cooling fan 3-pin, 2.54 mm pitch, 5 V Power button JST PH 4-pin (B4B-PH-SM4-TB) USB USB type B Programming 2×5-pin, 2.54 mm pitch (SWD) Motors 6 × 4-pin terminal blocks, one per driver Limit switches, inputs, outputs, E-stop, CAN, 24 V out, GND, HV_SEL, GND_SEL Pluggable terminal blocks along the edges CAN termination Two jumpers, CAN1 JUMPER and CAN2 JUMPER: on, each connects a 120 Ω resistor across its bus (CAN bus)

docs.title: Pin definitions
docs.text:
The microcontroller pins as the firmware defines them (iodefs.h), for anyone who writes firmware or probes the board:

#define PUL1 PC6     // step, joint 1          #define DIR1 PB15    // direction, joint 1
#define PUL2 PA10    // step, joint 5          #define DIR2 PA1     // direction, joint 5
#define PUL3 PC0     // step, joint 6          #define DIR3 PC1     // direction, joint 6
#define PUL4 PC3     // step, joint 4          #define DIR4 PA0     // direction, joint 4
#define PUL5 PC9     // step, joint 3          #define DIR5 PA8     // direction, joint 3
#define PUL6 PC5     // step, joint 2          #define DIR6 PB1     // direction, joint 2

#define SELECT1 PC7  // SPI chip select of driver 1 (joint 1)
#define SELECT2 PA9  // driver 2 (joint 5)
#define SELECT3 PC15 // driver 3 (joint 6)
#define SELECT4 PC2  // driver 4 (joint 4)
#define SELECT5 PC8  // driver 5 (joint 3)
#define SELECT6 PC4  // driver 6 (joint 2)
#define GLOBAL_ENABLE PA3   // ENABLE of all drivers

#define LIMIT1 PC12  // limit input of joint 6      #define LIMIT4 PD2   // limit input of joint 4
#define LIMIT2 PB3   // limit input of joint 2      #define LIMIT5 PB4   // limit input of joint 5
#define LIMIT3 PA15  // limit input of joint 3      #define LIMIT6 PC11  // limit input of joint 1

#define MISO PA6, MOSI PA7, SCK PA5   // SPI to the six drivers and the flash
#define FLASH_SELECT PA4              // chip select of the flash memory

#define LED1 PB2, LED2 PB10           // the two LEDs
#define SUPPLY_ON_OFF PC10            // switches the 24 V power stage
#define SUPPLY_BUTTON_STATE PC14      // reads the power button
#define INPUT1 PB6, INPUT2 PB5        // IN1, IN2 terminals
#define OUTPUT1 PC13, OUTPUT2 PB7     // OUT1, OUT2 terminals
#define ESTOP PB14                    // E-stop terminals
#define VBUS PB0                      // supply voltage sense
#define USB_D_PLUS PA12, USB_D_MINUS PA11
#define CAN1TX PB9, CAN1RX PB8        // CAN 1 (the gripper bus)
#define CAN1TX PB13, CAN1RX PB12      // CAN 2's pins (transceiver not populated)

iodefs.h defines CAN1TX and CAN1RX twice, the second time with CAN 2's pins, PB13 and PB12. The CAN driver does not use these names: CANInit() in CAN.cpp picks the pins itself.

docs.title: Wiring the robot
docs.text:
Figure 4.2: Wiring diagram of the robot to the control board.

Limit switches to 24 V and their LIMIT terminal; inductive sensors to 24 V, GND and the LIMIT terminal (brown, blue, black). The gripper's M8 socket to 24 V, GND, CAN H and CAN L. The finished wiring in PAROL6's base:

Figure 4.3: The connectors at the base.

docs.title: 5. Stepper drivers
docs.text:
Figure 5.1: Four ways to destroy the control board.

The board takes six TMC5160 driver modules in the StepStick format, configured over SPI by the firmware.

Orientation

A driver module inserted the wrong way round destroys the board the moment power is applied, permanently. The orientation is given by the two DIAG pins: they must point at the red arrows in the figure. Check all six before every power-on after the drivers were touched.

Figure 5.2: Driver orientation: the DIAG pins at the red arrows.

docs.title: Which drivers
docs.text:
Only the TMC5160 modules listed in the BOM are tested; a board bought with drivers has them fitted. A module from elsewhere must have the pinout in the figure, and:

  • Remove the two DIAG pins if they are soldered: the capacitors on the board are in their way and the module will not seat.
  • Cement the heatsink to the driver with thermal cement (not paste, not tape); a driver without a bonded heatsink overheats and fails, and takes the board with it.
Figure 5.3: The TMC5160 module pinout.

docs.title: Current
docs.text: The firmware sets each driver's running and holding current for its joint (Currents and temperatures and Firmware parameters). The modules' potentiometer, if they have one, is not used.

docs.title: Cooling
docs.text: The fan over the heatsinks must run whenever the motors are energised. A driver that gets too hot shuts its outputs down and its joint goes limp, and firmware 1 does not tell the PC; in PAROL6's base with the fan they stay far below that.

docs.title: Checking a driver
docs.text: The test firmware reads every driver over SPI about three seconds after power-on and prints whether it answers (joint N Connection is: GOOD or BAD) with its currents and fault flags, then turns every motor slowly (The test firmware). A driver that does not answer is not seated, dead, or in the wrong slot.

docs.title: The isolated I/O
docs.text:
Two inputs and two outputs on optocouplers, with their own supply rails HV_SEL and GND_SEL on the terminal blocks. You decide what feeds those rails:

Isolated supplyThe robot's 24 V

An external supply's negative to GND_SEL, positive to HV_SEL. The I/O then runs at that voltage, 24 V nominal and at least 12 V for the inputs, and a short or a surge on a sensor cannot reach the robot's electronics.

Figure 6.1: Isolated supply wiring.

Link the board's 24 V and GND terminals to HV_SEL and GND_SEL. The I/O shares the robot's supply, with a 2 A fuse protecting the outputs. Simpler, and enough for a pneumatic valve.

Figure 6.2: Non-isolated wiring.

The E-stop is on the robot's own supply in both cases.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: Between HV_SEL and IN1 or IN2: a switch, a push button, a relay contact, or the signal of a sensor fed from HV_SEL and GND_SEL. 12 to 50 V. The firmware reads them every cycle and reports them in the I/O byte of the packet.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Between GND_SEL and OUT1 or OUT2: a relay coil, a valve, a lamp. 0.5 A continuous, 1 A peak, 48 V maximum, with a flyback diode across any coil. The firmware sets them from the I/O byte of the PC's packet.

docs.title: The E-stop
docs.text:
Two connectors on the same input, for a normally closed contact. The firmware reads the input every cycle and reports it in the I/O byte; the PC software stops the robot when it sees the contact open (Emergency stop).

Figure 6.3: E-stop wiring.
  • The contact must be normally closed: an open circuit means stop, so an unplugged button or a cut wire stops the robot too. A normally open button does not work.
  • Both connectors share one microcontroller pin: a second button goes in series on the other connector.
  • Any NC switch works for a bench setup. The BOM's 19 mm E-stop and the printed housing go on the base.

docs.title: The power button
docs.text: A momentary push button with an LED, on the JST PH connector. A press switches the 24 V stage on; a press while on switches it off. The LED is fed from the button connector. The firmware reads the button on every pass of its main loop.

docs.title: 7. CAN bus
docs.text:
CAN 1 Transceiver fitted; terminals CAN H and CAN L; the gripper bus in PAROL6 CAN 2 Controller on the microcontroller, transceiver not populated Bit rate 1 Mbit/s, set by the firmware Termination One jumper per bus, CAN1 JUMPER and CAN2 JUMPER: with the jumper on, a 120 Ω resistor is connected between CAN H and CAN L; with it off, the bus is not terminated on the board

In PAROL6, CAN 1 runs with 24 V and GND to the M8 socket at the forearm. The firmware addresses one gripper at the CAN ID the PC's packet names (0 as the grippers ship), sends it a move, a calibrate, a clear-error or an empty status frame every cycle, and relays its answer to the PC: CAN bus in the Robot Manual, and the gripper manuals for the messages themselves.

A CAN bus is terminated at both of its ends, 120 Ω at each. In PAROL6 the ends are the board, with its CAN1 jumper, and the gripper, with its own termination switch. Nodes in the middle of a longer bus stay unterminated. The jumpers are on the board figure in Connectors and pinout.

docs.title: 8. Firmware
docs.text:
Two firmware programs exist for the board, both in the robot repository as PlatformIO projects:

Folder For Main firmware PAROL6 control board main software Running the robot with the commander software or the Python API Test firmware PAROL6 control board test code Checking the board and the wiring from a serial terminal (The test firmware)

A board from the shop carries the test firmware. Upload the main firmware before you use the robot.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
1. VS Code with the PlatformIO extension from its marketplace.
  2. A clone of the robot repository.
  3. An ST-Link programmer and the PAROL6 programming adapter, or an ST-Link whose cable carries exactly SWCLK, SWDIO, GND and 3V3 to the pins of the 2×5 header in the table below.
  4. On Windows, the ST-Link USB driver (STSW-LINK009) if PlatformIO cannot find the programmer.

Danger

Use the programming adapter, or the four named pins only. An ST-Link wired to the header with jumper wires without the adapter has destroyed boards: other pins of the header are not for it.

The 2×5 programming header, as labelled in the side view of the connections figure, left to right, the header to the left of the USB port:

Row Top RESET BOOT0 SWDIO none 3V3 Bottom GND GND CLK (SWCLK) none 3V3

An ST-Link needs four of them: SWDIO, CLK, GND and 3V3. Leave RESET and BOOT0 unconnected.

docs.title: Uploading
docs.text:
1. Disconnect the 24 V supply from the robot.
  2. Connect the adapter to the 2×5 header next to the USB port, and the ST-Link to the PC. The adapter supplies 3.3 V, which powers the microcontroller (not the motors) and turns the board on.
  3. In VS Code, Open Folder on the firmware's folder. PlatformIO downloads the toolchain the first time.
  4. Build and Upload (the arrow in PlatformIO's toolbar). The upload takes a few seconds.
  5. Disconnect the adapter. With it connected, the board cannot be switched off with the button and turns on by itself when the supply is connected.
  6. Reconnect the 24 V supply and press the power button.

Check

PlatformIO ends the upload with SUCCESS, and after step 6 the drivers click and the PC software connects. If not: Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Version
docs.text: #define VERSION 1 in constants.h. The firmware is released with the robot (tag V1) and has not changed since; the protocol it speaks is on The serial protocol.

docs.title: 9. The test firmware
docs.text:
The test firmware turns the board into a bench instrument. At power-on it checks the six stepper drivers over SPI and prints the result, then turns all six motors slowly, blinks the LEDs and toggles the two outputs; on request it prints the E-stop, the inputs, the supply voltage and the limit switches over USB. It is what every board ships with, and the right tool for a freshly wired robot before the base is closed.

The motors turn as soon as it starts

The test firmware enables all six drivers when it boots and turns every motor slowly, at 1000 steps per second, without being asked, with no limits and no homing, until the power is switched off. No command stops them: #STOP only ends a printout. Use it with the arm free to move or the motors unmounted, never on a robot folded against its stops.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
Upload the firmware if the board does not have it (Firmware), then open a serial terminal on the board's USB port: PlatformIO's monitor, PuTTY or screen. The board is a USB device, so the baud rate does not matter; PlatformIO's monitor uses the 3000000 set in the project's platformio.ini. Make the terminal send a line feed at the end of each line: the firmware acts on a command only when the line feed arrives, so a terminal that sends only a carriage return on Enter gets no answer. Two ways to power the board for the test:

  • the programming adapter's 3.3 V, with the 24 V supply disconnected: the board talks, but the drivers have no power and report errors;
  • the 24 V supply: the board is off until you press the power button, or supply 3.3 V from the adapter as well.

docs.title: What it does by itself
docs.text:
• About three seconds after power-on it reads every driver over SPI and prints a report per joint: joint N Connection is: GOOD or BAD, then the driver's current, hold and run current settings and its fault flags.
  • From then on all six motors turn slowly and keep turning.
  • Every second the two LEDs blink and outputs 1 and 2 toggle.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
# followed by the name, case as written, and the line feed. Four commands do something:

Command What it does #IO Prints, once a second, the E-stop input, input 1, input 2 and the supply voltage in millivolts #LIMIT Prints, once a second, Joint N is pressed for every limit switch that is triggered, numbered by joint #STOP Ends the #IO or #LIMIT printout; the motors keep turning #start Toggles the two LEDs

Every other name, including #STATUS, #STEP1 to #STEP6, #FLASH and #CAN, is answered with Unknown command: the parser knows the names, but the firmware does nothing with them. Test firmware commands is the reference list.

docs.title: Testing CAN
docs.text: CAN has its own test, next to the test firmware in the repository's PAROL6 control board test code folder and not part of its build: the sketch can_12_12 sends a frame with ID 0x446 every 500 ms at 1 Mbit/s and prints every frame it receives, and can_parol6_test.py is the PC side, a python-can script for a USB-CAN adapter (slcan, 1 Mbit/s; set its port, COM44 in the file) that prints the frames it receives with their node and command IDs.

docs.title: What good looks like
docs.text:
All six drivers answering, in the report at power-on:

Figure 9.1: Serial output with all drivers responding.

A driver missing or faulty:

Figure 9.2: Serial output with a faulty driver.

With good drivers and the 24 V on, the motors turn slowly at 200 to 300 mA. A triggered limit switch, with #LIMIT:

Figure 9.3: A limit switch triggered.

The I/O report, with #IO; change the E-stop or an input and the values follow:

Figure 9.4: The IO report.

Outputs 1 and 2 toggle every second, and the two LEDs blink.

docs.title: 10. The serial protocol
docs.text:
The PC and the board exchange one packet each per control cycle over USB, a virtual serial port (the PC software opens it at 3 000 000 baud, a setting USB ignores). The PC sends a command packet at 100 Hz; the board answers each valid packet with a telemetry packet. Both are binary, framed with start bytes, a length byte, two end bytes and a CRC byte, and together under 120 bytes. The byte-exact layout is on The serial protocol in the API reference; this page explains how it works.

Figure 10.1: Packet structure.

docs.title: The cycle
docs.text:
loop:
    read the power button; run the active command (jog, go-to-position, home, idle)
    while serial data is available:
        read a byte; look for the three start bytes 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF
        the next byte is the length: that many bytes follow, including the CRC and the end bytes
        when the end bytes are 0x01 0x02: unpack the packet into the commanded positions, speeds, command,
            outputs, gripper fields; read the E-stop and inputs; write the outputs; send the gripper its frame;
            pack and send the telemetry packet

A valid packet starts one robot cycle: the firmware does nothing on its own between packets except run the speeds it was last given. The PC must keep the packets coming; the time between the last two packets is measured with a 703 125 Hz timer (90 MHz / 128, so 1.422 µs per tick: 10 ms is 7031 ticks) and returned in the telemetry as timing_data, which is how the PC software checks that it keeps the 100 Hz loop.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
The command byte selects what the board does with the carrier data (the positions and speeds) in the same packet:

Command Name What the board does 255 Idle (dummy) The joints stand still: it sets their speeds but steps none; it only continues a homing in progress. The default between moves 123 Jog Runs each joint at its commanded speed (runSpeed) 156 Go to position with speed Runs each joint at the average of its commanded speed and the speed that would close the position error in one cycle: the tracking the planners use 100 Home Starts the homing sequence; idle packets continue it until done 101 Enable Enables the robot and resets the homing state 102 Disable Disables motion commands; the motors keep holding 103 Clear error Resets the homing state 69 Repeatability test A built-in two-pose cycle, for testing

Motion commands (100, 123, 156) are ignored while the robot is disabled. A jog or go-to packet ends a homing in progress; the homed bits in the telemetry change only by homing. The firmware does not check them before a move: the PC decides when a move is allowed.

docs.title: Passive data
docs.text: The I/O byte carries the two output states in every packet, and the gripper fields (ID, position, speed, current, command bits, mode) are forwarded to the gripper over CAN every cycle: a move when they change, a calibrate for mode 1, a clear-error for mode 2, and an empty status poll when nothing changed. They ride along with any command.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text: The board returns the six positions and speeds in motor steps, which joints are homed, the inputs, outputs and E-stop, two bytes of driver flags (temperature and position, reserved: the joint bits are cleared and the two spare bits set), the timing, the last command byte it received, and the gripper's data. Of that, the gripper reports only its position, current and status byte; the ID, speed and object-detection bytes are fixed values, and the object detection is read from two bits of the status byte (The serial protocol).

docs.title: Writing your own host
docs.text: Anything that frames the packets as on the reference page and keeps the 100 Hz cadence can drive the board: the commander software and the Python API are two such hosts, in Python. Start from the Python API's serial transport rather than from scratch; the Control ownership page says why two hosts must not talk to the board at once.

docs.title: 11. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Cause Remedy No life at all with 24 V connected The button; the supply; a reversed XT30 Check the supply's output, the JST button cable, the XT30 polarity. A reversed supply has usually destroyed the board The board is on but cannot be switched off 3.3 V on the programming header Unplug the ST-Link or adapter The board turns on when the supply is connected The same, or a motor was turned by hand Unplug the programmer; move an unpowered robot slowly The test firmware's report at power-on says Connection is: BAD for a joint Not seated; dead; wrong orientation Power off, check the orientation against the DIAG pins, reseat. A driver that was powered the wrong way round is dead, and the board may be too A motor hums but does not turn A phase open; a motor wire loose in the terminal Check the four wires of that joint's cable A motor turns the wrong way Normal for a new build Flip direction_reversed in the main firmware A switch does not show in #LIMIT Wiring; the switch; the wrong terminal Check 24 V to the switch and the signal wire; try the other terminals to find which input changes An inductive sensor never triggers Gap; no 24 V; the sensor is PNP NPN NO sensors only; brown 24 V, blue GND, black signal; gap of a millimetre or two The E-stop reads pressed with the button released Wiring open; the button is NO NC contact between the E-stop terminals The drivers are hot and shut down The fan The fan must run; 5 V, not PWM No serial port on the PC The board has no power; the cable; the driver (Windows) The board enumerates only when powered; try another cable and port The main firmware does not upload ST-Link driver; the adapter; the target not powered Install STSW-LINK009; check the adapter's 3.3 V; disconnect the 24 V supply

For anything the firmware reports to the PC, the robot-side pages apply: Troubleshooting in the Robot Manual.

docs.title: Build guide
docs.text:
PAROL6 is open hardware: you can print the parts, buy the rest from the bill of materials and build the robot yourself. This guide is the order to do it in, with the facts that are not in the assembly manual; the step by step assembly is in the building instructions PDF and the video playlist.

Warning

A self-built robot is yours to make safe: the motor currents, the wiring, the switches and the stops. Read the Safety chapter before the first power-on, as you would for a bought one.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. Bill of materials: what to buy
  2. Printing the parts: the material, the settings, the print table
  3. Mechanical assembly: the manual, the videos, the things to get right
  4. Electronics and wiring: the control board, the drivers, the motors, the switches
  5. Firmware and first run: the test firmware, the main firmware, directions, homing

docs.title: Kits
docs.text:
You do not have to source everything yourself. The shop sells the robot in every state between a bag of parts and a working arm:

What is in it You add Assembled robot the robot, built, tested and ready for the commander software nothing Full kit every part of the BOM except the printed parts and the power supply the printed parts, a 24 V 5 A supply Partial kit the hard-to-find parts: the board, the drivers, the bearings, belts, pulleys, connectors, sensors, switches, the pneumatics the gearboxes, the stepper motors and the power supply, which are heavy to ship and cheaper from a supplier near you; the printed parts Printed parts kit every printed part, in PETG, in several colours everything else Screw kit every screw and nut of the BOM, counted everything else Control board, programming adapter the electronics alone everything else

The partial kit is the best value for a builder with a printer: it carries the parts that are hard to find or easy to get wrong, and leaves out the three items a local supplier sells cheaper than we can ship them. A full kit skips the bill of materials; a printed parts kit skips the printing.

docs.text:

If you would rather not source the parts yourself, the shop's kits cover every part or the hard-to-find ones.

docs.title: Electronics and wiring
docs.text:
Figure 1: Four ways to destroy the control board.

The control board goes into the base with its fan and its six driver modules; the motors, switches, sensors, the gripper connector, the E-stop and the power connector are wired to it.

docs.title: The control board
docs.text: Everything about the board itself is in the Control Board Manual: the connectors, the pin map, the drivers. The two things that destroy boards, both on the Stepper drivers page: a driver module inserted the wrong way round, and a driver without its heatsink cemented on. Read that page before you plug anything in.

docs.title: Wiring the arm to the board
docs.text:
Figure 2: Wiring diagram: motors, switches, sensors and connectors to the control board.
  • Motors: one four-wire cable per joint, to the terminals marked with its joint number (J1_A+ to J6_B-).
  • Limit switches (joints 2, 3, 5): one lead to 24 V, the other to the LIMIT terminal the wiring diagram shows in that joint's group; polarity does not matter.
  • Inductive sensors (joints 1, 4, 6): brown to 24 V, blue to GND, black (signal) to the LIMIT terminal the wiring diagram shows in that joint's group.
  • The gripper connector: 24 V, GND, CAN H and CAN L from the board to the M8 socket at the forearm.
  • The E-stop: the NC contact to the two E-stop terminals.
  • Power: the GX16 socket on the base to the XT30 on the board, polarity checked twice.
  • The power button: the JST PH cable to the button connector.
  • The fan: 5 V, three-pin, on the fan header; not a PWM fan.

Wire each switch and sensor to the terminal the diagram shows for its joint, joints 1 and 6 included, and check each one with the test firmware's #LIMIT before you close the base.

The finished base looks like this:

Figure 3: The connectors on the base.

docs.title: Test before you close the base
docs.text:
Power the board with the test firmware and check every driver, switch, sensor, input and output from the serial terminal (The test firmware). It is far easier now than with the base closed and the arm on top. You can also test your motors here, before the arm is assembled, to see that each one works.

Every control board sold by Source Robotics comes with the test firmware preloaded. It is the firmware every board was tested with: each board is fully tested, every part of it, at the end of the production line.

docs.title: 1. The test firmware
docs.text:
A control board from the shop ships with the test firmware. Use it, with the base open and the motors not yet driving the arm, to check every driver, every switch and sensor, and the I/O from a serial terminal: on the bench before the arm is assembled, as in Electronics and wiring. At power-on it prints a report on each driver (joint N Connection is: GOOD or BAD) and turns every motor slowly; #LIMIT then shows the switches and #IO the E-stop, the inputs and the supply voltage. The test firmware has the commands and what good output looks like.

Danger

The test firmware turns all six motors slowly from the moment it boots until the power is switched off; no command stops them. On an assembled arm joints 1 to 5 reach their blockers within about a minute and keep pushing. Use it with the motors free to turn, never on an assembled robot.

Check

Six Connection is: GOOD lines in the report; #LIMIT names each switch while you press it; #IO follows the E-stop and the inputs and shows the supply near 24000 mV. If not: Control board troubleshooting.

docs.title: 2. Upload the main firmware
docs.text:
The main firmware is in the repository under PAROL6 control board main software; it is a PlatformIO project for VS Code. Install VS Code and the PlatformIO extension, open the folder, and upload with an ST-Link through the programming adapter, with the 24 V supply disconnected: Firmware has the procedure and the warnings.

Check

PlatformIO ends the upload with SUCCESS. If not: Control board troubleshooting.

docs.title: 3. First power-on
docs.text:
Unplug the programming adapter, plug in the supply, hold the forearm and press the button. Six clicks, and the arm holds. Start the commander software, connect, and open the joint jog menu.

Check

Six clicks, the fan runs, the arm holds itself, and the commander shows the robot's data. If not: First power-on: if nothing happens.

docs.title: 4. A joint turns the wrong way
docs.text:
Jog each joint briefly. The joint must turn as in the figure, which shows each joint's positive direction (Joint limits and directions). Before homing, the commander checks jogs against the joint limits with a position count that starts at 0, so some directions are refused with Error: Robot jog -> Position out of range:

  • Joint 2: press its right arrow (negative). It must turn opposite to the figure; its left arrow does nothing until the robot is homed.
  • Joints 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6: press the left arrow (positive). It must turn as in the figure.
Figure 1: Each joint turned 30 degrees in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey.

A joint that turns the other way is the most common first-run problem, and it is fixed in the firmware, not by rewiring:

// motor_init.cpp, in Init_Joint_N: switch between 0 and 1
Joint__->direction_reversed = 1;

Upload again and check again. Swapping one motor phase's wires has the same effect, if you prefer to open the base.

Check

The left arrows of joints 1 and 3 to 6 turn them as in the figure, and joint 2's right arrow turns it the opposite way.

docs.title: 5. Home
docs.text:
With every direction right, set joint 6 and check the tool's homing offset as in Before you press Home, then press Home and stay at the E-stop. The sequence is on Homing; if a joint grinds at a stop, press the E-stop and see Homing failures.

Check

Homing finishes, the simulator matches the robot, and the pin passes through the witness marks of each joint, which line up in the after-homing pose (Witness marks).

docs.title: The commander's terminal output
docs.text: While it runs, the commander prints the robot's data to its terminal: the positions, the homed and I/O bytes, the errors, the gripper data, and Time between 2 commands in ms, which should be near 0.010 (the number is in seconds, despite the label: 0.010 is 10 ms). Watch it for a few minutes while jogging: if it is often much higher, the PC is too slow (Communication).

docs.title: Mechanical assembly
docs.text: The assembly is documented step by step in the Parol building instructions PDF and shown in the video playlist. Read the whole manual once before you start: some steps cannot be undone without taking the joint apart again. This page lists what to get right.

docs.title: The building instructions
docs.text: Download the building instructions (PDF, 8 MB)

docs.title: Things to get right
docs.text:
• Bearings seated square: the tapered roller bearings carry the joint; a bearing that sits crooked makes the joint stiff in one direction and loose in the other.
  • Belt tension as in the belt tension video: maximum hand force for joints 3 and 5, slightly less for 1 and 4, with the tension bearings (Belts).
  • Threadlocker on every metal-to-metal screw, blue, and on all set screws (Couplers and threadlocker). The couplers between motors, gearboxes and shafts are where a loose screw costs the most.
  • The limit switches and sensors positioned so that the moving part presses the lever, or passes the sensor within a millimetre or two, before the joint reaches its mechanical stop.
  • Joint 1's blockers fitted: without them joint 1 can spin a full turn and tear its wires.
  • Wires and tubes with enough slack through each joint for its full range, and fixed so that they cannot be pinched by the belts.
  • Wire markings: the print table spreadsheet's Wire_markings sheet lists the colour code of the motor and sensor cables used on the reference robots, which helps when the base is wired.

docs.title: Small print beds
docs.text: The J1 turret blocker and the upper arm come split in STL/SMALL_PRINT_BED, with a README. Join the halves with the dowel pins and slow epoxy, clamp them straight, and let them cure before the joint is assembled.

docs.title: Custom couplers and flanges
docs.text: The repository's custom_couplers.md is a work in progress on machined alternatives to the shaft couplers, with a press-fit flange; use the BOM's couplers until it is finished.

docs.title: Before the electronics
docs.text: Turn every joint by hand through its range. Everything should move smoothly against the gearbox's resistance, with no clicks and no tight spots, and every switch should click as its joint reaches it.

docs.title: Material
docs.text: PETG. The motors run warm and the parts around them see 60 to 70 °C in long use, which PLA does not survive; PETG softens around 80 °C, prints without an enclosure, and bonds layers well. ABS or ASA work with an enclosure. The repository's PETG notes give the printing basics: hot end 220 to 250 °C, bed 60 to 90 °C with glue, a layer fan, and the warping is small.

docs.title: The files
docs.text: All parts are in the repository's STL folder, grouped by link: BASE, SHOULDER, UPPER_ARM, ELBOW, FOREARM, WRIST, ESTOP, GRIPPER_ATTACHMENTS, UTILITY, mounting plates, and SMALL_PRINT_BED for the split versions of the two largest parts. The print table below says how each was printed on the reference robots; it is a tested starting point, not a rule.

docs.title: Print table
docs.text:
The print table from the robot's repository, as it is. Every printed part with the settings it was printed with on the reference robots: supports, mass, infill, print time, cooling, layer height, top and bottom layers, perimeters. Click the table to enlarge it. The same table is in the repository as a PDF and as an Excel file.

Figure 1: The PAROL6 print table: part, position in the arm, supports, mass, infill type and percentage, print time, cooling, layer height, top and bottom layers, perimeters.

Print the pulleys with high infill and slow outer walls: their teeth carry the load. Check the first printed pulley against a belt before printing the rest.

docs.title: Tolerances
docs.text: Bearing seats and shafts are designed for a well-calibrated printer; a seat that is too tight is reamed, one that is too loose is shimmed with tape or a drop of epoxy. Test the fit of the tapered bearings in their seats before assembling a joint.

docs.title: Inserts
docs.text: Four M3 brass inserts are melted into their holes with a soldering iron; everything else screws directly into the plastic.

docs.title: PAROL6 End Effectors Guide
docs.text:
Document number: SR-3004

PAROL6 release: 1

Python API (parol6): v0.9.1

PAROL6 commander software: main

Revision: 2026.A

Published: 2026-11-03

Applies to: PAROL6 release 1, Python API (parol6) v0.9.1, PAROL6 commander software main

Original instructions

What goes on PAROL6's flange and how to set it up: the pneumatic and vacuum grippers from the robot's own files, Source Robotics' SSG-48 and MSG electric grippers, and a tool of your own. Each page says how the end effector mounts, how it connects, what to tell the firmware and the software, and how the commander software and the Python API drive it. The electric grippers have manuals of their own; here is only what is PAROL6-specific.

End effector Driven by Mounts with Commander Python API Manual Pneumatic gripper, SMC MHZ2-16D a 5/2 valve on OUTPUT1, 5 to 7 bar a printed holder on the joint 6 shaft coupler Output(1,HIGH), Output(1,LOW) select_tool("PNEUMATIC") this guide Vacuum gripper the same valve and an ejector a printed holder Output(1,HIGH), Output(1,LOW) select_tool("VACUUM") this guide SSG-48 adaptive electric gripper CAN and 24 V through the M8 connector coupler_connector_PAROL6 the Gripper tab, Gripper() select_tool("SSG-48") SSG-48 manual MSG compliant AI stepper gripper CAN and 24 V through the M8 connector ring_cover-PAROL6 the Gripper tab, Gripper() select_tool("MSG") MSG manual Your own tool 24 V and CAN, two air lines, two inputs and two outputs the shaft coupler, or the coupler template Output(1,HIGH), Output(1,LOW); the inputs in the IO tab set_tcp_offset(), a ToolConfig this guide

docs.title: In this guide
docs.text:
• The flange: the 8 mm shaft of joint 6, the connections at the forearm, the payload, the tool in the software
  • Pneumatic gripper
  • Vacuum gripper
  • SSG-48
  • MSG
  • Your own tool

Get the robot working before you attach a gripper: troubleshooting both at once is hard.

docs.title: Mounting
docs.text: Clamp onto the 8 mm shaft of joint 6 with a shaft coupler from the BOM, or print a holder with a coupler connector: the SSG-48 repository has a template, STEPS/coupler_connector_generic_STEP.STEP (and Gripper STL parts/connector_coupler_generic.STL), and the STL/WRIST/wrist.STL in the robot's files shows the mating geometry. Keep the tool within the payload and short: every millimetre past the flange is leverage against joints 4 and 5.

docs.title: The joint 5 homing feature
docs.text: Joint 5 finds its reference by driving the forearm's limit switch against a feature of the tool holder. Your holder needs a surface in the same place as the pneumatic gripper holder's; compare with Pneumatic_gripper_holder.STL. Then measure the homing offset: home, jog joint 5 until the pin fits the witness marks, and set j5_homing_offset in main.cpp to the steps that gives (Mastering).

docs.title: Connections
docs.text: Up to 24 V and CAN at the M8 connector, two air lines, and the control board's two inputs and two outputs at the base. A tool that needs more, a camera's USB for instance, runs its cable outside the arm, with enough slack for joints 4, 5 and 6 and fixed so the arm cannot catch it.

docs.title: The tool frame
docs.text:
The software positions the tool centre point. In the Python API, register the tool once with its transform from the flange, or set an offset at run time:

rbt.select_tool("NONE")
rbt.set_tcp_offset(0, 0, 120)                  # the tip, 120 mm along the tool's Z
index = rbt.set_tcp_transform(0, 0, 120, 0, 15, 0)   # with a rotation, intrinsic XYZ degrees
rbt.wait_command(index)

A permanent tool goes into the API's tool registry as a ToolConfig with its collision mesh, so that the collision checker knows its shape (Tools and the TCP). The commander software has no tool setting: its poses are for the standard pneumatic gripper, and a different tool means editing its robot model.

docs.title: Check before you run
docs.text: Jog joint 5 and joint 6 through their ranges slowly with the tool mounted and watch for contact with the forearm: the software's joint limits do not know the tool's shape.

docs.title: The flange
docs.text: Joint 6 ends in an 8 mm output shaft. Tools clamp onto it with a shaft coupler (8 mm bore, M4 set screws, three in the BOM) that bolts to the tool's holder; the SSG-48 and MSG grippers use a printed coupler connector made for this shaft. The coupler's set screws take blue threadlocker: joint 6 slipping on its shaft is the first thing to check when a tool's orientation drifts (Couplers and threadlocker).

docs.title: Connections at the forearm
docs.text:
M8 4-pin connector 24 V, GND, CAN H, CAN L for an electric gripper; wired from the control board's CAN 1 and 24 V Two pneumatic tubes, 4 mm From the two push-in fittings at the base, through the arm, to the forearm

The tubes and the gripper cable run through the arm and come out at the forearm. Joint 5 is held inside its limits by its stops. Joint 6 has no limit with the bare flange; with a tool, the tool's cable and tubes run from the forearm to the tool and wrap as joint 6 turns, so keep joint 6 within the turn they allow (Joint limits and directions).

docs.title: The tool in the software
docs.text:
The software must know the tool to compute the pose of its tip. The commander's kinematic model is built for the standard pneumatic gripper; the Python API has tool definitions with variants and a settable TCP offset (Tools and the TCP):

rbt.select_tool("PNEUMATIC")                       # default variant: vertical
rbt.select_tool("PNEUMATIC", variant_key="horizontal")
rbt.select_tool("SSG-48", variant_key="pinch")
rbt.select_tool("MSG", variant_key="150mm")
rbt.select_tool("VACUUM")
rbt.select_tool("NONE")                            # the bare flange

docs.title: Tool centre point
docs.text:
The tool centre point (TCP) is a6 = 50.5 mm from the joint 6 centre along the tool axis and a7 = 0 mm to the side. With nothing on the flange, the TCP is the flange's reference point. The sheet is the robot's model from robot_descriptions (version 2.15.1) with every joint at 0. Tell the software about the tool (Tools and the TCP); every tool is compared on Dimensions and kinematics.

Figure 1: PAROL6 with the flange only: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table.

docs.title: Homing and the tool
docs.text: Joint 5 homes against a feature of the tool holder. The pneumatic gripper holder and the SSG-48's coupler connector have it; a tool of your own needs it too, and the firmware's joint 5 homing offset must match the tool (Your own tool).

docs.title: Payload
docs.text: 1 kg near the base, 0.5 kg at full reach, the tool included. A gripper with a camera and a cable can be most of that. A short video shows the arm with a 1 kg payload: PAROL6 robot arm 1kg payload.

docs.title: MSG compliant AI stepper gripper
docs.text:
Source Robotics' modular stepper gripper: a STEPFOC driver in gripper mode, three rail lengths, three stepper lengths and a camera mount. It plugs into the M8 connector at the forearm and the control board drives it over CAN with the same commands as the SSG-48. Its own manual, MSG-gripper-docs, covers the gripper; this page covers PAROL6.

Stroke 55, 105 or 155 mm, with the 100, 150 or 200 mm rail Grip force about 20, 25 or 36 N per ampere with the 21.5, 40 or 60 mm stepper; up to about 31, 50 or 76 N Mass about 380 g plus the camera: mind the payload at full reach Shop MSG gripper

docs.title: Mounting
docs.text:
1. Replace the gripper's ring_cover with ring_cover-PAROL6 from the repository's Common parts: it bolts to the robot's last joint, and the coupler plate's shaft coupler (8 mm bore, two M4 clamp screws) takes the joint 6 shaft (Mounting on a robot).
  2. Slide the gripper onto the shaft, orient it with the camera looking down between the jaws, and tighten the two clamp screws with blue threadlocker (Couplers and threadlocker).
  3. Connect the PAROL6 gripper cable between the gripper and the M8 connector at the forearm.
  4. The camera is a plain USB camera with its own cable: route it outside the arm, with slack for joints 4, 5 and 6, and fix it so the arm cannot catch it.

Only the PAROL6 cable

PAROL6 and PAR6 put the four signals on different pins. The PAR6 cable, or a self-made cable with a wrong pin, puts 24 V on the CAN pins and destroys the gripper's driver. The gripper manual's cable page has the pinout to check your own against.

Leave the gripper's CAN node ID at 0 and its termination switch, reachable through the stepper cover, on: it is the last node on the robot's bus (CAN bus).

docs.title: Tool centre point
docs.text:
The tool centre point (TCP) is a6 = 134.3 mm from the joint 6 centre along the tool axis and a7 = 28.35 mm to the side. Both jaw variants share one TCP: an operating point, not a measured grasp centre. The sheet is the robot's model from robot_descriptions (version 2.15.1) with every joint at 0. Tell the software about the tool (Tools and the TCP); every tool is compared on Dimensions and kinematics.

Solid jawsSoft TPU jaws

Figure 1: PAROL6 with the MSG, solid jaws: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table.

Figure 2: PAROL6 with the MSG, soft TPU jaws: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table.

docs.title: The joint 5 homing offset
docs.text: Joint 5 homes against the tool, and the MSG's ring cover is not the pneumatic gripper holder that the firmware's default offset (8900) assumes. After the first homing, check joint 5 with the pin through the witness marks; if it is off, measure the offset and set j5_homing_offset in main.cpp as Mastering describes.

docs.title: Driving it
docs.text:
The gripper must be calibrated after every power-up: it opens fully and closes fully to find its end stops, and does not move before that. Clear any error first, then calibrate, then wait until the gripper reports itself calibrated before the first move: about 5 to 6 s on the longer rails.

Commander softwarePython API

The Gripper tab: after homing the robot press Clear gripper error, then Calibrate gripper, and wait until the tab shows Calibration status is: 1. Then set position, speed and current with the sliders and press Move GoTo. The feedback section shows the current, the position and the status (The GUI). In RBTscript, after clearing the error in the tab: Gripper_cal(), Delay(7), then Gripper(position, speed, current) (RBTscript).

rbt.select_tool("MSG", variant_key="150mm")           # 100mm, 150mm or 200mm: the rail
rbt.tool.calibrate()                                   # queued; the API counts it done after 2 s
rbt.delay(5)                                           # the rest of the calibration, with a margin
rbt.tool.set_position(0.8, speed=0.5, current=0.4)     # fractions of the ranges; 0.4 is 1180 mA
rbt.tool.close(current=0.4)
rbt.tool.open()
rbt.tool.release()                                     # drop the grip, the jaws stay
rbt.tool.stop()                                        # immediate: halt where the jaws are
Tool actions are queued with the motion, so a move after close() waits for the grip; a move on a gripper that was never calibrated is refused when its turn comes. The API does not read the calibrated bit and has no clear-error action at this version: clear an error in the commander's Gripper tab or with Motor GUI (Tools and the TCP, Tools).

docs.title: Current and force
docs.text:
The current limit is the grip force, and the slope depends on the stepper: about 20 N per ampere with the 21.5 mm stepper, 25 with the 40 mm, 36 with the 60 mm. Stay within the stepper's maximum, 1.5 A, 2.0 A or 2.1 A. The gripper manual's Force and speed has the curves.

The commander takes the current in milliamps, 100 to 1000 mA, which is within every stepper's maximum. The Python API takes it as a fraction of 100 to 2800 mA, a range above every stepper's maximum, so keep the fraction at or below the value for your stepper:

Stepper Maximum current Highest current= fraction 21.5 mm 1.5 A 0.51 40 mm 2.0 A 0.70 60 mm 2.1 A 0.74

docs.title: Status
docs.text: The robot passes the gripper's status byte through: calibrated, in motion, object detected (while closing, while opening, or none), and its error bits. The commander's Gripper tab shows the calibrated and E-stop error bits, and the whole status byte as a number (labelled Gripper object detection is). The Python API's tool.status() gives the jaw position and the current; its engaged and part_detected do not follow the status byte's bits at this version (Tool status). The gripper manual's errors page says what each error needs: Errors and recovery.

docs.title: Pneumatic gripper
docs.text: The standard tool: an SMC MHZ2-16D parallel gripper in a printed holder, driven by a 5/2 solenoid valve from one of the control board's outputs.

docs.title: Parts
docs.text: Gripper MHZ2-16D, two PC4-M5 push-in fittings Holder GRIPPER_ATTACHMENTS/Pneumatic_gripper_holder.STL (vertical) or Pneumatic_gripper_holder_horizontal.stl; Gripper_ARMS.STL for the fingers Valve 5/2 solenoid valve, 24 V, 4 mm tube ports Tube 4 × 2.5 mm pneumatic tube, 5 m Air 5 to 7 bar; stay below the lowest rating of the gripper, the valve and the fittings (Pneumatics)

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
The two tubes from the gripper leave the forearm and are joined to the two tubes that run through the arm to the base; the valve's two outputs go to the two fittings at the base. Swapping the two tubes swaps normally open and normally closed: choose the state the gripper should take without power.

The valve's coil goes between GND_SEL and OUTPUT1 on the control board, with the output supply set to the robot's 24 V or an isolated one (Inputs and outputs).

docs.title: Tool centre point
docs.text:
The tool centre point (TCP) is a6 = 62.3 mm from the joint 6 centre along the tool axis and a7 = 45.25 mm to the side. The TCP is the reference point of the original MHZ2-10D gripper, not a newly measured grasp centre. The sheet is the robot's model from robot_descriptions (version 2.15.1) with every joint at 0. Tell the software about the tool (Tools and the TCP); every tool is compared on Dimensions and kinematics.

Figure 1: PAROL6 with the pneumatic gripper: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table.

docs.title: Driving it
docs.text:
RBTscriptPython API 
Output(1,HIGH)    // the valve switches
Delay(0.5)
Output(1,LOW)     // and back


rbt.select_tool("PNEUMATIC")
rbt.tool.close()              # output 1 low
rbt.tool.open()               # output 1 high
rbt.write_io(0, 1)            # the same as open(), as a plain output
The tool's action lasts its estimated stroke, so a move queued after close() waits for the gripper. The API's open() switches output 1 high and close() switches it low: lay the tubes so that the gripper is open with the valve switched, or open() and close() come out the other way round.

docs.title: Orientation
docs.text: The vertical holder puts the gripper along the axis of joint 6; the horizontal holder turns it 90°, which reaches a table from the side. The Python API has a variant for each (vertical, horizontal); with the commander, remember that the DH dimensions a6 and a7 assume the vertical holder.

docs.title: SSG-48 adaptive electric gripper
docs.text:
Source Robotics' 48 mm electric gripper: a Spectral Micro BLDC driver in gripper mode. It plugs into the M8 connector at the forearm and the control board drives it over CAN; the commander software and the Python API both know it. Its own manual, SSG48-gripper-docs, covers the gripper; this page covers PAROL6.

Stroke 48 mm Grip force about 54 N per ampere, 5 to 80 N; on PAROL6 up to about 54 N from the commander, 70 N from the Python API Fingers fin-ray or pinch, printed: finger and pinch in the Python API Shop SSG-48

docs.title: Mounting
docs.text:
1. Fit coupler_connector_PAROL6 from the gripper's repository to the gripper. It carries a shaft coupler with an 8 mm bore and two M4 clamp screws for the joint 6 shaft, and the homing tab that joint 5 homes against: the tab goes on the same side as the gripper's cable connector, with an M3 × 12 screw in the marked hole, as the gripper's assembly manual shows on its last pages.
  2. Slide the gripper onto the joint 6 shaft, orient it, and tighten the two clamp screws, one on each side, with blue threadlocker (Couplers and threadlocker).
  3. Connect the PAROL6 gripper cable between the gripper and the M8 connector at the forearm.
Figure 1: The gripper connector at the forearm.

Only the PAROL6 cable

PAROL6 and PAR6 put the four signals on different pins. The PAR6 cable, or a self-made cable with a wrong pin, puts 24 V on the CAN pins and destroys the gripper's driver. The gripper manual's cable page has the pinout to check your own against.

Leave the gripper's CAN node ID at 0 and its termination switch on: it is the last node on the robot's bus (CAN bus).

docs.title: Tool centre point
docs.text:
The tool centre point (TCP) is a6 = 134.3 mm from the joint 6 centre along the tool axis and a7 = 0 mm to the side. The TCP lies on the joint 6 axis, with no sideways offset, for both jaw variants. The sheet is the robot's model from robot_descriptions (version 2.15.1) with every joint at 0. Tell the software about the tool (Tools and the TCP); every tool is compared on Dimensions and kinematics.

Solid jawsFin-ray jaws

Figure 2: PAROL6 with the SSG-48, solid jaws: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table.

Figure 3: PAROL6 with the SSG-48, fin-ray jaws: dimensions to the TCP and the DH table.

docs.title: The joint 5 homing offset
docs.text: Joint 5 homes against the tool, and the SSG-48's coupler sits differently from the pneumatic gripper holder. Set j5_homing_offset to 8035 in main.cpp of the control board firmware (the default, 8900, is for the pneumatic gripper) and upload (Firmware). Check with the pin through the joint 5 witness marks after the first homing, and master if needed (Mastering).

docs.title: Driving it
docs.text:
The gripper must be calibrated after every power-up: it opens fully and closes fully to find its end stops, and does not move before that. Clear any error first, then calibrate, then wait until the gripper reports itself calibrated before the first move: about 3 s.

Commander softwarePython API

The Gripper tab: after homing the robot press Clear gripper error, then Calibrate gripper, and wait until the tab shows Calibration status is: 1. Then set position, speed and current with the sliders and press Move GoTo. The feedback section shows the current, the position and the status (The GUI). In RBTscript, after clearing the error in the tab: Gripper_cal(), Delay(4), then Gripper(position, speed, current) (RBTscript).

rbt.select_tool("SSG-48")                             # or add variant_key="pinch"
rbt.tool.calibrate()                                   # queued; the API counts it done after 2 s
rbt.delay(2)                                           # the rest of the calibration, with a margin
rbt.tool.set_position(0.8, speed=0.5, current=0.4)     # fractions of the ranges; 0.4 is 580 mA
rbt.tool.close(current=0.6)
rbt.tool.open()
rbt.tool.release()                                     # drop the grip, the jaws stay
rbt.tool.stop()                                        # immediate: halt where the jaws are
Tool actions are queued with the motion, so a move after close() waits for the grip; a move on a gripper that was never calibrated is refused when its turn comes. The API does not read the calibrated bit and has no clear-error action at this version: clear an error in the commander's Gripper tab or with Motor GUI (Tools and the TCP, Tools).

docs.title: Current and force
docs.text:
The current limit is the grip force, about 54 N per ampere: 300 mA is about 16 N, 1 A about 54 N. Start low and raise it for a firmer grip; a high current with a high speed slams the jaws into the part. The gripper manual's Force and speed has the curve and the heat limits.

The commander takes the current in milliamps, 100 to 1000 mA, so its strongest grip is about 54 N. The Python API takes it as a fraction of 100 to 1300 mA: current=1.0 is 1.3 A, about 70 N.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: The robot passes the gripper's status byte through: calibrated, in motion, object detected (while closing, while opening, or none), and its error bits. The commander's Gripper tab shows the calibrated and E-stop error bits, and the whole status byte as a number (labelled Gripper object detection is). The Python API's tool.status() gives the jaw position and the current; its engaged and part_detected do not follow the status byte's bits at this version (Tool status). The gripper manual's errors page says what each error needs: Errors and recovery.

docs.title: Vacuum gripper
docs.text: A suction cup on a vacuum generator, fed by the same valve and tubes as the pneumatic gripper.

docs.title: Parts
docs.text: The BOM's vacuum section: a suction cup gripper, a vacuum generator (ejector) and a 4 mm to 6 mm coupler. The holder is GRIPPER_ATTACHMENTS/vacuum_gripper_holder.STL.

docs.title: Mounting
docs.text:
Print the holder and bolt the gripper to it. The gripper spins freely in the holder by default; to fix its orientation, tie it with a zip tie to the screw shown in the figure.

Figure 1: The vacuum gripper on the forearm.

docs.title: Air
docs.text:
A vacuum generator needs one supply line, so one of the valve's two ports is blocked: a short piece of tube with an M3 screw and threadlocker screwed into it does the job.

Figure 2: One valve port blocked with a tube and an M3 screw.

docs.title: Driving it
docs.text:
The valve switches the air to the ejector, which pulls the vacuum: Output(1,HIGH) holds, Output(1,LOW) drops. In the Python API, select_tool("VACUUM") gives tool.open(), which switches output 1 high, and tool.close(), which switches it low. With the tubing above, open() holds the part and close() drops it; write_io(0, 1) and write_io(0, 0) do the same.

Warning

The part drops the moment the air stops, with the E-stop, a valve fault or a power failure. Do not carry anything over something it can damage.

docs.title: PAROL6 GUI Guide
docs.text:
Document number: SR-4005

PAROL6 release: 1

PAROL6 commander software: main

Revision: 2026.A

Published: 2026-11-03

Applies to: PAROL6 release 1, PAROL6 commander software main

Original instructions

The graphical programs for PAROL6 and its grippers: which one to open for which job, how to install it, and what is on its screen. Programming the robot, in RBTscript or Python, is in the Programming Guide.

Commander software Waldo Commander Motor GUI What it is Source Robotics' desktop program: jogging, a 3D simulator, the RBTscript editor, the I/O and gripper tabs A community browser interface on the Python API: a simulator, Python programs, teaching by demonstration, an MCP server for LLMs Source Robotics' browser tool for the drivers inside the electric grippers For the first day, teaching poses, demos, simple sequences remote use, programs in the browser, AI-driven control setting up, testing and updating an SSG-48 or MSG gripper Runs on the PC at the robot, Python 3.10 or 3.11 a server at the robot, any browser any Chromium browser, with the CANvas adapter Talks to the control board over USB the Python API's controller the gripper's driver over CAN

docs.title: In this guide
docs.text:
• The commander software: Installation, The GUI
  • Waldo Commander
  • Motor GUI

One program owns the control board at a time: the commander and the Python API's controller cannot be connected together (Control ownership).

docs.title: Motor GUI
docs.text:
Motor GUI is Source Robotics' browser tool for its motor drivers, and so for the SSG-48 and MSG grippers, whose driver sits inside. It reaches the hardware through the browser's serial port access: nothing to install, a Chromium-based browser and the CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter.

On PAROL6 the control board drives the gripper, so Motor GUI is not part of everyday use. It is the tool when you:

  • update the gripper's firmware, over CAN, from the driver's GitHub releases, through the gripper's bootloader;
  • set up a self-built gripper, or restore a gripper's configuration: the setup page has presets for the SSG-48 and for the three MSG steppers. They are applied over UART, with the USB-to-serial adapter on the driver's UART port, not over CAN. A preset writes CAN ID 6, the PAR6 gripper's: change it to 0 before you apply it for PAROL6;
  • test a gripper off the robot: calibrate, open and close it, watch its position and current, run a cycle test, in the gripper panel.

The control board polls the gripper continuously while the robot is on, so use Motor GUI with the gripper off the robot's bus: the gripper on the CANvas adapter's CAN terminals and on a 24 V supply. Then follow the gripper manual's Motor GUI page, SSG-48 or MSG; the firmware update is on their Firmware pages (SSG-48, MSG).

docs.title: Waldo Commander (web)
docs.text:
Waldo Commander, by a member of the community, is a browser interface on top of the Python API: control from any device on the network, Python programs with an editor and step-through debugging, a 3D simulation to preview paths, teaching by demonstration recorded as Python, and a built-in MCP server through which an LLM can read the robot's status, write and run programs and drive the arm with your approval. It runs in simulator mode without a robot.

git clone https://github.com/Jepson2k/Waldo-Commander.git
cd Waldo-Commander
pip install -e ".[parol6]"
waldo-commander
Figure 1: The web commander.

It is built on waldoctl, the abstraction layer the Python API implements, so what it offers tracks the API's features. Its documentation is at jepson2k.github.io/Waldo-Commander.

docs.title: The commander software
docs.text:
The PAROL6 commander software is the desktop program for using the robot by hand: a GUI with joint and Cartesian jogging, a 3D simulator that mirrors the robot, a response log, a program editor and interpreter for RBTscript, the I/O tab and the gripper tab. It is written in Python with customtkinter and the Robotics Toolbox, runs a 100 Hz loop to the control board, and is the program to start with.

Figure 1: The commander window.

docs.title: In this guide
docs.text:
• Installation
  • The GUI: the windows, the menus, connecting, jogging, the tabs

Its program language, RBTscript, is in the Programming Guide: RBTscript, Examples.

docs.title: What it is and is not
docs.text:
It is the tool for the first day, for teaching poses, for demos and for simple sequences. It has no blending, no collision checking, no network interface and no tool selection: its kinematic model is the one with the pneumatic gripper. For programs that need those, the Python API. The two cannot be connected to the robot at the same time.

The experimental kinematics branch

The repository's experimental_kinematics branch resolves most Cartesian jogging errors but can command dangerous motion. The main branch is the safe one; use the other at your own risk.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or 3.11 (tested on 3.10.12 and 3.11.0; newer versions break some pinned dependencies).
  • Windows, Linux or macOS. On macOS, follow the Linux steps, as the repository's README says.
  • A PC that keeps the 100 Hz loop: What you need.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The commander goes into its own folder with its own virtual environment (.venv), on every operating system. It pins numpy 1.23.4 and the Python API needs numpy 2, so the two cannot share one Python: give each its own environment, as the Quick start does.

WindowsLinuxmacOS 

git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-commander-software.git
cd PAROL-commander-software
py -3.11 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
py -3.11 picks Python 3.11 when several are installed; py -3.10 works too. The robot's serial port is COM and a number: Device Manager lists it under Ports (COM & LPT).

sudo apt install python3.11 python3.11-venv python3.11-tk
git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-commander-software.git
cd PAROL-commander-software
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER     # access to the serial port; log out and in again once
Ubuntu's own Python is 3.10 on 22.04 and 3.12 on 24.04; where Python 3.11 is not in the distribution, the deadsnakes PPA has it (sudo add-apt-repository ppa:deadsnakes/ppa first). On 22.04 the system Python 3.10 with python3-venv and python3-tk works as well. The robot's serial port is ttyACM0 (ls /dev/ttyACM* lists it).

git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL-commander-software.git
cd PAROL-commander-software
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
With Python 3.11 from python.org; the repository's README says the Linux steps work on macOS.

After the activate line the prompt starts with (.venv). Activate the environment again in every new terminal before you start the program.

The repository's Windows and Linux guides list the packages one by one if requirements.txt fails: the robotics toolbox, swift, numpy and scipy are pinned to the versions that work together, and the Working dependency folder has the full module lists of PCs on which the software runs.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
For the first run, write the robot's port into the program: open GUI/files/Serial_sender_good_latest.py in a text editor and find these lines near the top:

if my_os == "Windows": 
    STARTING_PORT = 8 # COM3
else:   
    STARTING_PORT = 0

On Windows, replace 8 with the number of the robot's port (5 for COM5; Device Manager, Ports (COM & LPT), shows it). On Linux, 0 means /dev/ttyACM0. Save, then start the program from the activated virtual environment:

cd GUI/files
python Serial_sender_good_latest.py

Two windows open: the commander and the simulator. Enter the serial port at the bottom of the commander (COM5, or ttyACM0 on Linux) and press Connect, more than once if needed. On Linux, a permission error on the port is fixed with sudo chmod 666 /dev/ttyACM0, or by joining the dialout group.

docs.title: Check the loop
docs.text:
The terminal the program runs in prints the robot's data; Time between 2 commands in ms should sit near 0.010 while you jog. The value is in seconds, whatever the label says: 0.010 is the 10 ms cycle. If it is often much higher, the PC is too slow for the loop, and the robot will stutter (Communication).

Check

The commander shows the robot's data after Connect, and the simulator moves with the robot when you jog. If not: Communication.

docs.title: The GUI
docs.text:
Two windows: the commander, where everything is done, and the simulator, a 3D view of the robot that follows it once the robot is connected and homed.

Figure 1: The commander window, with the joint jog menu. Figure 2: The simulator window.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
Figure 3: The connection bar.

At the bottom: the serial port field and Connect. COMx on Windows, ttyACMx on Linux. The response log starts showing the robot's data when the connection is up; press Connect again if it does not. The Simulator and Real robot buttons have no function at present. Clear error resets the homing state; unlike Enable it does not re-enable a disabled robot.

docs.title: The Move menu
docs.text:
The left part of the window is the jog menu, with two variants:

Joint jog: six pairs of arrows, left for the positive direction and right for the negative. The speed slider below sets the jog speed as a percentage; it affects jogging only, not programs. Works before homing.

Cartesian jog: X, Y, Z and the rotations, in the WRF (the base) or the TRF (the tool), chosen with the switch; TRF is the default. The rotation buttons only work in the TRF: in the WRF they do nothing. Home the robot first (the software does not check), and the jog stops at a singularity (Configurations and singularities).

Figure 4: The Cartesian jog menu.

docs.title: The robot position
docs.text:
Figure 5: Joint angles, the tool pose and the speed slider.

The six joint angles and the tool pose in the WRF, live. Home starts the homing sequence; Enable clears errors and enables the robot; Disable disables it, the motors still holding. Park does not move the robot: it inserts a three-line program at the cursor of the program window, Begin(), a MoveJoint to the park pose with t=4, and End(), which you then run with Start.

docs.title: The program window
docs.text:
Figure 6: The program editor.

An RBTscript program, one command per line (RBTscript). Start runs it from Begin(), Stop halts it. Start first saves the editor's text: into the file you opened, if any, overwriting it, and into Programs/execute_script.txt.

Figure 7: Start and stop.

The command list inserts a command at the cursor: with Current selected, a motion command is inserted with the robot's current joint angles or pose as its arguments, which is how you teach a pose; with Custom the arguments are left for you.

Figure 8: The command list.

docs.title: The response log
docs.text:
Figure 9: The response log.

What the robot and the program are doing, and why a command was refused: the first place to look when something does not happen (Errors and recovery).

docs.title: The IO tab
docs.text:
Figure 10: The IO tab.

The state of the two inputs, and buttons for the two outputs.

docs.title: The Gripper tab
docs.text:
Figure 11: The gripper tab.

For the SSG-48 and MSG grippers. After homing: Clear gripper error, then Calibrate gripper, then wait until the tab shows Calibration status is: 1 (about 3 s for the SSG-48, 5 to 6 s for the MSG on its longer rails). Then set the position, speed and current with the sliders and press Move GoTo. The feedback section shows the gripper's position and current, its calibrated and E-stop error bits, and its whole status byte as a number (labelled Gripper object detection is). Change gripper ID sets the CAN ID the board addresses, 0 as the grippers ship.

docs.title: The Calibrate and Plot buttons
docs.text: The menu also has Calibrate and Plot. Both open the same panel, with Disable motor, Enable motor, Go to limit and a joint menu; none of them does anything in the current version.

docs.title: The Settings tab
docs.text:
Figure 12: The settings tab.

Dark or light mode, and the scaling of the GUI for your display.

docs.title: The terminal
docs.text: The terminal the program was started from prints a block of data every few seconds: the positions and speeds from the robot, the homed, I/O and error bytes, the timing, the gripper data, the commanded data and the GUI's state. Time between 2 commands in ms is the one to watch: near 0.010 is right. The value is in seconds, whatever the label says: 0.010 is the 10 ms cycle.

docs.title: PAROL6 Programming Guide
docs.text:
Document number: SR-4004

PAROL6 release: 1

Python API (parol6): v0.9.1

PAROL6 commander software: main

Revision: 2026.A

Published: 2026-11-03

Applies to: PAROL6 release 1, Python API (parol6) v0.9.1, PAROL6 commander software main

Original instructions

This guide is for everyone who makes PAROL6 do something: from a first RBTscript program in the commander software to a Python application on the API, a ROS 2 pipeline, or a program that an AI agent writes. It starts with the interfaces and how to choose, walks through the Python API and the commander software, and ends with ROS 2 and the other interfaces. The ideas the software is built on, the units, the frames, the kinematics, the configurations, the motion profiles, are in the Theory corner, a tab of their own. The API reference is where every method and command is listed, read from the API's source at the version named above.

  • Start here

    The interfaces at a glance: which program for which job, and what they have in common.

  • Theory corner

    Units, joints and poses, frames, kinematics, singularities, motion profiles, blending, control ownership, and more.

  • The Python API

    Installation, the controller, clients, motion, jogging and servoing, tools, status, errors, examples.

  • RBTscript

    RBTscript, the commander software's program language, and examples; the commander itself is in the GUI Guide.

  • ROS 2 and others

    ROS 2 and MoveIt, other interfaces: the serial protocol directly, the legacy API, AI agents.

  • API reference

    Every Python method, RBTscript, the serial protocol, firmware parameters.

docs.title: 1. The interfaces at a glance
docs.text:
Every way of programming PAROL6 ends at the same place: a packet to the control board every 10 ms with the joint speeds and positions to execute. What differs is who computes those packets and how you tell it what you want.

Commander software Python API ROS 2 + MoveIt Waldo Commander (community) What it is A desktop GUI with a simulator and a program editor A controller process and a Python client library A MoveIt configuration and a ros2_control interface on top of the Python API's controller A browser GUI on top of the Python API, with an MCP server for LLMs You write RBTscript, one command per line Python ROS 2 nodes, MoveIt plans Python, in the browser, or prompts Motion Joint and Cartesian moves, trapezoidal or quintic profiles, teach by jogging Planned moves (joint, linear, circular, spline, process), streamed jogs and servo targets, blending, five profiles, collision checking MoveIt planning What the API offers, plus teach by demonstration Tools SSG-48 and MSG gripper tab, outputs Registered tools with variants, TCP transforms, tool actions in the motion queue Through the bridge Through the API Simulator 3D window, needs the robot connected Simulator mode and a dry-run client, no robot needed RViz 3D preview, no robot needed Runs on The PC at the robot The controller at the robot; clients anywhere on the network Ubuntu 22.04 with ROS 2 Humble Any browser; the server at the robot Python 3.10 or 3.11 3.11 to 3.14 3.11 or newer Maturity Stable, no releases, main branch Pre-1.0, released often, interfaces can change between minors Demo and real-robot launch files Community project Best for The first day; teaching points; demos; simple sequences Everything else ROS users Remote use; AI-driven control

docs.title: Which one
docs.text:
• You have never run the robot: the commander software. The GUI shows the robot, the jog buttons check the wiring, and a three-line program is a minute's work.
  • You want to write programs: the Python API. Its controller runs the robot; your script, or several, talk to it; the dry-run client tests the script without a robot.
  • You have a ROS 2 stack: the MoveIt configuration, with the Python API's controller underneath.
  • You want to drive the arm from a browser or an LLM: Waldo Commander, a community project on the API.

docs.title: What they share
docs.text:
• The serial protocol to the control board, at 100 Hz.
  • The robot model: the joint limits, the gear ratios, the standby pose, the kinematics (Theory corner).
  • The rule that one program owns the board: the commander and the API's controller cannot be connected at the same time (Control ownership).
  • Homing after every power-up, and the E-stop handled by the PC software (Emergency stop).

docs.title: What they do not share
docs.text: Poses and programs do not transfer between the commander and the API without care: the commander's kinematic model assumes the pneumatic gripper, the API's assumes the tool you select, and the two have different speed limits and profiles. A pose taught in one is a starting point in the other, not a result.

docs.title: 4. ROS 2 and MoveIt
docs.text: PAROL6-ROS2-MOVEIT is a MoveIt 2 configuration for PAROL6 with the URDF, a simulation demo and launch files, tested on Ubuntu 22.04 with ROS 2 Humble.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text:
sudo apt install ros-humble-desktop ros-humble-moveit
mkdir -p ~/ros2_ws/src && cd ~/ros2_ws/src
git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/PAROL6-ROS2-MOVEIT.git
cd ~/ros2_ws && colcon build
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash && source install/setup.bash
LC_NUMERIC=en_US.UTF-8 ros2 launch parol6_moveit demo.launch.py
