RViz opens with the robot, and MoveIt plans and executes on the mock hardware.

docs.title: The real robot
docs.text:
real_robot.launch.py brings up the same stack on ros2_control, with a hardware interface and a bridge that talk to the Python API's controller, which must be running (parol6-server --serial ..., or its simulator mode). The hardware interface lives in parol6_ros2_control, a community repository, cloned next to the MoveIt package:

cd ~/ros2_ws/src
git clone https://github.com/grahas/parol6_ros2_control.git
cd ~/ros2_ws && colcon build
ros2 launch parol6_moveit real_robot.launch.py bridge_python:=/path/to/venv/bin/python3

The bridge_python must have the parol6 package installed. On Ubuntu 22.04 it does not install: the package needs Python 3.11 or newer, and on Linux its kinematics backend ships wheels only for glibc 2.39 or newer (Ubuntu 24.04), while 22.04 has Python 3.10 and glibc 2.35 (Installation). The interface's README gives the way round it: run parol6-server and the bridge on another machine, or under WSL2, where parol6 installs, and point the hardware interface's bridge_host parameter at it over the network.

docs.title: The URDF
docs.text: The robot description, URDF and MuJoCo with meshes and a version per tool, is in robot_descriptions, and an earlier URDF is inside the Python API (parol6/urdf_model). The gripper repositories have URDF and MJCF descriptions of the SSG-48 and MSG for attaching to it.

docs.title: Other ROS 2 projects
docs.text: parol6_commander, a web GUI on ROS 2 and MoveIt 2, and Parol6-firmware, alternative firmware with micro-ROS, are community projects (Community projects).

docs.title: Waldo Commander (web)
docs.text: A community browser interface on the Python API, with a simulator, programs in the browser, teaching by demonstration and an MCP server for LLMs: Waldo Commander in the GUI Guide.

docs.title: The serial protocol directly
docs.text: Anything that frames the packets of the serial protocol and keeps the 100 Hz cadence can drive the control board from any language. The Python API's serial transport and the commander's Serial_sender_good_latest.py are the two reference implementations.

docs.title: The legacy Python API
docs.text: PAROL6-python-API-Alvar was the first Python API: a headless commander (headless_commander.py) on the PC at the robot, listening for text commands over UDP on port 5001, and a thin client (robot_api.py) with functions like move_robot_joints, move_robot_pose, control_electric_gripper. It is frozen and kept for the projects built on it, including the Gemini vision demo. New work belongs on the current API.

docs.title: AI agents
docs.text: The current API's typed client, its dry-run preview and the MCP server in Waldo Commander are the paths for LLM-driven control: an agent writes Python against the client, previews it dry, and runs it with a human at the E-stop. The community list has examples (Community projects).

docs.title: The Python API
docs.text: Symptom Cause Remedy ping() returns None No controller, wrong host or port, a firewall Start parol6-server; check --host/--port; allow UDP 5001 ping() says hardware_connected=False No serial port given, or it failed to open --serial COM5, or connect_hardware("COM5"); check the port is free No status in stream_status() Multicast blocked, or a different group PAROL6_STATUS_TRANSPORT=UNICAST with PAROL6_STATUS_UNICAST_HOST; check PAROL6_MCAST_IF MotionError: MOTN_NOT_HOMED The robot is not referenced home(wait=True) MotionError: SYS_ESTOP_ACTIVE The E-stop is pressed or a protective stop is latched Release the button; reset() IK_TARGET_UNREACHABLE on a pose that looks fine Numerical IK, often around joint 4 Change the orientation slightly; start from another posture; a joint move first COMM_VALIDATION_ERROR or decode errors Client and controller of different versions The same version on both sides TimeoutError on a blocking move The move did not complete in timeout Longer timeout; stop() to cancel the queued move loop overbudget by +N% in the log The PC cannot keep 100 Hz Lower PAROL6_CONTROL_RATE_HZ; no DEBUG or TRACE logging; close other programs Jittery motion The same, or a long serial cable As above; a short shielded USB cable Motion refused with SYS_SELF_COLLISION where there is nothing A declared shape, a held object, the tool's mesh shapes(); the tool's variant; PAROL6_COLLISION_CHECK=0 to confirm, then fix the world A tool move fails with MOTN_GRIPPER_* Not calibrated; no gripper answering on CAN tool.calibrate(); the gripper's cable and manual

docs.title: The commander software
docs.text: Symptom Cause Remedy Connect does nothing Wrong port; the port in use; Linux permissions Try again; COMx/ttyACMx; chmod 666 The simulator shows a different pose Not homed Home A command in the program does nothing A typo in the name or the argument order; End() before it The response log; the exact syntax on RBTscript MoveCart stops half way A singularity A joint move, or another orientation Gripper() does nothing Not calibrated; an error latched; a value out of range Gripper tab: Clear gripper error, then Calibrate gripper; whole numbers, current 150 to 1000 mA The program runs once and stops No Loop() Add it, or End() is where you want it Import errors at start Wrong Python or package versions Python 3.10 or 3.11 and the pinned versions, in the commander's own virtual environment, activated (Installation) Time between 2 commands far above 0.010 (seconds, despite the label) The PC Communication

docs.title: Both
docs.text: The control board answers in text when you expected packets: it runs the test firmware; upload the main one (Firmware). Two programs cannot share the port (Control ownership).

docs.title: 2. The Python API
docs.text:
The Python API, package parol6, is two things: a controller process that owns the robot, talks to the control board over serial at 100 Hz, plans the motion and checks collisions; and a client library that sends it commands over UDP, from the same PC or any other on the network, with a blocking interface for scripts and an asynchronous one for applications. A dry-run client runs the same planning without a robot, for tests.

This chapter walks through it in the order you use it. The reference lists every method: Python API reference, read from the API's source at the version this site describes.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Installation
  • The controller: starting it, the serial port, simulator mode, the environment variables
  • Clients: the sync client, the async client, the dry-run client, the Robot lifecycle helper
  • Motion: joint, linear, circular, spline and process moves, speed and duration, blending, profiles
  • Jogging and servoing: streamed velocity and position targets
  • Tools and the TCP: selecting a tool, gripper actions, the TCP transform
  • I/O, delays and checkpoints
  • Status and waiting: queries, the status stream, waiting for commands
  • Errors
  • Examples

docs.title: In three lines
docs.text:
from parol6 import RobotClient
with RobotClient() as rbt:            # the controller runs already: parol6-server --serial COM5
    rbt.home(wait=True); rbt.move_j([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180], speed=0.5)

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Client["Your program"]
        RC["RobotClient / AsyncRobotClient"]
        DR["DryRunRobotClient (no robot)"]
    end
    subgraph Controller["parol6-server"]
        UDP["UDP 5001: commands and queries"]
        Q["Command queue"]
        MP["Motion planner (subprocess)"]
        SP["Segment player, 100 Hz loop"]
        ST["Status broadcast (multicast, 50 Hz)"]
    end
    CB["Control board (serial, 3 Mbaud, 100 Hz)"]
    RC -- commands --> UDP --> Q --> MP --> SP --> CB
    CB -- telemetry --> SP --> ST -- status --> RC

The controller is the only process that touches the serial port. The planner runs in a subprocess so that a long plan never delays the 100 Hz loop; the loop plays the planned segments and streams the jog and servo targets. Status goes out as multicast, so any number of listeners see the robot's state without asking.

docs.title: Clients
docs.text:
Three clients, one interface.

RobotClient AsyncRobotClient DryRunRobotClient Style Blocking calls async/await, status as an async generator Blocking, same methods Needs A running controller A running controller Nothing: plans in-process For Scripts, programs, tests on the robot GUIs, teleoperation, anything that streams Unit tests, previews, CI

All three are created with the controller's host and port (127.0.0.1, 5001 by default), work as context managers, and are closed with close().

docs.title: The sync client
docs.text:
from parol6 import RobotClient

with RobotClient(host="127.0.0.1", port=5001, timeout=2.0) as rbt:
    if not rbt.wait_ready(timeout=5):
        raise SystemExit("no controller")
    rbt.home(wait=True)
    index = rbt.move_j([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180], speed=0.5)    # waits by default (wait=True)
    print(rbt.pose(), rbt.angles())

A motion call returns the command index the controller assigned, or −1 if no acknowledgement arrived; a command the controller refuses raises MotionError. With wait=True the call blocks until that command completes and raises MotionError if it failed; with wait=False the call returns at once and wait_command(index) waits later. Queries return values or None on a timeout.

The defaults differ between the calls and between the clients:

Call RobotClient AsyncRobotClient timeout (used when waiting) move_j, move_l, move_c, move_s, move_p wait=True wait=False 10 s home wait=False wait=False 60 s tool_action and the rbt.tool methods wait=False wait=False 10 s

A move that runs longer than its timeout raises TimeoutError while it goes on running: give long moves a larger timeout.

docs.title: The async client
docs.text:
import asyncio
from parol6 import AsyncRobotClient

async def main():
    async with AsyncRobotClient() as rbt:
        await rbt.wait_ready(timeout=3)
        await rbt.home(wait=True)
        async for status in rbt.stream_status():
            print(status.angles, status.action_state)
            if status.completed_index >= 0:
                break

asyncio.run(main())

The same methods, awaited, with one difference: the moves return at once unless you pass wait=True (the table above). Plus stream_status(), which yields a copy of every status broadcast, and stream_status_shared(), which yields the same buffer each time for zero-copy hot paths. Slow consumers skip to the latest status.

docs.title: The dry-run client
docs.text:
from parol6 import DryRunRobotClient

with DryRunRobotClient() as rbt:
    rbt.home(wait=True)
    rbt.move_l([0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5)     # planned, collision-checked, not executed anywhere

The same calls run through the planner in your process and report what the controller would do: refused targets, collisions, durations. Its status and timing are a preview, not a measurement; the API marks that by advertising execution.preview.

docs.title: The bound tool
docs.text: rbt.tool is the tool object of the selected tool, with open(), close(), set_position(), calibrate(), release(), stop() and status() as the tool type has them (Tools and the TCP). It raises if no tool is selected.

docs.title: Several clients
docs.text: The controller serves any number of clients at once; the queue and the streamed motion are shared (Control ownership). A client that must know its command finished waits on its own index, never on "the robot stopped".

docs.title: The controller
docs.text: parol6-server is the process that owns the robot. Start it on the PC the control board is plugged into, and leave it running; clients connect and disconnect as they like.

docs.title: Starting it
docs.text:
parol6-server --serial COM5                # Windows
parol6-server --serial /dev/ttyACM0        # Linux
parol6-server --serial /dev/cu.usbmodem1   # macOS: ls /dev/cu.usbmodem* gives the name
parol6-server                              # no serial port: simulator mode
parol6-server --serial COM5 --log-level INFO

The options, from the source:

Option Default Meaning --host 0.0.0.0 UDP host address --port 5001 UDP port --serial — Serial port (e.g., /dev/ttyUSB0 or COM3) --baudrate 3000000 Serial baudrate -v, --verbose 0 Increase verbosity; -v=INFO, -vv=DEBUG, -vvv=TRACE -q, --quiet flag Enable quiet logging (WARNING level) --log-level — Set specific log level (one of TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL)

The serial port can also come from the environment (PAROL6_COM_PORT) or from the file the controller saves the last port to, so that a second start needs no option. Once running, connect_hardware("COM5") from a client connects or re-connects the port, and simulator(True) switches to the virtual arm.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
The Robot class starts and stops the controller as a subprocess, for scripts that should be self-contained:

from parol6 import Robot, RobotClient

with Robot(host="127.0.0.1", port=5001) as robot:      # starts parol6-server, waits until it answers
    with RobotClient() as rbt:
        rbt.wait_ready(timeout=5)
        rbt.simulator(True)
        rbt.home(wait=True)

Robot also carries the robot model (kinematics, limits, tools) that the clients use for previews.

docs.title: Simulator mode
docs.text: Without a serial port, or after simulator(True), the controller runs the same planner against a virtual arm and broadcasts its state. Everything works except the hardware: homing is instant, teleport() sets the pose, collisions are checked. Develop in the simulator and switch to the hardware with connect_hardware() or a restart with --serial.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text: The controller sends a packet to the board every 10 ms (100 Hz) and broadcasts status at 50 Hz. If the PC cannot keep up it logs loop overbudget by +N%, as a warning when it happens more than three times a minute (at DEBUG level otherwise); loop_stats() shows the figures. Lower PAROL6_CONTROL_RATE_HZ, close other programs, and keep logging at INFO or above: TRACE and DEBUG cost time.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Everything configurable without code, read at start-up:

Variable Default PAROL6_BLEND_HOLD_S 0.1 PAROL6_BUSY_THRESHOLD_MS 1.0 PAROL6_COLLISION_CHECK 1 PAROL6_COLLISION_CLEARANCE_M 0.005 PAROL6_COLLISION_JOG_LOOKAHEAD_S 0.15 PAROL6_COLLISION_PATH_SAMPLES 16 PAROL6_COLLISION_SRDF computed PAROL6_COM_FILE computed PAROL6_COM_PORT — PAROL6_CONTROL_RATE_HZ 100 PAROL6_EXECUTION_OVERRIDE_TRANSITION_S 1.0 PAROL6_MAX_BACKLOG_COUNT 500 PAROL6_MAX_BLEND_LOOKAHEAD 100 PAROL6_MCAST_GROUP 239.255.0.101 PAROL6_MCAST_IF 127.0.0.1 PAROL6_MCAST_PORT 50510 PAROL6_MCAST_TTL 1 PAROL6_PATH_SAMPLES 200 PAROL6_SERIAL — PAROL6_SETTLE_MAX_TICKS 20 PAROL6_STATUS_RATE_HZ 50 PAROL6_STATUS_STALE_S 0.5 PAROL6_STATUS_TRANSPORT MULTICAST PAROL6_STATUS_UNICAST_HOST 127.0.0.1 PAROL_TRACE 0

The ones you are most likely to touch: PAROL6_COM_PORT (the serial port), PAROL6_CONTROL_RATE_HZ and PAROL6_STATUS_RATE_HZ (the loop and broadcast rates), PAROL6_MCAST_GROUP and PAROL6_MCAST_PORT (where the status goes; PAROL6_STATUS_TRANSPORT=UNICAST with PAROL6_STATUS_UNICAST_HOST for networks without multicast), and PAROL6_COLLISION_CHECK (0 disables collision checking). A path or an expression as the default is marked computed: see config.py.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: The controller accepts any well-formed command on its UDP port from anyone who can reach it. That is by design, so that a GUI and a script can share it, and it means: run it on a trusted network, or bind --host 127.0.0.1.

docs.title: MotionError
docs.text:
A command the controller refuses or fails raises MotionError, carrying a RobotError with a code, a title, a cause, an effect and a remedy from the controller's catalog:

from parol6 import RobotClient, MotionError

with RobotClient() as rbt:
    try:
        rbt.move_l([900, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], speed=0.5)
    except MotionError as e:
        print(e)            # IK: target unreachable — ... — Verify target is within workspace...

The codes are on Errors. The ones you meet first:

Code When MOTN_NOT_HOMED Planned motion before the robot is referenced: home() first IK_TARGET_UNREACHABLE, IK_PARTIAL_PATH The pose, or part of a Cartesian path, has no solution SYS_ESTOP_ACTIVE The E-stop is pressed or a protective stop is latched: release, then reset() SYS_CONTROLLER_DISABLED The controller is disabled SYS_SELF_COLLISION The path collides with the robot itself or with a declared shape MOTN_CANCELLED The command was discarded by stop(), an E-stop, a stream taking the arm, a teleport, or a failure ahead of it in the queue COMM_VALIDATION_ERROR, COMM_DECODE_ERROR A malformed command; usually a version mismatch between client and controller

error() returns the current error, activity() the state with the error description, and the status stream carries error.

docs.title: ValueError and TimeoutError
docs.text: The client checks parameters before sending: a wrong number of angles, a speed outside (0, 1], a non-finite value, an unknown tool action raise ValueError locally. A blocking call whose completion is not confirmed in its timeout raises TimeoutError; the command stays queued, and stop() cancels it. A query that gets no reply returns None, except the TCP queries and bounded I/O writes, which raise rather than report a misleading value.

docs.title: ConnectionError
docs.text: A controller restart during a wait changes the session, and the wait raises ConnectionError: the index you were waiting for belongs to a controller that no longer exists.

docs.title: Recovering
docs.text: After Do stop() Nothing: the controller is enabled and holding; queue again estop() or the E-stop button Release the button; reset() reset_state() The shapes, tool, errors, pause, profile and speed are back to defaults; select the tool again; a protective stop stays until reset() A collision or stall on the hardware Stop; move the arm clear; home(calibrate=True) A failed command in the queue Everything behind it was cancelled: re-queue from the failed one

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The API's repository has runnable scripts in examples/; these are the shapes of program you will write most.

docs.title: A self-contained script
docs.text:
Starts the controller, runs in the simulator, moves, stops the controller.

from parol6 import Robot, RobotClient

with Robot(host="127.0.0.1", port=5001, normalize_logs=True):
    with RobotClient(timeout=2.0) as rbt:
        if not rbt.wait_ready(timeout=5.0):
            raise SystemExit("controller did not start")
        rbt.simulator(True)
        rbt.home(wait=True)                     # planned motion is refused until the robot is referenced
        print("pose:", rbt.pose()[:3], "angles:", rbt.angles())
        rbt.move_l([0, 0, 5, 0, 0, 0], rel=True, duration=1.0)

docs.title: Pick and place with an electric gripper
docs.text:
from parol6 import RobotClient

ABOVE_PICK  = [100, 300, 200, 90, 0, 90]
PICK        = [100, 300, 120, 90, 0, 90]
ABOVE_PLACE = [-100, 300, 200, 90, 0, 90]
PLACE       = [-100, 300, 120, 90, 0, 90]

with RobotClient() as rbt:
    rbt.select_tool("SSG-48")
    rbt.home(wait=True)
    rbt.tool.calibrate()                                # the API gives it 2 s
    rbt.delay(2)                                        # the rest of the SSG-48's calibration
    rbt.tool.open()
    for _ in range(3):
        rbt.move_j(pose=ABOVE_PICK, speed=0.5)
        rbt.move_l(PICK, speed=0.3)
        rbt.tool.close(speed=0.5, current=0.5)          # queued: the next move waits for the grip
        rbt.move_l(ABOVE_PICK, speed=0.3)
        rbt.move_j(pose=ABOVE_PLACE, speed=0.5)
        rbt.move_l(PLACE, speed=0.3)
        rbt.tool.open()
        rbt.move_l(ABOVE_PLACE, speed=0.3)
    rbt.home()

docs.title: A circle, a spline, a raster
docs.text:
From the API's showcase: three ways to draw a curve, in the XZ plane at a fixed Y.

import math
from parol6 import RobotClient

rbt = RobotClient()
rbt.home()
R, Y, ORI = 30, 340, [90, 0, 90]

def pt(cx, cz, deg):
    a = math.radians(deg)
    return [cx + R * math.cos(a), Y, cz + R * math.sin(a)] + ORI

rbt.move_j(pose=pt(0, 280, 0), speed=0.5)
rbt.move_c(via=pt(0, 280, 180), end=pt(0, 280, 0), speed=0.8)            # a full circle in one arc

waypoints = [pt(0, 140, i * 30) for i in range(12)] + [pt(0, 140, 0)]
rbt.move_l(waypoints[0], speed=0.8)
rbt.move_p(waypoints, speed=0.8)                                         # the same circle as a process path

spline = [[R * math.cos(t * 6 * math.pi), Y, 140 + t * 140] + ORI for t in (i / 36 for i in range(37))]
rbt.move_s(spline, speed=0.8)                                            # a sine wave up the three circles

for i in range(6):                                                       # a raster with blended corners
    y0, y1 = (0, 160) if i % 2 == 0 else (160, 0)
    z = 200 + i * 20
    rbt.move_l([280, y0, z, -180, -90, -180], speed=0.5, r=15)
    rbt.move_l([280, y1, z, -180, -90, -180], speed=0.5, r=15)
rbt.close()

docs.title: Following a target with a servo stream
docs.text:
import asyncio, math, time
from parol6 import AsyncRobotClient

async def main():
    async with AsyncRobotClient() as rbt:
        await rbt.home(wait=True)
        await rbt.move_l([0, 263, 272, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5, wait=True)   # to the circle's start
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        while time.monotonic() - t0 < 10:
            t = time.monotonic() - t0
            await rbt.servo_l([30 * math.sin(t), 263, 242 + 30 * math.cos(t), 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5)
            await asyncio.sleep(0.02)                   # 50 targets a second
        # the stream ends by itself a quarter second after the last target

asyncio.run(main())

The async client's moves return at once unless wait=True is given (the sync client waits by default). Without it, the first servo_l would take the arm from the move_l and cancel it.

docs.title: Switching an output between moves, and a checkpoint for the script
docs.text:
with RobotClient() as rbt:
    rbt.home(wait=True)
    rbt.move_l([0, 263, 200, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5, wait=False)
    rbt.write_io(0, 1)                                  # the valve, queued: it switches when the arm is at the part
    rbt.checkpoint("at_part")
    rbt.delay(0.5)
    rbt.move_l([0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5, wait=False)
    rbt.write_io(0, 0)                                  # queued after the second move
    rbt.wait_checkpoint("at_part", timeout=20)
    print("at the part")                                # the script learns it here, e.g. to trigger a camera
    rbt.wait_motion()

write_io is queued with the motion, so the valve switches between the two moves without the script's help; the checkpoint only tells the script when the queue got there.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 to 3.14.
  • Windows (x86-64), Linux (x86-64, ARM64) or macOS (ARM64): the kinematics backend, pinokin, ships wheels for these, for Python 3.11 to 3.14. Its Linux wheels need glibc 2.39 or newer: Ubuntu 24.04 or newer, not 22.04. Its macOS wheels need macOS 15 or newer.
  • The PC at the robot: the minimum PC of the Robot Manual. A client that only sends commands runs anywhere.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
From a clone of PAROL6-python-API, in a virtual environment:

WindowsLinuxmacOS 

git clone https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API.git
cd PAROL6-python-API
git checkout v0.9.1
py -3.11 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install .
The robot's serial port is COM and a number: Device Manager lists it under Ports (COM & LPT).

git clone https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API.git
cd PAROL6-python-API
git checkout v0.9.1
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install .
sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER     # access to the serial port; log out and in again once
The robot's serial port is /dev/ttyACM0 (ls /dev/ttyACM* lists it).

git clone https://github.com/PCrnjak/PAROL6-python-API.git
cd PAROL6-python-API
git checkout v0.9.1
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install .
Apple silicon (ARM64) only. The robot's serial port is /dev/cu.usbmodem and a number (ls /dev/cu.usbmodem* lists it).

The package pulls pinokin, numpy, scipy, Ruckig, TOPP-RA, numba, pyserial, msgspec, ormsgpack, psutil and the waldoctl interface layer. pip install -e . installs it editable for development.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
parol6-server --log-level=INFO

starts the controller in simulator mode when no serial port is given. In another terminal:

from parol6 import RobotClient
with RobotClient() as rbt:
    print(rbt.ping())

Check

It prints a PingResult with hardware_connected=False. Stop the server with Ctrl-C.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: The API is pre-1.0 and released often; a minor version can change an interface, and the controller and the client must be the same version, since they share the wire protocol. The release notes list the changes; this site describes v0.9.1.

docs.title: Digital I/O
docs.text:
The control board's two inputs, two outputs and the E-stop, as the firmware reports them:

state = rbt.io()                 # [in1, in2, out1, out2, estop], or None on a timeout
rbt.write_io(0, 1)               # output 1 high; logical index 0 = the first output
rbt.write_io(1, 0, timeout=1.0)  # raises TimeoutError if not confirmed in time

The firmware's I/O byte is [in1, in2, out1, out2, estop, ...], so logical output 0 is bit 2 of the byte; write_io does the mapping. is_estop_pressed() reads the E-stop alone. A per-call timeout bounds the setup, the retries and the reply; without one the client's defaults apply.

A write is queued with the motion: it takes effect when its turn in the queue comes, and it returns a command index that wait_command() waits on. The pneumatic gripper's open() and close() are output writes of the same kind. While the controller is disabled, after estop() or the E-stop until reset(), a write is refused with SYS_CONTROLLER_DISABLED, like a move.

docs.title: Switching an output at a point of a program
docs.text:
Queue the write between the two moves it belongs between. The output changes when the first move has finished, and the second move starts after it:

rbt.move_l([0, 263, 200, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5, wait=False)   # to the part
rbt.write_io(0, 1)                                              # output 1 high, once the arm is there
rbt.delay(0.5)                                                  # let the valve act
rbt.move_l([0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5, wait=False)   # away again
rbt.write_io(0, 0)                                              # output 1 low at the end
rbt.wait_motion()

A checkpoint() is for something outside the robot that must know when the queue reaches a point; the outputs do not need one.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
rbt.delay(1.0)                   # a second of nothing, in the queue

A queued delay holds the arm for its duration at its place in the queue; it is not time.sleep(), which would hold your script and not the robot. A paused queue keeps the delay's remaining time.

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text:
index = rbt.checkpoint("pick_done")
...
rbt.wait_checkpoint("pick_done", timeout=30)

A checkpoint is a labelled marker in the queue; wait_checkpoint() blocks until the queue reaches it, and the status stream reports last_checkpoint. It is how a program synchronises something outside the robot, a conveyor or a camera, with a point in the motion.

docs.title: Motion
docs.text: Planned motion: the client sends a target, the controller plans the trajectory in its planner subprocess, checks it for collisions and limits, queues it, and plays it. Every planned command returns a command index and runs in queue order.

docs.title: The five moves
docs.text:
Call Path Target move_j(angles) Straight in joint space: every joint moves proportionally, all finish together. The tool's path curves Six joint angles, or pose= a Cartesian pose solved once at the target move_l(pose) A straight line of the tool, orientation interpolated A pose in the WRF, or in the TRF with frame="TRF" move_c(via, end) A circular arc from the current pose through via to end Two poses move_s(waypoints) A cubic spline through the waypoints A list of poses move_p(waypoints) A process path: the waypoints joined by lines, run at constant tool speed with automatic blending at the corners A list of poses

rel=True on move_j and move_l makes the target relative to the current angles or pose; with frame="TRF" a relative move_l moves along the tool's own axes.

rbt.move_j([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180], speed=0.5)                 # joint move
rbt.move_j(pose=[100, 340, 334, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5)           # IK at the target, then a joint move
rbt.move_l([-50, 340, 334, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.3)                # straight line
rbt.move_l([0, 0, -20, 0, 0, 0], frame="TRF", rel=True, speed=0.2)   # 20 mm along the tool's -Z
rbt.move_c(via=[0, 250, 250, 90, 0, 90], end=[0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5)
rbt.move_s([[0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90], [50, 250, 200, 90, 0, 90]], speed=0.5)
rbt.move_p(waypoints, speed=0.8)

docs.title: Speed, acceleration, duration
docs.text:
speed and accel are fractions of the robot model's maxima in (0, 1], default 0.5 each. For a joint move they scale the leading joint; for a Cartesian move they scale the tool's linear and angular limits, with the joint limits as hard bounds. A duration in seconds times the move instead and speed is ignored; duration and speed are not combined. The move's actual speed is also capped by what the profile and the limits allow: a short move never reaches the asked speed.

rbt.move_l(target, speed=0.25, accel=1.0)      # a quarter of the Cartesian speed limit, full acceleration
rbt.move_l(target, duration=2.0)               # two seconds, whatever that takes

docs.title: Blending
docs.text: r, in millimetres, on move_j, move_l and move_c: the move does not stop at its target but blends into the next queued move within that radius (Blending). move_p blends on its own.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text: select_profile("TOPPRA") and the others set how the speed curve is shaped for all planned moves (Motion profiles); profile() reads it. The profiles of this version: TOPPRA, RUCKIG, QUINTIC, TRAPEZOID, LINEAR.

docs.title: Waiting
docs.text: wait=True, the default, blocks until the move completes and raises MotionError if it was cancelled or failed; TimeoutError if the timeout runs out first, in which case the move is still queued and stop() cancels it. wait=False returns the index for a later wait_command(); wait_motion() waits for the whole queue and for the arm to come to rest (Status and waiting).

docs.title: Execution speed and pause
docs.text: set_execution_speed(0.5) runs the queued trajectory at half its planned speed from now on, 10 to 100 %; pause() decelerates the queue to a hold and resume() continues it. Both keep the queue. A paused robot's execution_speed().paused is true once it has actually stopped.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text: A target outside the joint limits, a pose the IK cannot solve, a path that collides, an unhomed robot, a latched protective stop: the command is refused before anything moves, with a MotionError whose code says why (Errors). A refused command cancels nothing already queued; a command that fails while running cancels everything queued behind it.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
Every query is a request to the controller with a reply, returning None on a timeout:

rbt.ping()            # PingResult: hardware_connected
rbt.angles()          # [J1..J6] in degrees
rbt.pose()            # [x, y, z, rx, ry, rz], mm and degrees; pose("TRF") in the tool frame
rbt.joint_speeds()    # deg/s
rbt.tcp_speed()       # mm/s
rbt.io()              # [in1, in2, out1, out2, estop]
rbt.status()          # StatusSnapshot: pose, angles, speeds, io, tool_status
rbt.activity()        # what the robot does now: state, command, parameters, error
rbt.queue()           # the queued commands
rbt.error()           # the current RobotError, or None
rbt.reachable()       # remaining travel per joint and axis
rbt.tools(); rbt.profile(); rbt.tcp_offset(); rbt.tcp_transform(); rbt.shapes()
rbt.loop_stats(); rbt.status_rate(); rbt.execution_speed(); rbt.is_simulator()

docs.title: The status stream
docs.text:
The controller broadcasts its state at 50 Hz (set_status_rate() changes it) as multicast; the async client yields it as a stream:

async for s in rbt.stream_status():
    s.angles, s.speeds, s.pose, s.io, s.tool_status
    s.action_state, s.action_current, s.executing_index, s.completed_index, s.accepted_index
    s.error, s.homed, s.enabled, s.simulator_active, s.collision_active
    s.session_id, s.seq, s.mono_time_ns          # for recording: a session, a sequence, a timestamp

The fields are listed on Status fields. seq gaps mean missed broadcasts; session_id changes when the controller restarts; mono_time_ns is the time of the controller's snapshot, not of the sensor reading. The sync client's wait_status(predicate) waits for a status that satisfies a function.

docs.title: Waiting for a command
docs.text:
index = rbt.move_l(target, wait=False)
ok = rbt.wait_command(index, timeout=10)        # True when completed; raises MotionError if it failed

wait_command asks the controller for that command's exact result. Queued commands run in index order, so a wait on one covers everything queued before it; a jog or a tool.stop() can finish earlier than something queued before it, which is why a wait never infers success from the highest completed index. A command discarded by stop(), an E-stop, reset_state(), a teleport or a failure ahead of it raises MotionError with MOTN_CANCELLED at once; an unknown or expired result stays unconfirmed and the wait returns False at its timeout. The controller keeps its last 1024 completions and 1024 failures.

wait_motion() waits for the whole queue to run out and the arm to hold still for a settle window; wait_ready() polls ping() until the controller answers; is_robot_stopped() looks at the joint speeds only.

docs.title: What "done" means
docs.text: A blocking move returns when the controller reports the command complete: the trajectory played to its end and the arm at the commanded position, in counted steps. For a tool action, when the gripper's estimated travel time or its reported state says so. Neither is a measurement of the world: a program that needs to know the part is in the gripper checks where the jaws stopped (tool.status().positions) or reads a sensor. For the electric grippers, the tool status's part_detected does not follow the gripper's object-detection bits at this version (Tool status).

docs.title: Jogging and servoing
docs.text:
Streamed motion is for a hand on a button or a loop that computes the next target: a jog is a velocity held for a short time, a servo target is a position to go to now. Both bypass the queue and take the arm at once (the queue is cancelled). They end differently:

  • A jog runs for its duration (0.1 s by default), then the arm brakes to rest and holds. A held button sends a new jog before the last one runs out.
  • A servo stream ends about 0.25 s after the last target arrives, when the arm brakes to rest and holds.

docs.title: Jogging
docs.text:
rbt.jog_j(0, speed=0.3, duration=0.5)                             # joint 1 (index 0), 30 %, 0.5 s
rbt.jog_j(joints=[1, 2], speeds=[0.2, -0.2], duration=1.0)        # two joints
rbt.jog_l("WRF", "X", speed=0.2, duration=0.5)                    # the tool along world X
rbt.jog_l("TRF", axes=["Z", "RZ"], speeds_list=[0.2, 0.1], duration=0.5)

Speeds are signed fractions of the maximum in [−1, 1]; the controller clamps jogs to 80 % of the limits. A GUI sends a jog every few tens of milliseconds while the button is held; the controller de-duplicates repeated targets and extends the motion. A jog stops at a joint limit, and a Cartesian jog stops before a singularity.

docs.title: Servoing
docs.text:
rbt.servo_j([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180], speed=0.5, accel=0.5)       # go to these angles, now
rbt.servo_j(pose=[0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90])                          # via IK
rbt.servo_l([0, 263, 242, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5)                    # a straight line to the pose

A servo target is fire-and-forget: the controller plans a jerk-limited motion from where the arm is to the target and follows it, re-planning as new targets arrive. A stream of targets at 20 to 100 Hz gives smooth tracking of a moving goal, which is how teleoperation and following a camera are built. The stream ends a quarter second after the last target.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Cartesian jogs (jog_l) and servo targets need a homed robot, like planned motion; they are refused with MOTN_NOT_HOMED before it. Joint jogs (jog_j) work before homing, so that an arm can be jogged clear of an obstruction first.
  • It cancels the planned queue: every queued command fails with MOTN_CANCELLED. Do not interleave a servo stream with planned moves you still want.
  • Keep the targets reachable and the steps between them small; a target far from the current pose is a fast move at the asked speed.
  • Collision checking applies to jogs with a look-ahead (PAROL6_COLLISION_JOG_LOOKAHEAD_S).

docs.title: Status while streaming
docs.text: The status stream reports action_state and the actual angles at 50 Hz; stream_status() on the async client is the natural partner of a servo loop (Status and waiting).

docs.title: Tools and the TCP
docs.text: The controller needs to know the tool to compute the pose of its tip, to check it for collisions and to drive it. Tools are registered in the API with a transform, a collision mesh, variants and the actions they support.

docs.title: Registered tools
docs.text:
Key Tool Variants (default first) NONE Bare flange - no tool attached — PNEUMATIC Pneumatic gripper assembly (vertical/horizontal mounting) vertical, horizontal SSG-48 SSG-48 adaptive electric gripper (Spectral micro BLDC) finger, pinch MSG MSG compliant AI stepper gripper (StepFOC) 100mm, 150mm, 200mm VACUUM Vacuum gripper (pneumatic valve I/O) —

select_tool(key, variant_key) sets the active tool for everyone, queued with the motion; tools() lists them; rbt.tool.status() and the status stream's tool_status report the applied variant and the tool's state. Changing the tool or the variant clears any TCP correction.

rbt.select_tool("PNEUMATIC")                        # the default variant
rbt.select_tool("PNEUMATIC", variant_key="horizontal")
rbt.select_tool("SSG-48", variant_key="pinch")
rbt.select_tool("MSG", variant_key="150mm")

docs.title: Driving the tool
docs.text:
rbt.tool is the selected tool's object. The electric grippers (SSG-48, MSG) have position, speed and current as fractions of their ranges, and the actions calibrate, stop and release; the pneumatic and vacuum grippers have open and close on an output.

rbt.select_tool("SSG-48")
rbt.tool.calibrate()                                        # queued; the API gives it 2 s
rbt.delay(2)                                                # the rest of the SSG-48's calibration
rbt.tool.set_position(0.7, speed=0.5, current=0.4)          # 0 open, 1 closed
rbt.tool.close(speed=0.5, current=0.6)
rbt.tool.open()
rbt.tool.release()                                          # drop the grip, the jaws stay
rbt.tool.stop()                                             # immediate
print(rbt.tool.status())                                    # ToolStatus: state, engaged, part_detected, positions

The current fraction spans the tool's current range: 100 to 1300 mA for the SSG-48 and 100 to 2800 mA for the MSG, so current=0.4 is 580 mA on the SSG-48 and 1180 mA on the MSG. Keep an MSG within its stepper's rating (MSG).

docs.title: Calibrating
docs.text: The gripper has to be calibrated after every power-up: it opens fully and closes fully to find its end stops. calibrate() sends the calibration and counts it done after a fixed 2 s (200 control cycles); it does not read the gripper's calibrated bit. The gripper takes longer: about 3 s for the SSG-48, and about 5 to 6 s for the MSG on the longer rails. Queue a delay() after calibrate() to cover the rest with a margin, 2 s for the SSG-48 and 5 s for the MSG, before the first move. A gripper that has latched an error must be cleared first: the API has no clear-error action at this version, so use the commander's Clear gripper error or Motor GUI, then calibrate.

docs.title: Tool status
docs.text:
rbt.tool.status() returns a ToolStatus. For the electric grippers, positions is the jaw position (0 open, 1 closed) and channels the current in mA. engaged is taken from the gripper-speed field of the telemetry, which firmware 1 always reports as 1, so it reads true. part_detected is taken from bits 3 and 2 of the gripper's status byte, where the gripper manuals put the temperature and timeout errors (they put the object detection in bits 5 and 4). The calibrated and error bits are not in ToolStatus at this version. To know that a part is held, check the position the jaws stopped at, or use a sensor.

Tool actions are queued work: an action waits for the motion queued before it, the arm holds still while it runs, and the motion queued after it waits for it. A move on a gripper that was never calibrated is refused when its turn comes and, like any failing command, cancels what is queued behind it. stop() is the exception: it is immediate, halts the running action, and keeps the queue. tool_action(key, action, params) is the generic form the tool methods are built on.

docs.title: The TCP
docs.text:
The tool centre point is the point the robot positions: the registered tool's tip. Two corrections on top of it:

index = rbt.set_tcp_offset(0, 0, -190)           # a translation in the tool frame, mm
index = rbt.set_tcp_transform(0, 0, 25, 0, 90, 0) # translation and intrinsic XYZ rotation, degrees
rbt.wait_command(index)                           # queued: wait before relying on it
print(rbt.tcp_transform())                        # six values; tcp_offset() the three translations

Both are queued with the motion so that moves planned before the change keep their frame. set_tcp_offset clears a rotation; a tool change clears both. The correction applies to live FK, Cartesian planning, TRF motion and dry-run previews alike; the collision meshes stay on their links regardless.

docs.title: Your own tool
docs.text: Add a ToolConfig and register_tool("KEY", config) in parol6/tools.py: the transform from the flange, the collision mesh, the variants, and the actions if it is driven through the robot (Your own tool). The controller validates every tool action against the config before it is acknowledged.

docs.title: Held objects
docs.text: A program can declare the shape of what the gripper holds, attached to the flange, so that the collision checker accounts for it: shape.attach(...) on a shape from rbt.shapes(), applied with set_shapes(). The declaration is tied to the tool, the world and a fresh position reference; a change in any of them invalidates it and blocks motion until it is reconciled. The README of the API has the rules in full.

docs.title: 3. RBTscript
docs.text:
RBTscript is the program language of the commander software: one command per line, run by the commander's interpreter while its GUI shows the robot. It is the quickest way from a taught pose to a repeating sequence, and it is the limit of what the commander does: for blending, collision checking, tool selection and a network interface, the Python API.

  • RBTscript: the language, its units, every command
  • Examples

The commander itself, its installation and its windows, is in the GUI Guide.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Programs from the repository's GUI/files/Programs folder and the documentation. Paste one into the program window, read it against the simulator, and press Start. The speed slider does not slow a program: for a first run, lower v= or raise t= in the moves.

docs.title: A joint-space loop
docs.text:
Two poses, back and forth, with a timed first move.

Begin()
Delay(1)
MoveJoint(85.078,-111.195,143.513,-32.92,18.084,129.448,t=3)
Delay(1)
MoveJoint(66.129,-117.368,136.77,46.28,-29.588,149.293)
Delay(1)
Loop()

docs.title: Cartesian moves in the world frame
docs.text:
A joint move to a start pose, then straight-line moves: translations first, then changes of orientation. Watch the simulator to see the tool follow.

Begin()
Delay(1)
MoveJoint(90.0,-90.0,180.001,0.0,0.0,180.0,t=4)
Delay(1)
MoveCart(0.0,263.23,161.241,-90.0,0.0,-89.499)
Delay(1)
MoveCart(81.565,262.804,161.047,-90.135,-0.029,-89.578)
Delay(1)
MoveCart(81.649,194.981,160.077,-90.14,-0.043,-89.593)
Delay(1)
MoveCart(83.598,194.356,161.493,-91.155,1.306,-80.28)
Delay(1)
MoveCart(84.56,194.131,162.347,-48.387,1.261,-80.188)
Delay(1)
MoveCart(82.89,191.698,162.369,-40.587,26.026,-107.028)
Delay(1)
End()

The MoveCart lines have no t=, so each takes 3.6 s whatever its length (MoveCart). Give the long ones a t= for a slower first run.

docs.title: A move relative to the tool
docs.text:
80 mm back along the tool's X axis, from the start pose the program moves to first.

Begin()
Delay(1)
MoveJoint(90.0,-90.0,180.001,0.0,0.0,180.0,t=4)
Delay(1)
MoveCartRelTRF(-80,0,0,0,0,0)
Delay(1)
End()

docs.title: Pick and place with the gripper
docs.text:
From the repository: a joint move over the part, a Cartesian descent, a grip, a transfer and a release. Note the delays after each gripper command.

Begin()
Delay(1)
MoveJoint(89.209,-35.021,174.356,-1.463,-28.645,85.972,t=4)
Delay(1)
Gripper(255,20,120)
Delay(2)
MoveCart(-40.499,298.455,131.712,6.081,-0.739,-179.276)
MoveJoint(15.478,-56.126,178.673,-0.928,-54.084,85.5)
Delay(1)
Gripper(0,100,120)
MoveJoint(89.033,-49.402,174.486,-1.027,-43.341,85.596)
MoveCart(-41.535,300.316,17.635,6.141,-0.686,-179.224)
Delay(1)
Gripper(255,100,1000)
Delay(1)
MoveCart(-40.499,298.455,131.712,6.081,-0.739,-179.276)
MoveJoint(15.478,-56.126,178.673,-0.928,-54.084,85.5)
Gripper(0,100,100)
Delay(1)
End()

Before you run it:

  • It does not calibrate the gripper: clear the gripper's error and calibrate it in the Gripper tab first.
  • Gripper(255,20,120), Gripper(0,100,120) and Gripper(0,100,100) ask for 120 or 100 mA, below the about 150 mA the gripper needs to move: raise the current to at least 150 mA.
  • Gripper(255,100,1000) grips at 1000 mA and speed 100. Above about 700 mA, keep the speed low, or lower the current (Gripper).
  • The MoveCart lines have no t= and take 3.6 s each.

docs.title: Gripper test
docs.text:
Calibration, a few open and close cycles, then a small joint move and a Cartesian move.

Begin()
Gripper_cal()
Delay(3)
Gripper(100,60,600)
Delay(2)
Gripper(200,60,600)
Delay(2)
MoveJoint(85.192,-104.451,158.769,-1.983,-46.491,179.899,t=6)
Delay(1)
MoveCart(4.317,103.384,192.319,-84.465,1.447,-143.154)
Gripper(100,60,600)
Delay(2)
End()

Clear the gripper's error in the Gripper tab before you start it. Delay(3) is just the SSG-48's calibration time; Delay(4) leaves a margin, and the MSG needs Delay(7). The MoveCart has no t= and takes 3.6 s.

docs.title: Toggling an output
docs.text:
A pneumatic gripper, or a lamp, once a second, forever.

Begin()
Output(1,HIGH)
Delay(1)
Output(1,LOW)
Delay(1)
Loop()

docs.title: A dance
docs.text: Timed joint and Cartesian moves in quick succession: example_dance_2.txt in the repository, for a demo once the robot is known to run every pose in it.

docs.title: RBTscript
docs.text:
RBTscript is the commander's program language: one command per line, executed in order, synchronised to the 100 Hz control loop. It has motion in joint and Cartesian space, delays, outputs and the gripper, and a loop. There are no variables, conditions or arithmetic: a program is a sequence.

Begin()
MoveJoint(90,-90,180,0,0,180,t=3)
MoveCart(0,263,242,90,0,90)
Delay(1)
Loop()

docs.title: Units
docs.text: Angles in degrees, positions in millimetres, speed and acceleration in percent of the robot's maximum, time in seconds, gripper position and speed 0 to 255, gripper current in milliamps (Units).

docs.title: MoveJoint
docs.text:
MoveJoint(j1, j2, j3, j4, j5, j6, v=0, a=0, t=0, trap|poly, speed)

Moves all joints to the given angles; the path is a straight line in joint space, all joints stopping together. The tool's path curves.

Argument Meaning Unit j1 … j6 The target joint angles degrees v Speed of the leading joint, the one with the longest way % (0 to 100) a Acceleration and deceleration of the leading joint % t Duration of the move; overrides v and a seconds trap, poly The profile, as a bare word: poly (quintic polynomial) or trap (trapezoidal). "trap" in quotes or func=trap is ignored without a message and gives the default speed The word speed as the last argument: track the speed curve only

The arguments must be in this order. The rules:

  • With t, the move takes that long; the profile is polynomial unless the word trap follows, and a trapezoid with t spends a third of the time in each phase.
  • With v and a, the profile is trapezoidal, for the leading joint; the other joints get what makes them finish together.
  • With neither, a conservative trapezoid.
  • With speed last, only the speed curve is tracked: smoother and quieter, and the robot may stop a few steps short of the target (Target, commanded and actual).
MoveJoint(0,-90,180,0,0,180,t=4)
MoveJoint(0,-90,180,0,0,180,t=4,trap)
MoveJoint(0,-90,180,0,0,180,v=50,a=50)
MoveJoint(0,-90,180,0,0,180)
MoveJoint(0,-90,180,0,0,180,speed)

docs.title: MovePose
docs.text:
MovePose(x, y, z, Rx, Ry, Rz, v=0, a=0, t=0, trap|poly, speed)

Like MoveJoint, but the target is a pose in the WRF: the inverse kinematics is solved once at the target and the robot moves in joint space to the configuration it found, which may not be the one you expected. The same arguments and rules as MoveJoint.

docs.title: MoveCart
docs.text:
MoveCart(x, y, z, Rx, Ry, Rz, v=0, a=0, t=0, trap|poly, speed)

Moves the tool in a straight line to the pose, in the WRF. The joints' motion is whatever the straight line requires, and the move stops if it meets a singularity; the robot does not deviate from the line to avoid one. The timing rules differ from MoveJoint:

  • With t, the move takes that long and the profile is trapezoidal unless the word poly follows, the opposite of MoveJoint.
  • Without t, every move takes 3.6 s, however long it is, so a long move without t is fast. v and a are accepted but only checked for range. Give t for every Cartesian move.

docs.title: MoveCartRelTRF
docs.text:
MoveCartRelTRF(x, y, z, Rx, Ry, Rz, v=0, a=0, t=0, trap|poly, speed)

A straight-line move relative to the current tool frame: MoveCartRelTRF(-80,0,0,0,0,0) moves 80 mm along the tool's −X. For rotations about more than one axis, use two commands, one axis each. The timing rules are those of MoveCart.

docs.title: SpeedJoint, SpeedCart
docs.text: Listed in the command menu, but neither works. SpeedJoint() passes the program check and has no action: the program stops on that line until you press Stop. SpeedCart() fails the check, and a program that contains it is refused; so are the menu's Get_data and Timeouts.

docs.title: Timing and flow
docs.text: Command Meaning Begin() Must be the first line; a program that does not start with it is refused End() Stops the program; the last line must be End() or Loop(), or the program is refused Loop() Restarts at the line after Begin() Delay(t) Waits t seconds; t must be more than 0.01, and Delay(0.01) is refused and stops the program

docs.title: I/O
docs.text:
Output(1,HIGH)
Output(1,LOW)

Sets output 1, with no space after the comma. In the current version Output(2,HIGH) and Output(2,LOW) are refused by a bug in the check (Invalid Output() command) and stop the program, so only output 1 can be switched from a program. Input() appears in the menu but has no action: a program stops on it until you press Stop; Home() behaves the same.

docs.title: Gripper
docs.text:
Gripper_cal()
Delay(4)
Gripper(position, speed, current)
Delay(2)

Gripper_cal() calibrates the SSG-48 or MSG gripper. Clear the gripper's error first, with the Gripper tab's Clear gripper error (RBTscript has no command for it), and add a delay for the calibration to finish: Delay(4) for the SSG-48 (about 3 s) and Delay(7) for the MSG (5 to 6 s on the longer rails). Activating it is the Gripper tab's Activate option, which is on by default. Gripper() moves it, with whole numbers only: position 0 (open) to 255 (closed), speed 0 to 255, current 100 to 1000 mA, the current being the grip force; below about 150 mA the gripper does not move. A value outside these ranges is logged as Gripper() invalid input value, the line is skipped and the program goes on. The program continues at once, so add a Delay() for the gripper to arrive.

Danger

A current above about 700 mA with a high speed slams the jaws into the part and can damage the gripper, the robot and the part. Start low.

A gripper error (not calibrated, E-stop, timeout) stops the gripper until it is cleared in the Gripper tab.

docs.text: The commands on one page: RBTscript commands.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Where you look things up. The Python API pages are generated from the API's source at v0.9.1: the signature and the docstring of every public method of RobotClient, the tool methods, the registered tools, the error codes, the environment variables and the controller's options, with notes written around them. The build fails when a page names a method the API no longer has, and the tests fail when a method is on no page.

  • Python API

    Every method by category: motion, jogging and servoing, control, queries, synchronization, tools, I/O, configuration, the status fields, the errors, the controller.

  • RBTscript

    Every command of the commander's program language, with its arguments.

  • The serial protocol

    The packets between the PC and the control board, byte by byte, and the command codes.

  • Firmware and test firmware

    The firmware's parameters per joint, and the test firmware's commands.

docs.title: Firmware parameters
docs.text: The per-joint parameters of the control board's main firmware (constants.h, motor_init.cpp, main.cpp at release V1): what a builder edits when mastering, fitting a different tool, reducing the currents, or fixing a joint's direction. Steps are 32-microstep motor steps. Firmware says how to upload a change.

docs.title: Currents (constants.h)
docs.text:
Define Value Note MICROSTEP 32 MOTOR1_MAX_CURRENT 2000 mA motor rated 2100 MOTOR2_MAX_CURRENT 2000 mA motor rated 2100 MOTOR3_MAX_CURRENT 1900 mA motor rated 2000 MOTOR4_MAX_CURRENT 1700 mA reduced: the motor is enclosed in the forearm MOTOR5_MAX_CURRENT 1700 mA reduced: enclosed MOTOR6_MAX_CURRENT 965 mA motor rated 1000 VERSION 1

The driver is set to MOTORx_MAX_CURRENT × 0.85 as the running current and hold_multiplier of that for holding (the per-joint table below has both); the driver rounds them to its own current steps.

docs.title: Per joint (motor_init.cpp)
docs.text:
Parameter J1 J2 J3 J4 J5 J6 reduction_ratio 6.4 20 18.0952 4 4 10 standby_position (steps at standby) 10240 −32000 57905 0 0 32000 homed_position (steps from the switch to standby) 13500 19588 23020 −10200 8900 (j5_homing_offset) 15900 joint_range_positive_steps 14000 −1200 92605 7500 6400 64000 joint_range_negative_steps −14000 −51587 34700 −7500 −6400 0 limit_switch_trigger (input level when triggered) 0 (inductive) 1 (switch) 1 (switch) 0 (inductive) 1 (switch) 0 (inductive) direction_reversed 1 0 1 0 0 1 hold_multiplier 0.7 0.8 0.8 0.8 0.8 0.88 Running current, MOTORx_MAX_CURRENT × 0.85 1700 mA 1700 mA 1615 mA 1445 mA 1445 mA 820 mA Holding current, the running current × hold_multiplier 1190 mA 1360 mA 1292 mA 1156 mA 1156 mA 722 mA Driver position / LIMIT input 1 / 6 6 / 2 5 / 3 4 / 4 2 / 5 3 / 1

Joint 1's standby of 10240 steps is +90° (90 / 0.05625 × 6.4): the firmware homes to the pose the software reports as J1 = 90°. The firmware's "standby" is what these pages call the after-homing pose: the standby pose turned 90° about joint 1 (Joint limits and directions).

docs.title: Joint 5 and the tool (main.cpp)
docs.text: Variable Value Note j5_homing_offset 8900 the pneumatic gripper holder; 8035 for the SSG-48

docs.title: Homing speeds and distances (main.cpp, home_all)
docs.text: The approach speeds in steps/s: J1 −2050, J2 −2550, J3 −2550, J4 5550, J5 −5050, J6 −9550; the back-off distances 850 (J1), 1050 (J2, J3), 1550 (J4, J5, J6) steps; the slow re-approach −750 steps/s for joints 1 to 3, ±4050 for 4 and 5, −8050 for 6. The firmware uses the second, slow trigger as the reference.

docs.title: The serial link
docs.text: Serial.begin(3000000); the timing counter runs at 90 MHz / 128 = 703 125 Hz.

docs.title: RBTscript commands
docs.text:
The commands of the commander software's program language, as its interpreter accepts them. One command per line; arguments in the order given; angles in degrees, positions in millimetres, speed and acceleration in percent, time in seconds. RBTscript in the guide has the rules and examples.

Command Arguments What it does Begin() Must be the first line, or the program is refused End() Stops the program; the last line must be End() or Loop() Loop() Restart at the line after Begin() Delay(t) t seconds, more than 0.01 Wait; Delay(0.01) is refused MoveJoint(j1,j2,j3,j4,j5,j6, v=, a=, t=, trap\|poly, speed) six joint angles; v, a in % for the leading joint; t duration; the bare word trap or poly; the word speed A move to joint angles, straight in joint space MovePose(x,y,z,Rx,Ry,Rz, v=, a=, t=, trap\|poly, speed) a WRF pose, then as MoveJoint IK at the target, then a joint-space move MoveCart(x,y,z,Rx,Ry,Rz, v=, a=, t=, trap\|poly, speed) a WRF pose; t; poly or trap; speed A straight-line move of the tool in the WRF; stops at a singularity. With t: trapezoidal unless poly. Without t: always 3.6 s MoveCartRelTRF(x,y,z,Rx,Ry,Rz, v=, a=, t=, trap\|poly, speed) a pose relative to the tool frame A straight-line move relative to the tool; timing as MoveCart SpeedJoint() No action: the program stops on it until Stop SpeedCart() Not accepted: a program containing it is refused Output(n,HIGH\|LOW) output 1; HIGH or LOW, no space Sets output 1; Output(2,...) is refused in the current version and stops the program Input(), Home() No action: the program stops on it until Stop Gripper_cal() Calibrates the electric gripper (clear its error in the Gripper tab first; activation is the tab's Activate option); follow with Delay(4) for the SSG-48, Delay(7) for the MSG Gripper(position, speed, current) whole numbers: 0 to 255; 0 to 255; mA, 100 to 1000 Moves the electric gripper; continues at once, so follow with a Delay()

Rules for MoveJoint and MovePose: t overrides v and a and makes the profile polynomial unless the word trap follows; v with a makes it trapezoidal; neither gives a conservative trapezoid; speed as the last argument tracks the speed curve only and may stop short of the target. MoveCart and MoveCartRelTRF are trapezoidal with t unless poly follows, and take 3.6 s for any move without t. The list is in the commander's PAROL6_ROBOT.py as Commands_list.

docs.title: The serial protocol
docs.text: The packets between the PC and the control board, from the firmware's main.cpp (Unpack_data, Pack_data). Serial over USB at 3 000 000 baud; the PC sends one command packet per 10 ms cycle and the board answers each valid packet with one telemetry packet. Multi-byte values are big-endian; positions and speeds are signed 24-bit integers in motor microsteps and microsteps per second. The serial protocol in the Control Board Manual explains the cycle.

docs.title: PC → board: the command packet
docs.text: Offset after the length byte Size Field Meaning — 3 Start bytes 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF — 1 Length 52: the number of bytes that follow, CRC and end bytes included 0 18 Joints[6] Commanded position of each joint, 3 bytes each, signed, microsteps 18 18 Speed[6] Commanded speed of each joint, 3 bytes each, signed, microsteps/s 36 1 Command The command byte, below 37 1 Affected joint Bit per joint; reserved 38 1 InOut Bits from the MSB: bit 2 = output 1, bit 3 = output 2; the rest reserved 39 1 Timeout Reserved 40 2 Gripper position 0 to 255 42 2 Gripper speed 0 to 255 44 2 Gripper current mA 46 1 Gripper command Bits from the MSB: 0 activate, 1 action, 2 E-stop, 3 release direction 47 1 Gripper mode 0 operate, 1 calibrate, 2 clear error 48 1 Gripper ID The gripper's CAN ID 49 1 CRC Reserved: carried, not checked by firmware 1 50 2 End bytes 0x01 0x02

docs.title: Command bytes
docs.text:
Value Name Effect 255 Idle (dummy) The joints stand still (speeds are set, no joint is stepped). Continues a homing in progress 123 Jog Runs each joint at its commanded speed 156 Go to position with speed Runs each joint at the average of the commanded speed and the speed that closes the position error in one cycle 100 Home Starts the homing sequence 101 Enable Enables motion, resets the homing state 102 Disable Disables motion; the motors hold 103 Clear error Resets the homing state 69 Repeatability test A built-in two-pose cycle

The gripper fields are forwarded over CAN every cycle: a move frame when any of them changed, a calibrate for mode 1, a clear error for mode 2, an empty status poll otherwise.

docs.title: Board → PC: the telemetry packet
docs.text:
Offset after the length byte Size Field Meaning — 3 Start bytes 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF — 1 Length 56 0 18 Position[6] Actual position of each joint, 3 bytes each, signed, microsteps 18 18 Speed[6] Actual speed of each joint 36 1 Homed Bits from the MSB: joint 1 to joint 6 homed; bits 6 and 7 set 37 1 IO Bits from the MSB: input 1, input 2, output 1, output 2, E-stop (1 = closed, not pressed); bits 5 to 7 set 38 1 Temperature error Bits from the MSB: joint 1 to joint 6, reserved, reported cleared by firmware 1; bits 6 and 7 set 39 1 Position error Bits from the MSB: joint 1 to joint 6, reserved; bits 6 and 7 set 40 2 Timing data Ticks of 1.422 µs between the last two valid packets (90 MHz / 128); 7031 = 10 ms 42 1 Timeout error Reserved 43 1 XTR2 The last command byte received 44 1 Gripper ID Always 0 in firmware 1 (not reported by the gripper) 45 2 Gripper position 0 to 255 47 2 Gripper speed Always 1 in firmware 1 (not reported by the gripper) 49 2 Gripper current mA 51 1 Gripper status The gripper's status byte, bits from the MSB: activated, moving to a position, object detection (bits 5 and 4, bit 5 the low bit: 0 moving, 1 object while closing, 2 object while opening, 3 at position), temperature error, timeout error, E-stop error, calibrated 52 1 Object detection Always 1 in firmware 1; the real value is in the status byte's object-detection bits 53 1 CRC Reserved 54 2 End bytes 0x01 0x02

The gripper's status byte and object detection are as the gripper manuals define them.

docs.title: Test firmware commands
docs.text:
The commands the test firmware (PAROL6 control board test code) acts on: # followed by the name, case as written, and a line feed (a terminal that sends only a carriage return gets no answer). None takes an argument. The test firmware in the Control Board Manual shows the output.

The motors turn from power-on

The test firmware turns all six motors slowly from the moment it boots until the power is switched off; no command stops them.

Command What it does #IO Prints, once a second, the E-stop input, input 1, input 2 and the supply voltage in mV #LIMIT Prints, once a second, Joint N is pressed for every triggered limit switch #STOP Ends the #IO or #LIMIT printout; the motors keep turning #start Toggles the two LEDs

The parser (SerialPacketParser.cpp) also recognises STATUS, STEP1 to STEP6, INPUT, ESTOP, OUT1TOGGLE, OUT2TOGGLE, LED1TOGGLE, LED2TOGGLE, SUPPLYV, ONOFF, CAN and FLASH, but main.cpp has no action for them (the FLASH test is commented out): each is answered with Unknown command. The driver report (joint N Connection is: GOOD or BAD, the currents and fault flags) is printed once, about three seconds after power-on, not on a command.

docs.title: Python API reference
docs.text:
The public methods of RobotClient (the sync client; the async client has the same methods, awaited, plus the two status streams), generated from the API's source at v0.9.1. rbt in the signatures is a client, rbt = RobotClient().

The conventions, once: angles in degrees in order J1 to J6, poses as [x, y, z, rx, ry, rz] in millimetres and degrees, speed and accel as fractions in (0, 1], duration in seconds, r a blend radius in millimetres, joints indexed from 0 in jog calls. A motion call returns the command index (≥ 0), or −1 if no acknowledgement arrived; a query returns None on a timeout; a refused or failed command raises MotionError (Errors).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The hardware connection, the motion profile, the TCP corrections, the collision world and the status rate. Tools and the TCP and The controller in the guide.

docs.title: connect_hardware
docs.text:
rbt.connect_hardware(port_str: str) -> int

Connect to robot hardware via serial port.

rbt.connect_hardware("/dev/ttyUSB0")
Parameter Meaning port_str Serial port path (e.g., '/dev/ttyUSB0' or 'COM3').

Returns: 1 if acknowledged, 0 on failure.

Raises:

  • ValueError: If port_str is empty.

docs.title: select_profile
docs.text:
rbt.select_profile(profile: str) -> int

Set the motion profile (e.g. "TOPPRA").

rbt.select_profile("TOPPRA")
Parameter Meaning profile Motion profile type ('TOPPRA', 'RUCKIG', 'QUINTIC', 'TRAPEZOID', 'LINEAR') Note RUCKIG is point-to-point only; Cartesian moves will use TOPPRA.

Returns: 1 once the profile is selected, 0 when no reply arrives.

Raises:

  • MotionError: when profile is not a profile name.

Note

The profiles of this version: TOPPRA, RUCKIG, QUINTIC, TRAPEZOID, LINEAR. Motion profiles says what each does.

docs.title: set_tcp_offset
docs.text:
rbt.set_tcp_offset(x: float = 0, y: float = 0, z: float = 0) -> int

Set TCP offset in mm, composed on top of the current tool transform.

The offset shifts the effective TCP point in the tool's local frame. Subsequent motion (especially TRF relative moves) will use the new TCP. Returns the queued index; await wait_command(index) to confirm application. This translation-only setter clears user TCP rotation. Call with (0, 0, 0) to reset. Changing tools resets the offset.

rbt.set_tcp_offset(0, 0, -190)  # pencil tip 190mm from gripper

docs.title: set_tcp_transform
docs.text:
rbt.set_tcp_transform(
    x: float = 0,
    y: float = 0,
    z: float = 0,
    roll: float = 0,
    pitch: float = 0,
    yaw: float = 0,
) -> int

No docstring.

docs.title: tcp_offset
docs.text:
rbt.tcp_offset() -> list[float]

Query current TCP offset in mm [x, y, z].

offset = rbt.tcp_offset()

docs.title: tcp_transform
docs.text:
rbt.tcp_transform() -> list[float]

No docstring.

Note

set_tcp_transform(x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw): millimetres and intrinsic XYZ degrees relative to the registered tool. Both setters return a queued index; wait for it before relying on the correction. The TCP queries raise TimeoutError instead of returning a misleading zero when the controller does not answer.

docs.title: set_shapes
docs.text:
rbt.set_shapes(shapes: list) -> int

Replace the program-layer collision-world shapes (keep-out barriers).

Collision-enabled shapes are added to the controller's checkers so motion is blocked against them; an empty list clears the program layer. Installation-layer shapes (robot config) are unaffected.

Acknowledged: returns 1 only after the controller confirms the world was applied; 0 on timeout. Raises MotionError if the controller rejects the shapes.

rbt.set_shapes([Box(name="table", x=0.6, y=0.4, z=0.02,
                    pose=(0.3, 0, -0.01, 0, 0, 0))])

Note

Shapes are the program layer of the collision world: boxes and other primitives with a pose in metres and extrinsic XYZ radians, collision-enabled or visual only, attachable to the flange as held objects. The installation layer, from the robot's configuration, is not affected.

docs.title: set_status_rate
docs.text:
rbt.set_status_rate(hz: float) -> int

Set the rate the controller broadcasts status at.

rbt.set_status_rate(100)

docs.title: Control
docs.text: Commands that change what the controller is doing: stops, the protective stop and its reset, pause and execution speed, simulator mode, teleport, and the state reset. They are system commands: immediate, not queued, and accepted also while the controller is disabled, except teleport, which is refused then. Control ownership.

docs.title: stop
docs.text:
rbt.stop() -> int

Stop all motion — cancel the active move and clear the queue.

The controller stays enabled and holding position; the next motion command is accepted immediately.

rbt.stop()

Returns: 1 if acknowledged, 0 on failure.

Reset program state — world shapes, tool selection, errors, pause, motion profile and execution speed — and discard the queue, each discarded command failing with MOTN_CANCELLED.

docs.title: teleport
docs.text:
rbt.teleport(angles_deg: list[float], tool_positions: list[float] | None = None) -> int

Instantly set joint angles and optional tool positions (simulator only).

The pose is exact, so the arm counts as homed afterwards and planned motion may follow. Whatever was driving the arm is cancelled with MOTN_CANCELLED.

rbt.teleport([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180])
rbt.teleport([90, -90, 180, 0, 0, 180], tool_positions=[1.0])

Returns: 1 once the pose is applied, 0 when no reply arrives.

Raises:

  • ValueError: for a non-finite angle, one outside the hard joint limits, or a tool position outside [0, 1].
  • MotionError: off the simulator (SYS_NOT_SIMULATOR), when the tool positions do not match the fitted tool's DOF count, or while the controller is disabled.

docs.title: The wire protocol
docs.text:
Clients and the controller exchange msgpack messages over UDP: a command or query with a request ID, and an OK, an error, a response or a status. The protocol version is checked in every status broadcast, and a client that speaks another version raises ProtocolVersionError. The command and query types of this version:

Commands: CmdType.PING and the others, 54 in all, the queries among them; queries: PING, STATUS, ANGLES, POSE, IO, SPEEDS, TOOL, QUEUE, CURRENT_ACTION, LOOP_STATS, PROFILE, TOOL_STATUS, ENABLEMENT, ERROR, TCP_SPEED, IS_SIMULATOR, TCP_OFFSET, SHAPES, STATUS_RATE, TCP_TRANSFORM, EXECUTION_SPEED, COMMAND_COMPLETION. The definitions are parol6/protocol/wire.py; a program in another language can speak the protocol from them, though the Python client is the supported path.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
The error codes of the controller, with the catalog text a MotionError carries, from the source at v0.9.1. The number ranges: 10 to 19 inverse kinematics, 20 to 29 trajectory planning, 30 to 39 motion execution, 40 to 49 communication, 50 to 59 system and safety. MOTN_CANCELLED uses the number shared with the waldoctl interface, so that a client sees one code for a discarded command whichever arm raised it. Errors in the guide says how to recover.

Code Number Title Cause Effect Remedy IK_TARGET_UNREACHABLE 10 IK: target unreachable Target pose has no valid IK solution. Motion command rejected. Pipeline halted. Verify target is within workspace. Try different orientation. IK_PARTIAL_PATH 11 IK: partial path failure Only {valid}/{total} poses along the path are reachable. Motion command rejected. Pipeline halted. Shorten the move, add intermediate waypoints, or adjust orientation. TRAJ_EMPTY_RESULT 20 Trajectory: empty result Trajectory generation returned no waypoints. Motion command rejected. Check motion parameters. Start and end may be too close. TRAJ_NO_STEPS 21 Trajectory: no steps Trajectory calculation produced zero steps. Motion command rejected. Increase duration or reduce speed fraction. MOTN_HOME_TIMEOUT 30 Homing timeout Robot did not start homing sequence within timeout. Home command aborted. Check serial connection and robot power. Ensure E-stop is released. MOTN_GRIPPER_TIMEOUT 31 Gripper timeout Gripper command timed out in state {state}. Gripper command aborted. Check gripper connection and calibration. MOTN_GRIPPER_UNKNOWN 32 Gripper: unknown state Gripper entered an unknown internal state. Gripper command aborted. Reset the controller and recalibrate the gripper. MOTN_SETUP_FAILED 33 Command setup failed Command could not be initialized. Command rejected. Pipeline halted. Check command parameters and robot state. MOTN_TICK_FAILED 34 Command execution error Unexpected error during execution. Command aborted. Robot stopped. Check robot state. May need to re-home. MOTN_NOT_HOMED 35 Robot not homed MOTN_CANCELLED shared Command cancelled The command was cancelled by {scope} before it finished. The motion did not run to completion. Re-issue the command if the motion is still wanted. COMM_QUEUE_FULL 40 Command queue full Motion queue at maximum capacity. Command rejected. Wait for current motions to complete. COMM_UNKNOWN_COMMAND 41 Unknown command No handler for received command type. Command ignored. Check client library version matches server. COMM_DECODE_ERROR 42 Command decode error Failed to decode command. Command ignored. Check command encoding. Possible version mismatch. COMM_VALIDATION_ERROR 43 Command validation error Invalid parameters. Command rejected. Check parameter ranges and types. SYS_STATUS_RATE_INVALID 55 Status rate not achievable Status is broadcast every Nth control tick, so {requested} Hz does not divide the {control} Hz control loop evenly. Broadcast rate unchanged. Pick a rate that divides {control} Hz: {allowed}. SYS_CONTROLLER_DISABLED 50 Controller disabled Motion command sent while controller is disabled. Command rejected. Call reset() to re-enable the controller. SYS_ESTOP_ACTIVE 51 E-stop active Emergency stop is currently engaged. All motion stopped. Queue cleared. Release the E-stop button and call reset(). SYS_PORT_SAVE_FAILED 52 Serial port save failed Could not save serial port configuration. Port may not persist across restarts. Check file permissions and disk space. SYS_PROFILE_INVALID 53 Invalid motion profile Unrecognized motion profile: Profile not changed. Use one of: TOPPRA, RUCKIG, QUINTIC, TRAPEZOID, LINEAR. SYS_NOT_SIMULATOR 56 Simulator-only command {detail} is only available on the simulator. Command rejected; the arm is unchanged. Switch to the simulator with simulator(True), or drive the arm with a planned move. SYS_SELF_COLLISION 54 Self-collision predicted Planned configuration would self-collide at sample {sample} of {total}: {pairs} Motion command rejected before dispatch. Choose a different target, add intermediate waypoints, or disable via PAROL6_COLLISION_CHECK=0.

A RobotError has the fields code, title, cause, effect and remedy, and str(error) joins them.

docs.title: I/O
docs.text: The control board's digital inputs and outputs. The firmware's I/O byte is [in1, in2, out1, out2, estop, ...]; reads return the first five, writes take the logical output index 0 or 1. I/O, delays and checkpoints in the guide.

docs.title: write_io
docs.text:
rbt.write_io(index: int, value: int, *, timeout: float | None = None) -> int

Set digital output by logical index (0 = first output pin).

The firmware I/O byte layout is [in0, in1, out0, out1, estop, ...] so logical output index 0 maps to bit position 2.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

timeout bounds command acceptance. TimeoutError leaves application unconfirmed; None uses the client defaults.

rbt.write_io(0, 1)   # Set first output HIGH

The read side is io() under Queries, and is_estop_pressed().

docs.title: Motion
docs.text: Planned moves: queued, run in order, each returning its command index. wait=True (the default) blocks until the command completes and raises MotionError if it failed or was cancelled; wait=False returns at once for a later wait_command(). Either duration or speed times a move, not both. Motion in the guide explains the choices.

docs.title: home
docs.text:
rbt.home(wait: bool = False, calibrate: bool = False, timeout: float = 60.0) -> int

Home the robot to its home position.

Uncalibrated (first home after power-on), this runs the full referencing sequence: each joint seeks its limit switch, then the robot moves to standby. Calibrated, it returns to standby with a normal planned, collision-checked joint move — unless calibrate=True, which re-runs the referencing sequence. The referencing sequence is firmware-driven and ignores the collision world, so clear keep-out geometry from the joints' sweep first.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

rbt.home()
Parameter Meaning wait If True, block until motion completes calibrate If True, always run the referencing sequence timeout Maximum time to wait in seconds (only used when wait=True)

Note

The referencing sequence is the firmware's (Homing): it ignores the collision world, and it takes about half a minute. A later home() is a planned joint move to the API's standby, the after-homing pose.
