docs.title: Status fields
docs.text:
The fields of the status buffer the controller broadcasts, as stream_status() yields it and status() summarises it, from the source at v0.9.1. Arrays are numpy arrays.

Field Type session_id int seq int mono_time_ns int pose np.ndarray angles np.ndarray speeds np.ndarray io np.ndarray tool_status ToolStatus joint_en np.ndarray cart_en_wrf np.ndarray cart_en_trf np.ndarray action_current str action_params str action_state ActionState executing_index int completed_index int last_checkpoint str error RobotError \| None queued_segments int queued_duration float tcp_speed float simulator_active bool collision_active bool collision_pairs list[tuple[str, str]] scene_epoch int accepted_index int homed bool enabled bool torques np.ndarray torques_ext np.ndarray warnings list[tuple] link_health dict drive_health dict loop_health dict homing dict cart_en dict[str, np.ndarray]

docs.title: Meaning
docs.text:
Field Meaning session_id, seq, mono_time_ns The status publisher's lifetime (changes on restart), a sequence number (gaps mean missed broadcasts), and the monotonic time of the controller's snapshot pose The tool pose as a 4×4 matrix, flattened (16 values), in the WRF angles, speeds Joint angles in degrees and speeds in deg/s, J1 to J6 io [in1, in2, out1, out2, estop] tool_status The selected tool's ToolStatus; key NONE when no tool is fitted joint_en, cart_en_wrf, cart_en_trf, cart_en Enablement: whether each joint, and each Cartesian axis in each frame, can still move in the positive and negative direction (12 values: six axes, two directions) action_current, action_params, action_state What the controller is executing, its parameters, and the state: idle, executing, error executing_index, completed_index, accepted_index The index of the command running, the highest completed, and the latest accepted last_checkpoint The label of the last checkpoint reached error The current RobotError, or None queued_segments, queued_duration How much motion is queued, in segments and in seconds of estimated duration (tool actions included) tcp_speed The tool's linear speed in mm/s simulator_active Simulator mode collision_active, collision_pairs Whether the collision checker is on, and the pairs it currently reports scene_epoch Changes when the collision world changes: re-query shapes() homed, enabled Whether the robot is referenced, and whether motion is enabled torques, torques_ext Reserved for arms with torque sensing; zero on PAROL6 warnings, link_health, drive_health, loop_health Diagnostics: warnings, the serial link, the drives, the control loop timing homing The progress of a homing sequence

The buffer's freedrive property is always false: PAROL6's steppers cannot be back-driven. mode is an alias of action_state.

docs.title: Jogging and servoing
docs.text: Streamed motion: takes the arm at once and cancels the planned queue (MOTN_CANCELLED for every discarded command). A jog ends when its duration runs out; a servo stream ends about 0.25 s after the last target. Then the arm brakes to rest. Speeds are signed fractions in [−1, 1] for jogs and fractions in (0, 1] for servo targets. jog_j works before homing; jog_l and the servo targets need a homed robot. Jogging and servoing in the guide.

docs.title: stream_status (async client only)
docs.text:
rbt.stream_status() -> AsyncIterator[StatusBuffer]

Async generator that yields status updates from multicast broadcasts.

async for status in client.stream_status():
    print(f"Angles: {status.angles}")

This generator terminates automatically when close is called on the client, so callers do not need to manually cancel their consumer tasks.

Each yielded StatusBuffer is a copy - safe to store or process async. For zero-copy hot paths, use stream_status_shared instead.

Slow consumers automatically skip to the latest state (desired for real-time).

docs.title: stream_status_shared (async client only)
docs.text:
rbt.stream_status_shared() -> AsyncIterator[StatusBuffer]

Zero-copy async generator that yields the shared status buffer.

async for status in client.stream_status_shared():
    # Process immediately - don't store references
    print(f"Angles: {status.angles}")

WARNING: The same buffer instance is yielded on every iteration. Do not store references to the yielded object - data will be overwritten on the next iteration. For safe storage, use stream_status or call status.copy().

This generator terminates automatically when close is called on the client.

Slow consumers automatically skip to the latest state (desired for real-time).

docs.title: Synchronization
docs.text: Waiting for the controller, for a command, for a checkpoint or for the arm to come to rest; and the two queued markers, delays and checkpoints. Status and waiting in the guide says what "done" means.

docs.title: wait_ready
docs.text:
rbt.wait_ready(timeout: float = 5.0, interval: float = 0.05) -> bool

Poll ping() until server responds or timeout.

Parameter Meaning timeout Maximum time to wait for server to respond interval Polling interval between ping attempts

Returns: True if server responded to PING, False on timeout

docs.title: wait_command
docs.text:
rbt.wait_command(command_index: int, timeout: float = 10.0) -> bool

Wait until a specific command index has been completed.

Queries exact success in the controller's last 1024 completions: a later command that finishes first — a jog, a tool.stop() — does not complete an unfinished one queued before it. Queued commands, tool actions among them, run in index order, so a wait on one covers everything queued ahead of it. Unknown or expired results are never inferred successful from the status high-water mark. A command that ended as a failure — cancelled by stop()/estop() (MOTN_CANCELLED) or failed by the pipeline — raises MotionError.

Parameter Meaning command_index The command index to wait for (returned by motion commands). timeout Maximum time to wait in seconds.

Returns: True if the command completed within timeout, False otherwise.

Raises:

  • MotionError: If the pipeline errored at or before command_index.

docs.title: wait_motion
docs.text:
rbt.wait_motion(
    timeout: float = 10.0,
    settle_window: float = 0.25,
    speed_threshold: float = 0.5,
    angle_threshold: float = 0.5,
) -> bool

Wait until the queue has run out and the arm has come to rest.

First waits for the latest command the controller has accepted — every command this client queued, and each newer one the status stream reports accepted — to end, then for the arm to hold still for settle_window. A command that failed or was cancelled ends the wait like one that completed; wait_command() tells which.

rbt.wait_motion()
Parameter Meaning timeout Maximum time to wait in seconds settle_window How long robot must be stable to be considered stopped speed_threshold Max joint speed to be considered stopped (deg/s) angle_threshold Max angle change to be considered stopped (degrees)

Returns: True if robot stopped, False if timeout

Raises:

  • ConnectionError: If the controller session changes while a command is still being waited on.

docs.title: wait_status
docs.text:
rbt.wait_status(predicate: Callable[[StatusBuffer], bool], timeout: float = 5.0) -> bool

Wait until a multicast status satisfies predicate(status) within timeout.

docs.title: checkpoint
docs.text:
rbt.checkpoint(label: str) -> int

Insert a checkpoint marker in the motion queue.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

rbt.checkpoint("pick_done")
Parameter Meaning label Checkpoint label for progress tracking

docs.title: wait_checkpoint
docs.text:
rbt.wait_checkpoint(label: str, timeout: float = 30.0) -> bool

Wait until a checkpoint with the given label has been reached.

rbt.wait_checkpoint("pick_done")
Parameter Meaning label Checkpoint label to wait for timeout Maximum wait time in seconds

docs.title: delay
docs.text:
rbt.delay(seconds: float) -> int

Insert a non-blocking delay in the motion queue.

Returns the command index (≥ 0) on success, -1 on failure.

rbt.delay(1.0)

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: Selecting a tool, the generic tool action, and the methods of the bound tool object rbt.tool. Tool actions are queued with the motion; tool.stop() is immediate. Tools and the TCP in the guide.

docs.title: Registered tools
docs.text: Key Tool Variants (default first) NONE Bare flange - no tool attached — PNEUMATIC Pneumatic gripper assembly (vertical/horizontal mounting) vertical, horizontal SSG-48 SSG-48 adaptive electric gripper (Spectral micro BLDC) finger, pinch MSG MSG compliant AI stepper gripper (StepFOC) 100mm, 150mm, 200mm VACUUM Vacuum gripper (pneumatic valve I/O) —

docs.title: select_tool
docs.text:
rbt.select_tool(tool_name: str, variant_key: str = '') -> int

Set the active end-effector tool on the controller.

rbt.select_tool("PNEUMATIC")
Parameter Meaning tool_name Name of the tool ('NONE', 'PNEUMATIC', 'SSG-48', 'MSG', 'VACUUM') variant_key Optional variant within the tool type.

Returns: Command index (>= 0) if queued, 0 on failure.

docs.title: tool_action
docs.text:
rbt.tool_action(
    tool_key: str,
    action: str,
    params: list | None = None,
    *,
    wait: bool = False,
    timeout: float = 10.0,
) -> int

Send a generic tool action command.

Returns the command index (>= 0) on success, -1 on failure. The action and its parameters are checked before anything is sent: a malformed one raises ValueError. A key naming a tool other than the selected one is refused by the controller.

A tool action is queued work: it runs in queue order with motion, the arm holding still while it does, so a wait on it covers the motion queued ahead of it, and one sent after a blended move ends the blend there. A move before a completed calibrate is refused when its turn comes, failing its own index; a tool action that fails cancels what is queued behind it (MOTN_CANCELLED). A pause holds the tool actions still queued. stop(), estop(), reset_state(), a teleport, or a jog or servo stream taking the arm discards them and halts the one running where the jaws are, keeping the grip.

stop alone acts at once, on the tool fitted now: it halts the action running, failing it as cancelled by a tool stop, keeps what is queued behind it, and holds the next queued tool action until the jaws are still.

Electric grippers take move [position, speed, current] (exactly three fractions in [0, 1]; current spans the tool's current_range), calibrate, stop (halt in place, keep grip) and idle (release, the jaws left where they are); set_position/open/close map onto move. Pneumatic grippers take open, close, and move/set_position [position].

rbt.tool_action("PNEUMATIC", "open")
Parameter Meaning tool_key Tool registry key (e.g. "PNEUMATIC", "SSG-48", "MSG") action Action name (e.g. "open", "close", "move", "calibrate") params Positional parameters (meaning defined by tool config) wait If True, block until action completes timeout Maximum time to wait in seconds (only used when wait=True)

Note

The actions of the electric grippers: move with [position, speed, current] as fractions, calibrate, stop, idle (release). Of the pneumatic and vacuum grippers: open, close, and move (or set_position) with [position], below 0.5 opening and from 0.5 closing. The tool methods below call these.

docs.title: tool.set_position (electric)
docs.text:
rbt.tool.set_position(
    position: float,
    *,
    speed: float = 0.5,
    current: float = 0.5,
    **wait_kwargs: Any,
) -> int

Moves the jaws to position, 0 open and 1 closed, at speed (a fraction of the gripper's speed range) and with current as the current limit, the grip force. current is a fraction of the tool's current range: 100 to 1300 mA for the SSG-48, 100 to 2800 mA for the MSG, so current=0.5 is 700 mA or 1450 mA. Queued: it waits for the motion before it, and the motion after it waits for the jaws to arrive, stop on a part or stall. Refused when its turn comes on a gripper that was never calibrated.

docs.title: tool.open (electric)
docs.text:
rbt.tool.open(*, speed: float = 0.5, current: float = 0.5, **wait_kwargs: Any) -> int

set_position(0.0, ...): the jaws fully open.

docs.title: tool.close (electric)
docs.text:
rbt.tool.close(*, speed: float = 0.5, current: float = 0.5, **wait_kwargs: Any) -> int

set_position(1.0, ...): the jaws close until they reach the end or stop on a part.

docs.title: tool.calibrate (electric)
docs.text:
rbt.tool.calibrate(**kwargs: object) -> int

Sends the gripper its calibration: it opens fully and closes fully to find its end stops. Queued. The API counts it done after a fixed 2 s (200 control cycles) and does not read the gripper's calibrated bit; the SSG-48 needs about 3 s and the MSG 5 to 6 s, so queue a delay() after it (Calibrating). There is no clear-error action: a latched gripper error is cleared from the commander or Motor GUI.

docs.title: tool.release (electric)
docs.text:
rbt.tool.release(**kwargs: object) -> int

Drop the grip, freeing the jaws for manual handling, once the commands queued ahead of it have run. The jaws stay where they are.

docs.title: tool.stop (electric)
docs.text:
rbt.tool.stop(**kwargs: object) -> int

Halt the jaws where they are, keeping the grip, ahead of anything still queued: the action running fails as cancelled, and the queue behind it is kept. On an uncalibrated gripper, which has no position to hold, this releases instead.

docs.title: tool.set_position (pneumatic)
docs.text:
rbt.tool.set_position(position: float, **kwargs: float | int) -> int

Binary position: < 0.5 opens, >= 0.5 closes.

docs.title: tool.open (pneumatic)
docs.text:
rbt.tool.open(**kwargs: float | int) -> int

Switches output 1 high, queued with the motion; the action lasts the tool's estimated stroke (a single control cycle for the vacuum gripper). Which way the gripper moves depends on the tubing.

docs.title: tool.close (pneumatic)
docs.text:
rbt.tool.close(**kwargs: float | int) -> int

Switches output 1 low, queued with the motion; otherwise as open().

Every tool object also has status(), returning the ToolStatus of the selected tool: key, state, engaged, part_detected, fault_code, positions, channels and variant_key. For the electric grippers, Tool status says where each field comes from.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text:
• Questions and discussion: the Source Robotics Discord.
  • A problem with the robot's hardware, its files or the control board firmware: an issue in the robot repository; see Report a problem for what to include.
  • A problem with the commander software: an issue in PAROL-commander-software.
  • A problem with the Python API: an issue in PAROL6-python-API.
  • A mistake on a page of this site: every page ends with a link to edit it and one to report it; see Contributing.
  • Orders and hardware: source-robotics.com.

Before you ask, Troubleshooting goes through the common symptoms, and the commander's terminal output or the API's error() tells most of what anyone will ask you for.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: The documentation lives in Source-Robotics/PAROL-docs. A small fix, a typo, a wrong number, a missing link, can be made from the browser: every page ends with a link to edit it on GitHub, which opens a pull request. For anything larger, open an issue first and say what you want to change.

docs.title: House rules
docs.text:
• Write for the reader who has the robot in front of them: what to do, in what order, and why when the why matters. Short sentences, one idea each.
  • Facts come from the files: the firmware, the software's source, the BOM. When a page and the code disagree, the code is right and the page is fixed; a change to a command is made in the code first.
  • Version facts live in versions.yml, never in a page. The API reference is generated from the Python API's source: edit the notes around the markers, not the markers' output.
  • Link to a page of this site with its relative path, so that the build checks it; link to code on GitHub by its permanent URL.
  • Images under 2400 px, with the exact file name (the live site is case-sensitive).
  • Run python tools/test_tools.py and mkdocs build --strict before you open a pull request. Both run on every push.

The text and the images you contribute are published under CC BY-SA 4.0, the code examples under MIT.

docs.title: Report a problem
docs.text:
A report that can be acted on says what you did, what happened, and what the robot said. Include:

  1. The robot: bought or self-built; control board version (v2.0 with terminal blocks, or v1.2); the firmware (main, from which commit, and whether you changed constants.h or motor_init.cpp).
  2. The software: commander (which commit, which Python version, which OS) or Python API (pip show parol6), or something else.
  3. What you did: the exact steps, the program or script, the jog, the command.
  4. What happened: and what you expected instead. A short video helps for anything mechanical.
  5. What the robot said: the commander's response log and terminal output, or the API's exception text and the controller's log.
  6. The PC: processor and OS, for anything about timing or communication.

Where to file it is on Getting help. A problem with a gripper goes to the gripper's own repository, with the same facts.

docs.title: Theory corner
docs.text: The theory behind a six-axis robot arm and its software, explained in the order you meet it: what a joint angle and a pose are, which frames the numbers are in, how the software goes from one to the other, why some poses cannot be reached and some moves cannot be made, what shape a move has in time, and who is in charge of the robot at any moment. Each page says how the idea shows up in PAROL6's software. None of it needs maths beyond what is on the page, and none of it is needed to run the robot: read it when you want to know why the robot does what it does.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text:
• Units
  • Joints, directions and the standby pose
  • Reference frames
  • Pose and orientation
  • Forward and inverse kinematics
  • Configurations and singularities
  • Workspace and reach
  • Homing and mastering
  • Motion profiles
  • Blending
  • Target, commanded and actual
  • Control ownership
  • Steppers, open loop and backlash
  • Further reading

docs.title: Robot types
docs.text:
Industrial robots are sorted by their joints and how they are arranged: vertically articulated arms, Cartesian gantries, cylindrical and polar arms, SCARA arms, delta robots. PAROL6 is a vertically articulated arm with six revolute joints, the most common industrial type, and the ideas on these pages are the ones every such arm uses. The last three joints meet in a point, a spherical wrist, which the pages on kinematics return to.

Figure 1: A robot with a spherical wrist (left) and one without (right).

docs.title: Blending
docs.text:
A program with many waypoints stops at each one unless told otherwise, and every stop costs time and a jolt. Blending lets the robot pass near a waypoint without stopping: when the tool comes within a radius of the waypoint, it starts the next move, and the path rounds the corner.

  • The tool does not pass through a blended waypoint; it cuts the corner inside the radius. A waypoint where the tool must be exactly, a pick or a place, is not blended.
  • The blend radius is in millimetres of the tool's path.
  • A blend needs the next move to be known when the current one starts: in the Python API the moves are queued, so the controller looks ahead and blends.

docs.title: In the Python API
docs.text:
move_j, move_l and move_c take r, the blend radius; r=0 stops at the target. move_p is the process move: a list of waypoints run at constant tool speed with automatic blending at every corner, for scan and dispensing paths. A tool action or a delay() queued after a blended move ends the blend there: the arm stops for it. The zig-zag example in the API's repository shows a raster scan with blends.

rbt.move_l([200, 0, 250, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5, r=15)
rbt.move_l([200, 160, 250, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5, r=15)
rbt.move_l([250, 160, 250, 90, 0, 90], speed=0.5)          # stops here

docs.title: In the commander software
docs.text: RBTscript has no blending: every move ends at rest. Make the path with fewer, longer moves, or with MoveCart through points far enough apart that the stops do not matter.

docs.title: Configurations
docs.text:
The same tool pose can be reached with the elbow up or down, the wrist flipped or not, the base facing the target or turned 180° with the arm reaching backwards. Each combination is a configuration. A joint move keeps the configuration it is in unless the target is in another; a Cartesian move cannot change configuration at all, because that would mean passing through a pose where two configurations meet, which is a singularity.

Three choices with two answers each make eight configurations. The figure shows all eight for one tool pose: PAROL6 with nothing on the flange, the tool centre point 250 mm in front of the base and 230 mm up, the tool tilted 30° from vertical. The flange is in exactly the same place and orientation in every picture; only the joints differ. The teal dot marks the centre of the flange and the arrow its axis, the same in every picture.

  • Shoulder right or left: the wrist centre in front of the joint 1 axis, or behind it with joint 1 turned about 180° and the arm reaching back over itself.
  • Elbow up or down: the elbow above or below the line from the shoulder to the wrist centre.
  • Wrist flipped or not: joint 5 positive or negative; joints 4 and 6 turn by 180° to keep the tool where it is.
Figure 1: The eight configurations of PAROL6 for one tool pose: elbow up or down, shoulder right or left, wrist flipped or not; of these, only (a) is within the joint limits.

Mathematically all eight reach the pose. On the real robot, the joint limits rule most of them out: for this pose only (a) is within every joint limit (Joint limits and directions), and several of the others would also hit the robot itself. The poses were solved and drawn from PAROL6's model in robot_descriptions, the same model the limits come from.

The practical rule: teach the poses of a program in the configuration you want, and make the move between two configurations a joint move (MoveJoint, move_j), never a Cartesian one.

How the software chooses, when a target is given as a pose:

  • The Python API solves every pose starting from the joints where the robot is, so it keeps the current configuration, in Cartesian moves and in joint moves to a pose alike.
  • The commander software solves MovePose starting from the standby pose, so it takes the configuration nearest to standby, whichever the robot is in; its Cartesian moves keep the current one.

To be sure of the configuration, give the target as joint angles.

docs.title: Singularities
docs.text:
When the arm moves in Cartesian space, the software converts a tool velocity into six joint velocities every cycle. In most poses that works. In some poses two joint axes line up, and a motion of the tool in a certain direction would need infinite joint speed, or the joints can turn without the tool moving: a singularity. The maths divides by something that goes to zero. Near it, small tool motions ask for huge joint speeds; at it, the move is impossible.

The three singularities of a six-axis arm with a spherical wrist:

When Looks like You meet it Wrist Joint 5 at 0°: the axes of joints 4 and 6 in one line The wrist straight; the standby pose is a wrist singularity whenever the tool points the way the forearm does Shoulder The wrist centre on the joint 1 axis. The shoulder axis is 23.4 mm in front of it, so the arm leans back to get there: with joint 3 at 180°, at joint 2 = −133.1° The wrist straight above the middle of the base working close to the joint 1 axis, above the base Elbow Joint 3 at 256.2°: the upper arm and the line from the elbow to the wrist centre in one line, the wrist centre 362.3 mm from the shoulder axis The arm fully stretched at full reach Figure 2: The wrist singularity: joint 5 at 0°, so the axes of joints 4 and 6 lie in one line. Figure 3: The shoulder singularity: the wrist centre on the joint 1 axis, here with joint 2 at −133.1° and joint 3 at 180°. Figure 4: The elbow singularity: joint 3 at 256.2°, so joints 2 and 3 and the wrist centre lie in one line, the arm fully stretched.

The angles are the ones the software shows, from PAROL6's model. The wrist centre is where the axes of joints 4, 5 and 6 meet. The elbow singularity is the outer edge of the workspace (Workspace and reach): singularities are part of its boundary, with the joint limits.

docs.title: What PAROL6 does
docs.text:
• The commander software stops a Cartesian move or jog when it reaches a singularity; the robot stays where it stopped. It does not deviate from the path to go around.
  • The Python API refuses a Cartesian command whose path it cannot solve, before anything moves, and a jog that would enter a singular region stops.

Some industrial controllers can bend the path slightly to pass a singularity; PAROL6 keeps the path and stops instead. The demonstration video shows what singularities look like on an industrial arm.

docs.title: Avoiding them
docs.text:
Singularities are a property of the geometry, so they are avoided by design, with trial and error:

  • Keep the wrist bent: a few degrees of joint 5 away from 0° at the poses where you work.
  • Place the parts so that the arm reaches them with a bent elbow, not at full stretch, and off the axis of joint 1.
  • Mount the gripper at an angle, or on a plate that turns it, so that the working orientation needs a bent wrist.
  • When a move keeps failing, make it a joint move, or add an intermediate pose.
  • Run the program in the simulator: a stop or a refusal in the simulator is a singularity you can see.

docs.title: Control ownership
docs.text:
Only one program can own the control board, and inside the Python API only one source can drive the arm at a time. Knowing who is in charge saves confusion and collisions.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Clients
        G[GUI]
        P[Your script]
    end
    subgraph Controller["Controller: one owner of the arm"]
        Q["Planned queue: move_*, home, tools, in order"]
        S["Streamed motion: jog_*, servo_*, at once"]
    end
    B[Control board]
    G --> Q
    P --> Q
    P --> S
    S -. cancels .-> Q
    Q --> B
    S --> B

docs.title: One host on the serial port
docs.text: The control board executes whatever packets arrive on its USB port. The commander software and the Python API's controller each take the port exclusively; the second one to try gets an error or silence. Stop one before you start the other.

docs.title: Inside the Python API
docs.text:
The controller owns the arm. Clients send it commands; it accepts commands from any number of clients on the network, without authentication, so a GUI and a script can both be connected. What happens when they both command motion:

  • Planned motion (move_*, home, delay, tool actions, checkpoints) goes into one queue, in the order it arrives, and runs in that order, together with the output writes (write_io), the tool selection (select_tool) and the TCP corrections. Every queued command gets an index; wait_command(index) waits for that one.
  • Streamed motion (jog_*, servo_*) takes the arm at once: it cancels the planned queue (every discarded command fails with MOTN_CANCELLED). A jog runs for its duration; a servo stream drives the arm while targets keep coming and ends about a quarter of a second after the last one. Then the arm brakes to rest and holds.
  • stop() cancels the active move and clears the queue, from any client. estop() does the same and latches a protective stop until reset().
  • pause() holds the queue where it is; resume() continues it; set_execution_speed() scales it between 10 and 100 %.
  • System commands (simulator, connect_hardware, select_profile, set_shapes) take effect at once and change the controller's state for everyone. A queued select_tool does too, when its turn comes.

The rule for a program that shares the controller: own the arm for the duration of a task by queuing it, wait for your indices, and expect MotionError if someone else stopped you.

docs.title: The firmware
docs.text: The firmware's enable and disable commands (101, 102) decide whether it accepts motion at all; the E-stop makes the PC software send disable or latch a stop (Emergency stop). Between packets the firmware keeps the last speeds it was given, which is why a host must never stop sending while a joint is in motion.

docs.title: Simulator versus hardware
docs.text: The controller runs against the hardware or in simulator mode, where the same planner drives a virtual arm and the status stream reports it. simulator(True) switches; is_simulator() tells; teleport() sets the virtual arm's pose. The dry-run client goes further: it runs the planner in the client's own process, with no controller at all, for tests and previews (Clients).

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
Good places to go deeper into the concepts of this chapter:

  • Robot Academy: Peter Corke's video lectures on kinematics, frames and control, the basis of the Robotics Toolbox the commander software uses.
  • Automatic Addison: practical tutorials, including how to assign DH frames and how to find the DH table.
  • Robogrok: a robotics course with the maths worked out.
  • Robotics coursework collection: a curated list of courses and books.
  • Robotics Explained: short explanations of the vocabulary.
  • How do robot manipulators move? on Robotic Sea Bass: motion planning from the ground up.
  • How many axes does my robot need? on Robohub.
  • Singularities demonstrated on an industrial arm.

The Python API's repository has a docs folder and a README that go into its architecture, the motion planner and the collision checker beyond what this guide covers.

docs.title: Homing and mastering
docs.text: Stepper motors without encoders know nothing about where they are when the power comes on. Two procedures give PAROL6 its position: homing, every time, and mastering, once per robot.

docs.title: Homing
docs.text:
Each joint drives to a switch or sensor whose position in the mechanics is known from the CAD model, then moves a fixed number of steps from there to the after-homing pose. After that the firmware's step counters hold the joint positions, and every move is counted from them. The process is the one 3D printers use. The sequence and what can go wrong are in the Robot Manual's Homing.

In the software: the commander's Home button, the API's home(). The API tracks whether the robot is referenced and refuses planned motion before it (MOTN_NOT_HOMED); a home() on a referenced robot is a planned joint move back to the after-homing pose, and home(calibrate=True) runs the firmware's sequence again.

docs.title: Mastering
docs.text:
The fixed number of steps from the switch to the after-homing pose is measured on the reference robot. Printers and switches vary, so on another robot the homed pose is a fraction of a degree off per joint. Mastering measures the error with the witness marks, pins through holes in neighbouring links that line up in the after-homing pose, and corrects the number in the firmware (Mastering).

Figure 1: Witness marks on PAROL6.

Mastering affects the absolute accuracy, whether the pose the software reports is the true pose. It does not affect the repeatability, whether the robot returns to the same place every time, which comes from the mechanics and the switches alone. A program taught on an unmastered robot runs correctly on that robot; it runs offset on another.

docs.title: When the position is lost
docs.text: A collision, a stall, a move by hand or a power failure breaks the count, and nothing in the robot can tell. Home again. A program that must not run with a wrong position checks something external before it starts: a sensor on an input, a camera, a touch.

docs.title: Joints, directions and the standby pose
Numbering
docs.text:
Joints are numbered 1 to 6 from the base up: J1 turns the whole arm about the vertical axis, J2 is the shoulder, J3 the elbow, J4 rotates the forearm, J5 pitches the wrist, J6 rotates the tool. The Python API indexes joints from 0 in its jog calls (jog_j(0, ...) is J1) and lists angles in order J1 to J6 everywhere.

Joints 4, 5 and 6 are also called wrist 1, wrist 2 and wrist 3, as in the robot model and ROS. The forearm is also called the lower arm: both names mean the link from the elbow to the wrist.

Figure 1: Each joint turned 30 degrees in its positive direction, in colour, over the pose in grey.

docs.title: Positive direction
docs.text: Each joint has a positive direction, the one in which its angle increases, drawn as the arrows in the figure on Joint limits and directions. The commander's left arrows jog positive, the right arrows negative. The firmware has a per-joint flag that inverts the motor so that the hardware agrees with this convention; a new build sets it per joint on the first run.

docs.title: Joint space and the standby pose
docs.text:
A set of six joint angles is a point in joint space: it describes the arm's configuration completely, and a joint move is a straight line in it, every joint moving proportionally and finishing at the same time.

The reference point is the standby pose, the pose of the Denavit-Hartenberg table; after homing the robot stands in it turned 90° about joint 1:

Pose J1 J2 J3 J4 J5 J6 Standby 0° −90° 180° 0° 0° 180° After homing 90° −90° 180° 0° 0° 180°

Every joint angle the software reports is measured in this convention. At J1 = 0° the arm points along the base's X axis, away from the electronics box; homing ends with J1 a quarter turn further, at 90°, and the software reports 90° there. The Python API calls that after-homing pose its standby.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Each joint has a software limit in both directions, enforced by the planner and by the jog, and a mechanical stop a little past it (Joint limits and directions). The limits are in the robot model (PAROL6_ROBOT.py in both programs); a tool or a base that changes the real clearance does not change them.

docs.title: Forward and inverse kinematics
docs.text: Kinematics is the geometry of the arm: how the joint angles decide where the tool is, and the other way round.

docs.title: The kinematic diagram and the DH table
docs.text:
A kinematic diagram shows the links and joints without the shapes: six revolute joints, their axes, and the distances between them. The Denavit-Hartenberg convention writes that down as four numbers per joint, a link length, a link offset, a joint angle and a link twist, and PAROL6's table is in the Robot Manual (Dimensions and kinematics). The commander software's robot model is built from this table; the Python API loads the robot's URDF, which carries the same geometry, and computes the kinematics numerically with Pinocchio.

The sheet below shows both at once for PAROL6 with nothing on the flange: the robot's real outline with every joint at 0, the joint centres J1 to J6, the dimensions a1 to a7 between them, and under it the DH table those dimensions make. The Robot Manual has the same sheet for every gripper.

Figure 1: PAROL6, flange only: the dimensions a1 to a7 between the joint centres, and the DH table they make.

docs.title: Forward kinematics
docs.text: From six joint angles to the pose of the tool. It is a chain of transformations, one per joint, multiplied together, and it always has exactly one answer: the software runs it every cycle to show you where the tool is. rbt.pose() is forward kinematics of the current angles plus the tool's transform.

docs.title: Inverse kinematics
docs.text:
From a pose of the tool to the joint angles that reach it. It is the hard direction. The spherical wrist helps: the first three joints decide where the wrist centre is, and the last three decide the orientation from there, so the problem splits in two. Even so:

  • A pose can have several solutions: elbow up or down, wrist flipped or not, the base turned the other way. The software picks the one nearest the current configuration.
  • A pose can have no solution: out of reach, or an orientation the wrist cannot make from that position. The move is refused (IK_TARGET_UNREACHABLE in the API, an inverse kinematics error in the commander).
  • Near a singularity the solution exists but demands enormous joint speeds; the next page.

The Python API solves the inverse kinematics numerically, which is general but can fail on poses a closed-form solver would find, especially around joint 4; re-planning from a slightly different pose or starting posture usually helps. MovePose in RBTscript and move_j(pose=...) in the API solve the kinematics once, at the target, and move in joint space; MoveCart and move_l solve it all along a straight line, which is where the next page matters.

docs.title: Motion profiles
docs.text: A move has a start, an end and a time; the profile is how the speed changes in between. The profile decides how smooth the move is, how much it shakes the arm, and whether the steppers can follow it.

docs.title: Trapezoidal
docs.text:
Accelerate at a constant rate, cruise at the maximum speed, decelerate at the same rate. The speed curve is a trapezoid; the acceleration jumps between +a, 0 and −a, which is felt as a jerk at the three corners. With the commander's t= argument, each third of the move is one phase.

Figure 1: A trapezoidal velocity profile.

docs.title: Polynomial
docs.text:
A quintic (fifth-order) polynomial through the start and end positions with zero speed and zero acceleration at both ends: the speed rises and falls as a smooth bell, the acceleration is continuous, and the move starts and ends from rest without a jolt. Slower in the middle for the same total time, and the arm likes it better.

Figure 2: A quintic polynomial velocity profile.

docs.title: In the commander software
docs.text: MoveJoint, MovePose, MoveCart and MoveCartRelTRF take the bare word trap or poly after the other arguments (func="trap" is ignored). A MoveJoint or MovePose with t= defaults to polynomial, with v= and a= it is trapezoidal, and with neither it runs a conservative trapezoid. A MoveCart or MoveCartRelTRF with t= defaults to trapezoidal, and without t= it always takes 3.6 s (RBTscript).

docs.title: In the Python API
docs.text:
select_profile() sets the profile for all planned moves. The profiles of the version this site describes: TOPPRA, RUCKIG, QUINTIC, TRAPEZOID, LINEAR.

Profile What it is TOPPRA Time-optimal path following: the fastest run along the given path within the joint speed and acceleration limits. The default RUCKIG Jerk-limited point-to-point motion: acceleration ramps instead of jumping. Joint moves only; a Cartesian move under it runs TOPPRA QUINTIC The quintic polynomial above, C² smooth TRAPEZOID Trapezoidal, with parabolic blends at the corners LINEAR Straight interpolation, no smoothing: for tests

The move's speed and accel fractions scale the limits the profile works within; a duration fixes the time instead. Streamed jogs and servo targets use their own jerk-limited profile in the controller, not the selected one.

docs.title: Why the profile matters for a stepper arm
docs.text: A stepper follows a speed command exactly until the torque runs out; a sudden acceleration demand at a corner is where it runs out first. Smooth profiles, lower accelerations and lower currents go together: if a joint loses steps at the start of moves, a quintic or jerk-limited profile at the same speed often fixes it.

docs.title: Pose and orientation
docs.text: A pose is a position and an orientation together: where the tool is and which way it points. Six numbers: x, y, z in millimetres and three angles in degrees, [x, y, z, Rx, Ry, Rz], in the frame you name, the WRF unless you say TRF.

docs.title: Position
docs.text: The tool centre point's coordinates in the frame. For the standard pneumatic gripper the TCP is between the finger tips; for a selected tool in the API it is the tool's registered point, moved by any offset you set.

docs.title: Orientation
docs.text:
Three angles describe how the tool frame is rotated relative to the reference frame. There are many conventions; PAROL6's software uses roll, pitch and yaw as rotations about X, Y and Z, which is what the commander shows as Rx, Ry, Rz and what the API's pose() returns and its motion commands take. The API's set_tcp_transform() takes its angles as intrinsic XYZ rotations, Rx · Ry · Rz; its collision shapes take extrinsic XYZ in radians. When a pose from one program goes into another, check the convention before trusting the numbers.

The same position can be reached with many orientations, and the orientation is what a program usually gets wrong first: a few degrees off puts a finger into the table. The Python API examples on this site use [90, 0, 90], the orientation the tool has after homing: horizontal, pointing forward, away from the base. A tool pointing down at the table has other angles; jog it there and read them.

Figure 1: The same position with two orientations.

docs.title: Reading a pose from the robot
docs.text: Jog to where you want to be and read the pose: the commander's position display, or rbt.pose(). That is how poses are taught. A taught pose contains the tool's transform: taught with one tool, it is wrong for another.

docs.title: Rotating about several axes
docs.text:
A rotation about X followed by one about Y is not the same as Y then X, and three angles at once are hard to predict. Rotate about one axis per command when you can, especially in the tool frame:

MoveCartRelTRF(0, 0, 0, 0, 45, 0)
MoveCartRelTRF(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 45)

docs.title: Reference frames
docs.text: A frame is a coordinate system: an origin and three axes, X, Y and Z, at right angles. A position is three numbers in a frame; the same point has different numbers in different frames. PAROL6's software uses two frames you choose between, and several it keeps to itself.

docs.title: The right-hand rule
docs.text: All frames are right-handed: with the right hand's thumb along X and the index finger along Y, the middle finger points along Z. For rotations, the thumb along the axis, the fingers curl in the positive direction. Every orientation angle in the software follows this rule.

docs.title: WRF, the world reference frame
docs.text: Fixed to the robot's base: the origin on the axis of joint 1 at the base's mounting surface, Z up, X and Y along the base. Everything that does not move with the arm is described in it: the table, the parts, the positions a program teaches. MoveCart in RBTscript and move_l in the API take WRF poses by default.

docs.title: TRF, the tool reference frame
docs.text:
Fixed to the tool: the origin at the tool centre point, Z along the tool's approach direction, X and Y across it. It moves with the arm. A move in the TRF is relative to where the tool is now: "100 mm forward along the tool" is MoveCartRelTRF(0,0,100,0,0,0) or move_l([0,0,100,0,0,0], frame="TRF", rel=True), and it goes in a different world direction every time, depending on the tool's orientation. Approaching a part along the gripper's axis, retreating after a grip, and rotating the tool about its own axis are TRF moves.

Figure 1: The tool frame at the end effector.

docs.title: Jogging in a frame
docs.text: The commander's Cartesian jog and the API's jog_l take the frame: WRF jogs move the tool along the base's axes, TRF jogs along the tool's own. Switch to TRF to go straight in or out of a part whatever its angle.

docs.title: The frames inside
docs.text: The kinematic model keeps a frame at every joint, each defined relative to the previous one by the Denavit-Hartenberg parameters, and a frame at the flange. The tool frame is the flange frame moved by the tool's transform; the Python API's tool definitions and set_tcp_transform() set that transform (Tools and the TCP). The commander's model has the pneumatic gripper's transform built in.

docs.title: Actuators
docs.text: Robots are moved by actuators: servo motors with encoders, stepper motors, brushless motors, pneumatic and hydraulic cylinders. PAROL6 uses stepper motors, which move in discrete steps on command, hold position with their current, and need no sensor to be positioned: the cheapest way to get six precise axes, and the reason the robot has no encoders and no brakes.

docs.title: How a stepper works
docs.text:
A stepper has 50 pole pairs and two windings; energising the windings in sequence pulls the rotor one step, 1.8°, at a time, 200 steps per turn. The driver can set the currents to intermediate values and hold the rotor between full steps: microstepping, 32 positions per step on PAROL6, 6400 per turn. A microstep is a real position only while the torque against it is small; under load the rotor lags up to a full step behind the commanded microstep, which is why the resolution on paper is finer than the accuracy in practice.

A stepper's torque falls as its speed rises, because the windings' inductance limits how fast the current can reverse. Above a certain speed, at a certain load, it stalls: it stops following the steps, buzzes, and the position is lost. The speed and acceleration limits of the software exist to stay below that.

docs.title: Open loop and closed loop
docs.text:
Open loop: the controller commands and assumes the result. Simple, cheap, no sensors, and no way to know when something went wrong. Closed loop: a sensor measures the result and the controller corrects the difference; accurate, robust against load, and more complex. PAROL6's joints are open loop: the step count is the position, and a lost step is an error nobody sees. The safeguards are the margins in the limits, the homing that resets the count, and the user's eyes.

The electric grippers are different: their drivers run the motor in closed loop with an encoder, a brushless motor on the SSG-48's Spectral Micro and a stepper on the MSG's STEPFOC. That is what makes a force-controlled gripper possible (End effectors).

docs.title: Position, velocity and torque control
docs.text: A joint can be controlled in position (go there and hold), velocity (turn at this speed) or torque (push this hard). PAROL6's firmware offers velocity (the jog command) and a velocity-plus-position tracking (the go-to command); the planner on the PC turns position targets into those. Torque control, which collaborative robots use to be safe around people, is not possible with open-loop steppers: the robot cannot feel.

docs.title: Backlash
docs.text: The play between gear teeth, in a belt's mesh and in a coupler: when a joint reverses, the motor turns a little before the output follows. PAROL6's planetary gearboxes have 15 to 20 arc-minutes of it, the belts less. It shows as a small position error that depends on the direction of the last move, and as a slight looseness at the tool. The cure is preload (tight belts), approaching a pose always from the same direction, and keeping the couplers tight (Couplers and threadlocker).

docs.title: Encoders
docs.text: An encoder measures a shaft's rotation: incremental ones count from a start, absolute ones know the angle at power-up. PAROL6 has none on its joints; adding them is a common modification, and the community has closed-loop driver projects. The gripper drivers have an absolute magnetic encoder on their motor.

docs.title: Target, commanded and actual
docs.text:
Three positions exist at every moment, and they differ.

  • The target is where you asked the robot to go: the end of the move.
  • The commanded position is where the planner says the robot should be right now, on the trajectory it computed from the profile, sent to the control board in this cycle.
  • The actual position is where the motors are, as the control board counts their steps: what rbt.angles() and the commander's display show.

docs.title: Why commanded and actual differ
docs.text:
The board receives a speed and a position every 10 ms and runs the stepper at that speed until the next packet. Two things pull the actual position away from the commanded one:

  • The PC is not a real-time machine; the packets are 10 ms apart on average, not exactly, and a late packet lets the motor run a little too long or short.
  • A stepper cannot make the very small speed changes at the start and end of a smooth profile exactly; it rounds them.

If the board followed the speed alone, the errors would add up over a long move and the robot would miss the target by a few steps. So the planners use the go-to-position command (156), in which the board runs each joint at the average of the commanded speed and the speed that would close the position error within one cycle: the speed curve gives the smoothness, the position curve pulls the error back to zero every cycle, and the robot arrives exactly.

Figure 1: Commanded (blue) and actual (red) speed on a trapezoidal move; the robot spends a third of the time in each phase. Figure 2: Position with speed-only tracking and with speed-and-position tracking: the second reaches the target exactly. Figure 3: The same with a polynomial profile.

The commander's RBTscript exposes the choice: a move with speed as its last argument tracks the speed curve only, which is smoother and quieter and may stop short of the target; without it, speed and position are tracked.

docs.title: What the software reports
docs.text: The commander shows the actual joint angles and the actual tool pose; the Python API's status stream carries the actual angles and speeds, plus executing_index and completed_index for where the queue is. "Actual" means "counted steps": a lost step moves the real arm away from all three without any of them noticing (Homing and mastering).

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Robotics mixes units, and PAROL6's software converts between them at several places. The rule is: the interfaces speak degrees and millimetres, the firmware speaks motor steps, and the maths in between is in radians and metres.

Quantity At the interface (commander GUI, RBTscript, Python API) Inside the software At the firmware Joint angle degrees radians motor steps (microsteps) Position millimetres metres — Orientation degrees (three angles) rotation matrices, radians — Joint speed commander: percent of the maximum; API: a fraction of the maximum in (0, 1] rad/s steps per second Tool speed commander: percent; API: a fraction m/s, rad/s — Acceleration percent, or a fraction rad/s², m/s² steps/s² Time seconds seconds 10 ms cycles; the timing counter in 1.422 µs ticks Gripper position commander: 0 to 255; API: a fraction 0 to 1 0 to 255 Gripper current commander: milliamps; API: a fraction of the tool's current range milliamps

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The firmware knows nothing but steps: 200 full steps per motor turn, 32 microsteps each, 6400 per turn, times the joint's gear ratio for a turn of the joint (Drives, ratios and resolution). The PC software converts with the two constants it keeps in its robot model:

degrees per step = 360 / (200 × 32) / ratio          # 0.05625° / ratio
steps = degrees / 0.05625 × ratio

docs.title: Speed fractions
docs.text: The Python API's speed and accel are fractions of the robot model's maxima, in (0, 1], not percentages: a speed=0.5 joint move runs the leading joint at half its maximum speed, and the others proportionally so that all finish together. A duration above zero overrides the speed: the move takes that long, whatever the speed fraction says. The commander's speed slider is a percentage applied to its own, lower, maxima.

docs.title: Angles wrap
docs.text: Joint 3 reports about 105° to 295° and joint 6 0° to 360°, both with the standby at 180°; joints 1, 2, 4 and 5 report signed angles. Orientation angles wrap at ±180°: a pose with Rz = 179° and one with Rz = −181° are the same, and a program that compares angles must take that into account.

docs.title: Reach
docs.text: The furthest the flange centre gets from the axis of joint 1, within the joint limits: 408 mm. The standard pneumatic gripper's tool centre point gets to 434 mm. A longer tool reaches further and weighs on joints 4 and 5.

docs.title: Workspace
docs.text:
Figure 1: Where the flange centre can go in the arm's plane, within the joint limits, in mm.

The shaded region is everywhere the centre of the flange can go in the plane of the arm, within the joint limits of the robot's model; the dotted line is the same for the wrist centre. It reaches 408 mm in front of the joint 1 axis and 359 mm behind it, 523 mm above the mounting surface and 25 mm below it. A tool adds its own length. The region is computed from the limits only: the arm's own parts, the tool and the table can block some of it.

The volume the tool can reach. The reachable workspace is every point it can touch with some orientation: a near-sphere of the reach, minus the base, minus the volume behind the elbow that the limits of joints 2 and 3 exclude. The dexterous workspace is the part of it where the tool can take any orientation, much smaller, around the middle of the reach and in front of the robot. A program that needs a particular orientation at a point needs that point in the dexterous workspace, and the way to find out is to jog there and try.

docs.title: Payload across the workspace
docs.text: 1 kg close to the base, 0.5 kg at full reach: the torque on joints 2 and 3 grows with the distance, and the steppers' torque does not. A heavy tool shrinks the workspace in which the arm moves without losing steps.

docs.title: Placing the task
docs.text: Faster cycles and a larger usable workspace come from the layout, not from the program: put the work in front of the robot at mid reach, at a height that keeps the elbow bent, and away from the joint 1 axis. Move the robot or the fixture rather than fighting the kinematics. The Python API's reachable() reports how much travel each joint and axis has left from the current pose, which tells you how close to a limit the program works.
